🎯 EX267 Exam Strategy

Master the 2-Hour Performance-Based Exam

Hands-on CLI + OpenShift Console tasks. Pass: 68% (210/300). Here's your battle-tested strategy.

First 5 Minutes — Setup Ritual

  • ✅ Set up aliases: alias ogp='oc get pods', alias oaf='oc apply -f', export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"
  • ✅ Verify context: oc whoami, oc project
  • ✅ Check cluster health: oc get nodes, oc get clusteroperators
  • ✅ Set mental checkpoints: 30min → 60min → 90min → 110min → 120min
  • ✅ Write down key numbers: GPU types (A100=80GB, H100=80GB), MIG max=7, NVLink=900GB/s

3-Pass Time Management

1
Pass 1 (0-30 min)

Easy tasks first (project creation, data connections). Flag harder ones.

2
Pass 2 (30-100 min)

Medium tasks (notebooks, pipelines, model serving). Process flagged items.

3
Pass 3 (100-120 min)

Hard tasks (GPU, troubleshooting). Review, verify, never leave blank.

Top 10 Mistakes That Cost Points

  • 1. Not switching project context: Always run oc project <name> first
  • 2. Forgetting to create PVC for notebooks: Data science needs persistent storage — check PVC status
  • 3. Not labeling GPU nodes: oc label node <name> nvidia.com/gpu.present=true
  • 4. Using kubectl when oc is needed: Routes, BuildConfigs, DeploymentConfigs need oc
  • 5. Ignoring SCC for AI workloads: GPU pods need privileged or custom SCC
  • 6. Not verifying model endpoints: Always curl the inference endpoint after deploy
  • 7. Forgetting data connection YAML syntax: Triple-check S3 credentials in secrets
  • 8. Pipeline step timeout too short: AI training can take minutes — set appropriate timeouts
  • 9. Not using oc explain for CRDs: OpenShift AI uses many custom resources
  • 10. Skipping verification: Always run oc get or oc describe after every change

Exam Day Checklist

  • ✅ Quiet room, stable internet, system test completed 24h before
  • ✅ Government-issued ID ready, webcam and microphone working
  • ✅ Bookmarked docs.openshift.com reference pages (pre-loaded in exam browser)
  • ✅ Scratch paper for key numbers and YAML skeletons
  • ✅ Water nearby, no electronics on desk except exam computer
  • ✅ 39 chapters studied + 12 labs completed + 90+ practice questions done!

📝 YAML Skeleton Templates — Copy-Paste Ready

5 Must-Memorize YAML Skeletons for EX267
  # 1. DataScienceCluster (core AI config)
  apiVersion: datasciencecluster.opendatahub.io/v1
  kind: DataScienceCluster
  metadata: { name: default-dsc }
  spec:
    components:
      dashboard: { managementState: Managed }
      workbenches: { managementState: Managed }
      datasciencepipelines: { managementState: Managed }
      kserve: { managementState: Managed, serving: { name: Knative } }
      modelregistry: { managementState: Managed }

  # 2. InferenceService (KServe)
  apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
  kind: InferenceService
  metadata: { name: ${MODEL_NAME} }
  spec:
    predictor:
      model:
        modelFormat: { name: ${FORMAT} }  # pytorch, tensorflow, onnx, sklearn
        storageUri: ${S3_URI}             # s3://bucket/model-path

  # 3. Data Connection Secret
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Secret
  metadata: { name: ${CONN_NAME}, labels: { opendatahub.io/dashboard: 'true' } }
  stringData:
    AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${KEY}
    AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${SECRET}
    AWS_S3_ENDPOINT: ${ENDPOINT}
  type: Opaque

Chapter 1: What is OpenShift? 🟢 Beginner

Chapter 1: What is OpenShift? — The Enterprise Kubernetes Platform

Before diving into OpenShift AI, notebooks, and GPU workloads, let's understand why OpenShift exists, what problems it solves, and how it transforms the way we deploy and manage applications. We'll use our anihpj/jobpost Django app to make every concept concrete and practical.

Architecture & Fundamentals ~35% RHOAI Relationship with OCP

🎯 What You'll Learn in Chapter 1

  • ✅ The problems that existed before OpenShift — manual deploys, SSH nightmares, scaling chaos
  • ✅ What OpenShift actually IS — the clear, simple definition beyond "enterprise Kubernetes"
  • ✅ OpenShift vs vanilla Kubernetes — why Red Hat's platform adds so much value

Understanding OpenShift Fundamentals Matters on EX267

The EX267 exam tests your ability to work within the OpenShift ecosystem. While Chapter 1 isn't directly tested with CLI commands, understanding why OpenShift exists and how its components fit together helps you reason through every task. Key concepts to internalize:

  • OpenShift IS Kubernetes — Every kubectl command works on OpenShift. The oc CLI is kubectl + OpenShift-specific features (Routes, BuildConfigs, DeploymentConfigs).
  • Security by Default — Unlike vanilla K8s, OpenShift runs containers as random UIDs (not root!) and enforces Security Context Constraints (SCCs). This matters for GPU workloads.
  • Operator Framework — OpenShift's secret weapon. Operators automate installation, configuration, and lifecycle management of complex software — including the entire OpenShift AI stack.

1.1 The World Before OpenShift — Why We Need a Platform

Imagine you've built anihpj — a Django app with a jobpost module where employers list jobs filtered by Skills, Location, and Author. Now you want to deploy it to production. Without a platform like OpenShift, here's what your life looks like:

💀 The "Without OpenShift" Nightmare Scenario

You SSH into a server at 3 AM because the Django process crashed. You manually restart it. There's no load balancing — one server handles everything. When traffic spikes (new job postings go viral), the server buckles. To scale, you buy a new server and configure everything from scratch — nginx, Postgres, Django, SSL certs, monitoring. This takes days. Then something else breaks.

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — The "Why" Behind All of This

Before Kubernetes and OpenShift, deploying applications was like building a house by hand — every brick placed manually, every wire run individually. If a wall cracked at 3 AM, YOU had to fix it. If more people wanted to live there, YOU had to build an extension.

OpenShift changes this completely: It's like having a smart building that automatically fixes cracks, adds rooms when needed, routes visitors to the right entrance, and has 24/7 security guards. You just describe what you want the building to do, and the platform handles the rest.

This is the fundamental shift: from imperative ("do this, then this, then this") to declarative ("I want 3 copies of my app running, always healthy, with automatic failover"). You declare the desired state; OpenShift makes it happen and keeps it that way.

The Evolution of Deployment

Computing has evolved through five major eras. Each solved problems of the previous one — but introduced new challenges:

🖥️
1990s
Bare Metal

One app = one server. anihpj would be the ONLY thing running. Wasteful and expensive.

❌ No AI
💻
2000s
Virtual Machines

Multiple VMs per server. anihpj gets its own VM. Heavy overhead — each VM runs a full OS.

⚠️ Heavy
📦
2013+
Docker Containers

Lightweight, portable packaging. anihpj in a container. But who manages 100 containers?

🟡 Close
☸️
2015+
Kubernetes

Container orchestration. Auto-healing, scaling, load balancing. You assemble the pieces.

✅ Platform
🤖
2023+
OpenShift AI

K8s + all batteries included + AI/ML operators. Notebooks, pipelines, GPU scheduling.

✅ AI Ready

1.2 OpenShift Defined — The Simple Answer

Here's the simplest, most accurate definition:

📖 OpenShift Defined

OpenShift is "Enterprise Kubernetes with batteries included." It's a production-ready Kubernetes platform built by Red Hat that comes pre-integrated with everything you need: container registry, CI/CD pipelines, monitoring, logging, service mesh, OAuth authentication, web console, and operator framework. Think of Kubernetes as the engine — OpenShift is the fully assembled car with GPS, air conditioning, and safety features already installed.

🔴
OKD (Upstream)

The open-source community distribution of OpenShift. Like Fedora is to RHEL. Free, community-supported, cutting-edge features. Great for learning and testing.

☸️
OpenShift Container Platform

Red Hat's enterprise product. Fully supported, security-hardened, certified. Includes 24/7 support, security patches, and validated integrations. What you'll use in production.

Quick Facts

Created byRed Hat (2011)
Built onKubernetes + Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS
Written inGo (like Kubernetes)
LicenseApache 2.0 (open source)
Container RuntimeCRI-O (lightweight, Kubernetes-native)
Default CNIOVN-Kubernetes
Latest Version4.16+ (as of 2025)

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "But What IS Kubernetes Really?"

If OpenShift is a fully-equipped kitchen, Kubernetes is the rulebook for how kitchens should work. Kubernetes defines concepts like "a Pod is a group of containers," "a Service routes traffic to Pods," and "a Deployment ensures N copies are always running." OpenShift takes these rules and builds a complete, working kitchen with all appliances, safety systems, and management tools already installed.

Key insight: When you learn OpenShift, you're ALSO learning Kubernetes. Every Kubernetes concept (Pod, Service, Deployment, Namespace, ConfigMap, Secret) exists in OpenShift. OpenShift just adds more — Routes, BuildConfigs, ImageStreams, Operators, SCCs. Think of it as Kubernetes++.

1.3 OpenShift vs Kubernetes — What's Actually Different?

This is the question every newcomer asks. Here's the honest comparison:

Kubernetes is like buying all the raw ingredients to build a kitchen — flour, eggs, appliances — and assembling everything yourself. OpenShift is like walking into a fully equipped professional kitchen where everything is already installed, tested, and ready to cook. You can still customize everything, but you start from a working baseline.

💡 The OpenShift Difference

With vanilla Kubernetes, you'd need to set up: a container registry, a CI/CD tool, an ingress controller, TLS certificates, a monitoring stack, and a logging system — all separately. With OpenShift, all of these are built-in and pre-configured. You focus on your code; the platform handles everything else.

1.6 When NOT to Use OpenShift

OpenShift is powerful, but it's not always the right choice:

⚠️ Scenarios Where OpenShift Might Be Overkill
  • Personal hobby projects — If you're deploying a personal blog, use minikube, k3s, or even Docker Compose. OpenShift's overhead isn't justified.
  • Tiny teams with no K8s experience — OpenShift simplifies Kubernetes, but you still need to understand K8s concepts. Learning curve exists.
  • Serverless-only architectures — If everything runs on AWS Lambda / Cloud Functions, you don't need a full container platform.
  • Tight budget constraints — OpenShift licensing costs real money. Managed cloud K8s (EKS, AKS, GKE) may be cheaper for small deployments.

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — How OpenShift Components Work Together (Step by Step)

Scenario: You deploy anihpj. Here's exactly what happens behind the scenes:

1. You run oc new-app anihpj:latest → CLI sends request to API Server (the front door — ALL requests go through it).

2. API Server authenticates you (OAuth: "Who are you?") and authorizes (RBAC: "Are you allowed?"). If approved, it writes the desired state to etcd (the cluster's database).

3. The Scheduler watches for unassigned Pods. It scores every worker node: "Which has enough CPU/RAM? Which is least loaded?" It picks the best node and updates etcd.

4. The Kubelet on the chosen node sees the assignment. It tells CRI-O: "Pull image anihpj:latest and run it." CRI-O pulls the image, creates the container with a random UID (security!), and starts gunicorn.

5. The Controller Manager constantly reconciles: "Are 3 replicas running? Is one unhealthy? Create a replacement!" This reconciliation loop is Kubernetes' most powerful concept.

6. Kube-Proxy writes iptables rules so traffic to the Service IP gets load-balanced across all healthy Pods. The Route (HAProxy) handles external TLS termination.

🎯 Key Insight: You never told OpenShift "run this on node 5, open port 8080, set up iptables rule X." You declared "I want 3 copies of anihpj, always healthy." The platform figured out the rest. This is declarative infrastructure — the paradigm shift that makes OpenShift so powerful.

1.8 Key OpenShift Concepts — The Terminology You MUST Know

OpenShift introduces several concepts beyond standard Kubernetes. Master these 12 terms — they appear in every EX267 task:

📁
Project

Kubernetes Namespace + security + resource isolation. All your anihpj resources live inside a Project. oc new-project anihpj-dev

🛣️
Route

Kubernetes Ingress + TLS on steroids. Exposes Services externally with automatic certificate management. oc expose svc/anihpj

🏗️
BuildConfig

Defines HOW to build your container image — from Git, Dockerfile, or source code (S2I). Triggers on code push.

🔄
DeploymentConfig

Kubernetes Deployment + triggers + lifecycle hooks + rollback. OpenShift-native deployment management.

🖼️
ImageStream

Virtual view of container images. Tracks tags across registries. Auto-triggers deployments when images update.

📋
Template

Parameterized YAML. Defines an entire application stack with variables. oc new-app --template=...

🤖
Operator

Automated app lifecycle management. Encodes human operator knowledge in software. The heart of OpenShift AI.

🔒
SCC

Security Context Constraint. Pod security policies on steroids. Controls what pods CAN do (run as root? use host network?).

📦
S2I

Source-to-Image. Build container images from source code — NO Dockerfile needed! Python, Node.js, Java builders included.

⚙️
MachineConfig

Node-level OS configuration. Managed by Machine Config Operator. Immutable RHEL CoreOS — declarative config only.

📊
ClusterVersion

Manages the OpenShift version and orchestrates updates. Upgrades the entire cluster — control plane + workers.

⚙️
ConfigMap/Secret

Same as K8s — separate configuration from code. Secrets for passwords/API keys. ConfigMaps for app settings.

1.9 Understanding OpenShift Projects — Your First Sandbox

A Project is OpenShift's version of a Kubernetes Namespace — but with additional security, resource isolation, and management features.

📖 Project = Namespace + Superpowers

A Project automatically includes: network isolation (NetNamespace), RBAC bindings for your team, resource quotas to prevent runaway workloads, and annotations for the OpenShift console. When you create a Project, OpenShift does MUCH more than just create a Namespace.

Terminal — Creating your first Project 
# Create your first project for anihpj development
oc new-project anihpj-dev \
  --description="Development environment for anihpj job board" \
  --display-name="anihpj Development"

# Switch to the project
oc project anihpj-dev

# Check project details
oc status
oc get quota
oc describe project anihpj-dev

OpenShift AI is NOT a separate product — it's a set of Operators and components that run ON TOP of OpenShift Container Platform:

OpenShift AI = OCP Foundation + AI/ML Layer on Top

  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The DataScienceCluster CRD is the single configuration object that controls ALL AI components. One YAML file enables or disables notebooks, pipelines, model serving, and GPU support:

DataScienceCluster CRD 
apiVersion: datasciencecluster.opendatahub.io/v1
kind: DataScienceCluster
metadata:
  name: default-dsc
spec:
  components:
    dashboard:
      managementState: Managed       # Web console AI tab
    workbenches:
      managementState: Managed       # Jupyter notebooks
    datasciencepipelines:
      managementState: Managed       # Elyra + kfp pipelines
    kserve:
      managementState: Managed       # Single-model serving
      serving:
        name: Knative                # Auto-scaling runtime
    modelregistry:
      managementState: Managed       # Model version registry

1.12 Real-World Companies Using OpenShift AI

🏦
Finance — Fraud Detection

Major banks run fraud detection models on OpenShift AI. They need: scalable inference (KServe), auditable model registry, SCC-hardened pods for PCI compliance, and automated retraining pipelines. Key tools: Model Registry, Pipelines, TrustyAI for bias monitoring.

🏥
Healthcare — Medical Imaging AI

Hospitals use GPU-accelerated OpenShift for medical image analysis. They need: GPU node scheduling with taints/tolerations, large PVCs for imaging datasets, HIPAA-compliant network policies, and model explainability. Key tools: GPU Operator, KServe explainers.

🛒
Retail — Recommendation Engines

E-commerce platforms run recommendation models on OpenShift AI. They need: multi-model serving (ModelMesh) for 100+ models, canary deployments for A/B testing, and scale-to-zero for cost savings. Key tools: ModelMesh, Knative KPA.

🏛️
Government — Classified AI Workloads

Government agencies deploy AI on air-gapped OpenShift clusters. They need: offline operator catalogs, FIPS-compliant encryption, strict SCC policies, and comprehensive audit logging. Key tools: SCC, audit logs, disconnected install.

1.13 The Shipping Port Analogy — How OpenShift Orchestrates Everything 🚢

Think of AI computing like a global shipping operation. This analogy helps you understand how every OpenShift component works together:

🚢 The Shipping Port — How OpenShift Orchestrates Everything

OpenShift = The Port Authority that manages EVERYTHING. Kubernetes = The port rulebook. OpenShift adds the staff, security gates, control tower, and automated systems.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Takeaway: OpenShift is Kubernetes redesigned from the ground up to be enterprise-ready. It's like comparing building your own house from raw materials vs. moving into a fully furnished apartment with security, utilities, and maintenance already included. You can still customize everything — but you start from a working, secure baseline.

📝 Chapter 1 Practice Questions — Test Your Understanding

Q1
What is the relationship between OKD and OpenShift Container Platform?
Click to reveal answer & explanation
✅ Answer

OKD is the upstream open-source community distribution (like Fedora to RHEL). OpenShift Container Platform is Red Hat's enterprise product with full support, security hardening, and certified integrations.

📖 Explanation

The same way Fedora is the upstream for RHEL, OKD is where new features are tested first. OCP adds enterprise features: 24/7 support, FIPS compliance, certified operators, and long-term stability guarantees.

Q2
Which container runtime does OpenShift 4.x use by default, and why was Docker replaced?
Click to reveal answer & explanation
✅ Answer

OpenShift uses CRI-O, a lightweight, Kubernetes-native container runtime. Docker was replaced because it required a daemon (dockerd), ran with root privileges, and wasn't purpose-built for Kubernetes.

📖 Explanation

CRI-O implements the Kubernetes Container Runtime Interface (CRI) directly — no extra daemon, no root requirement, smaller attack surface. It's maintained by Red Hat and version-aligned with OpenShift releases.

Q3
What is a Security Context Constraint (SCC) and how does it differ from Kubernetes Pod Security Standards?
Click to reveal answer & explanation
✅ Answer

SCCs are OpenShift's pod security mechanism that control what actions pods can perform — running as root, using host network, accessing host filesystem, etc. They're more granular than K8s Pod Security Standards and are enforced at admission time.

📖 Explanation

Default SCCs include: restricted (denies root, host access), anyuid (allows any UID), privileged (full access). For GPU workloads, you often need privileged SCC because GPU drivers require host device access.

Q4
Your anihpj Django app needs to be accessible at https://jobs.example.com. What OpenShift resource do you use?
Click to reveal answer & explanation
✅ Answer

You use an OpenShift Route with TLS termination. Command: oc create route edge anihpj --service=anihpj --hostname=jobs.example.com

📖 Explanation

A Route is OpenShift's enhanced Ingress. The edge type means the router terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP to the pod. Other types: passthrough (TLS to pod), re-encrypt (router decrypts then re-encrypts).

Q5
Explain the difference between a Kubernetes Namespace and an OpenShift Project.
Click to reveal answer & explanation
✅ Answer

An OpenShift Project is a Kubernetes Namespace PLUS additional OpenShift features: automatic RBAC bindings, network isolation (NetNamespace), resource quotas, and console annotations. oc new-project creates all of these; kubectl create ns only creates the namespace.

📖 Explanation

When you run oc new-project anihpj-dev, OpenShift automatically: creates a Namespace, adds the creating user as admin, sets up network isolation, creates default RBAC roles, and registers the project in the console. A plain Namespace has none of these.

Q6
What is the DataScienceCluster CRD and what components does it control?
Click to reveal answer & explanation
✅ Answer

It's the single YAML configuration that controls ALL OpenShift AI components: Dashboard, Workbenches (notebooks), DataSciencePipelines, KServe (model serving), and ModelRegistry.

📖 Explanation

Each component has a managementState field (Managed or Removed). Setting a component to Managed installs and configures it automatically via the OpenShift AI Operator.

apiVersion: datasciencecluster.opendatahub.io/v1
kind: DataScienceCluster
metadata: { name: default-dsc }
spec:
  components:
    dashboard: { managementState: Managed }
    workbenches: { managementState: Managed }
    datasciencepipelines: { managementState: Managed }
    kserve: { managementState: Managed }
Q7
Which OpenShift product variant would you choose for an air-gapped (disconnected) government deployment?
Click to reveal answer & explanation
✅ Answer

OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) deployed on-premise using User-Provisioned Infrastructure (UPI).

📖 EXPLANATION
# Air-gapped deployment:
openshift-install create install-config  # Set platform: none
# Mirror registry: oc adm release mirror → local registry
# Disconnected operators: CatalogSource → local mirror
# FIPS: fips: true in install-config.yaml
Q8
How does OpenShift handle certificate management for internal services?
Click
✅

Service-ca operator auto-generates TLS certs for annotated services. Auto-rotates at 80% of validity. Pods need restart to pick up new certs.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Annotate service for auto-TLS:
metadata:
  annotations:
    service.beta.openshift.io/serving-cert-secret-name: anihpj-tls
# Auto-created Secret: anihpj-tls with tls.crt + tls.key
Q9
What is the relationship between OperatorHub and OLM?
Click
✅

OperatorHub is the catalog (app store). OLM (Operator Lifecycle Manager) is the installer — handles dependency resolution, upgrades, CRD lifecycle.

📖 EXPLANATION
OperatorHub → browse/search operators
    ↓ (click Install)
OLM → Subscription → InstallPlan → CSV (ClusterServiceVersion) → Operator Pod
# Key objects: Subscription, InstallPlan, CSV, OperatorGroup
Q10
How does OpenShift's GitOps model (ArgoCD) differ from imperative CLI operations?
Click
✅

GitOps: desired state in Git → ArgoCD continuously reconciles cluster to match. CLI: one-time commands. GitOps provides audit trail, rollback, and drift detection.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: { name: anihpj-ml }
spec:
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/ml-platform
    path: openshift/
  destination: { server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, namespace: anihpj-ml }
  syncPolicy: { automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true } }
⚠️ Chapter 1 — Common EX267 Mistakes
  • Confusing Routes with Ingress: They serve the same purpose but Routes are OpenShift-native and have more features (TLS termination types, wildcard support). Always use oc expose svc or oc create route — NOT kubectl ingress commands.
  • Forgetting OpenShift runs as random UID: If your container image expects to run as root, it WILL fail on OpenShift. Always test with oc run test --image=your-image --command -- id to see what UID you get.
  • Mixing up Project and Namespace: kubectl create ns creates a bare namespace without RBAC or network isolation. oc new-project creates the full OpenShift project with all security features.

Chapter 2: Containers, Docker & Podman — The Foundation of OpenShift 🟢 Beginner

Chapter 2: Understanding Containers — The Building Blocks of OpenShift

Containers are the fundamental unit of deployment in OpenShift. Before you can deploy anihpj on OpenShift, you need to understand what containers are, how Docker and Podman differ, and how to build production-ready container images. This chapter gives you the container mastery every OpenShift developer needs.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📦 Containers 🐳 Docker

🎯 What You'll Learn in Chapter 2

  • ✅ What containers really are — the shipping analogy that explains everything
  • ✅ Docker vs Podman vs CRI-O — which one OpenShift actually uses and why
  • ✅ How to build a production-ready Dockerfile for anihpj (multi-stage, non-root)
  • ✅ Container registries — where images live and how OpenShift's internal registry works
  • ✅ Container security — why OpenShift runs containers as random UIDs
  • ✅ Why Docker alone isn't enough — the orchestration gap that OpenShift fills

2.1 What is a Container? (The Shipping Analogy)

The best way to understand containers is through the shipping industry analogy:

Physical Shipping Containers → Software Containers
  🌍 PHYSICAL WORLD                              💻 SOFTWARE WORLD
  ─────────────────────────────────              ──────────────────────────────
  📦 Shipping Container                          📦 Software Container
     • Standard size (20ft/40ft)                    • Standard format (OCI image)
     • Fits on any ship, truck, train               • Runs on any container runtime
     • Contents isolated from other containers      • Process isolated from other containers
     • Stackable, portable, predictable             • Stackable, portable, predictable

  🚢 Container Ship                              ☸️ OpenShift Cluster
     • Carries thousands of containers              • Runs thousands of pods
     • Automated loading/unloading (cranes)         • Automated scheduling (kubelet)
     • Port authority manages everything            • Control plane manages everything

Container Image = The blueprint (like a shipping container specification). Container = The running instance (like an actual loaded container on a ship).

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — Containers vs Virtual Machines

This is the most important distinction for newcomers:

Virtual Machine: Each VM has its own full operating system (kernel + user space). A server running 10 VMs runs 10 copies of Linux. Heavy, slow to start (minutes), gigabytes of RAM overhead.

Container: All containers on a host share the SAME Linux kernel. Each container only has the application and its dependencies. A server running 100 containers runs ONE kernel. Light, starts in milliseconds, megabytes of overhead.

This is why OpenShift can run hundreds of pods on a single node — they're containers, not VMs. The isolation comes from Linux kernel features (namespaces and cgroups), not from running separate operating systems.

2.2 Docker vs Podman vs CRI-O — Which Does OpenShift Use?

FeatureDockerPodmanCRI-O (OpenShift)
ArchitectureDaemon-based (dockerd)DaemonlessDaemonless, K8s-native
Root Required?Yes (by default)No (rootless)No (runs as rootless)
Image Builddocker buildpodman build / buildahBuildah + S2I
K8s Integrationdockershim (removed in 1.24)Via CRI-O or containerdNative CRI implementation
OpenShift Default❌ Not used✅ For building✅ Runtime since OCP 4.x
Best ForLegacy, developmentDevelopment, buildingProduction Kubernetes
📖 Key Fact

OpenShift uses CRI-O as its container runtime — NOT Docker. CRI-O is purpose-built for Kubernetes, lighter weight, and more secure. For building images, OpenShift supports Dockerfiles, Podman, Buildah, and S2I (Source-to-Image).

2.3 Building Containers for OpenShift — The anihpj Dockerfile

Here's a production-ready multi-stage Dockerfile for deploying anihpj on OpenShift:

Dockerfile — anihpj/jobpost Production Build 
# ===== STAGE 1: BUILD =====
FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/python-311 AS builder
USER 0
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# ===== STAGE 2: RUNTIME =====
FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/python-311
USER 1001  # OpenShift runs as random UID — match with numeric user
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app /app
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8080", "--workers", "4"]
💡 OpenShift Dockerfile Best Practices
  • Use UBI (Universal Base Image) — Red Hat's official images are optimized for OpenShift
  • Don't use root — OpenShift runs containers as random UIDs. Your app must work without root
  • Use numeric USER — USER 1001 works better than USER appuser on OpenShift
  • Multi-stage builds — Keep runtime images small by separating build from runtime
  • EXPOSE the right port — OpenShift Services forward to the port you EXPOSE (typically 8080)

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — Dockerfile Line-by-Line

FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/python-311 AS builder — Start from Red Hat's official Python image. "AS builder" names this stage so we can copy from it later.

USER 0 — Temporarily switch to root (UID 0) for the build stage. We need root to install packages. This is OK because it's ONLY the build stage — the runtime stage drops root.

COPY requirements.txt . — Copy ONLY the requirements file first. Why? Docker caches layers. If requirements.txt hasn't changed, the pip install layer is cached — builds are 10x faster.

FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/python-311 — Second FROM starts a NEW, clean stage. The build tools (gcc, headers) from stage 1 are gone — keeping the final image small and secure.

USER 1001 — Switch to a non-root user. OpenShift will override this with a random UID, but setting a non-zero value is good practice and signals intent.

COPY --from=builder — Copy ONLY the needed artifacts from the build stage. The final image doesn't contain compilers, dev headers, or source code — just the running app.

2.4 Container Registries — Where Images Live

OpenShift includes an internal container registry — no need for Docker Hub or external registries:

🏗️BuildS2I / Docker / BuildConfig
→

→

2.5 Running Containers on OpenShift — Beyond docker run

With OpenShift, you don't use docker run. You use oc new-app — a single command that creates the Deployment, Service, and ImageStream:

Terminal
# Deploy anihpj from a Docker image (5 commands → 1)
oc new-app registry.example.com/anihpj:latest --name=anihpj

# Or deploy directly from Git source (S2I auto-detects Python/Django)
oc new-app https://github.com/anihs/anihpj.git --name=anihpj

# Expose the app via a Route
oc expose svc/anihpj

# Check everything
oc status

2.6 OpenShift Build Strategies — S2I, Docker, Custom

📦
Source-to-Image (S2I)

Build images from source code — NO Dockerfile needed! Python, Node.js, Java builders included. Best for: standard frameworks like Django. Recommended for anihpj.

🐳
Docker Build

Use your existing Dockerfile. Full control over the build process. Best for: custom dependencies, ML libraries, complex setups.

2.7 Container Security Basics — Running as Non-Root

⚠️ Why Root Containers Are Dangerous

A container running as root can: escape the container in certain scenarios, access host filesystems, modify kernel parameters, and install malicious software. OpenShift prevents this by default — every container runs as a random UID from a high range (typically 1000650000+).

💡 Making Your Image OpenShift-Compatible
  • Don't use USER root — use USER 1001 or any non-zero UID
  • Make sure files are world-readable (OpenShift's random UID needs access)
  • Don't write to root-owned directories (use /tmp or a mounted volume)
  • Test with: oc run test --image=your-image --command -- id

2.8 Multi-Stage Docker Builds for anihpj — Step by Step

Multi-stage builds dramatically reduce image size — from 1.2GB down to ~350MB for a typical Django app:

Collect static

→

needed

ChallengeDocker AloneOpenShift Solution

Rolling updateManual scriptoc rollout + automated

📝 Chapter 2 Practice Questions

Q1
Why does OpenShift use CRI-O instead of Docker?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

CRI-O is daemonless, K8s-native, and more secure. Docker's daemon was unnecessary overhead for Kubernetes.

📖 Explanation

CRI-O directly implements the Kubernetes Container Runtime Interface — no extra daemon, no root requirement, smaller attack surface.

Q2
You build a Dockerfile with USER root. Will it run on OpenShift?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

Likely FAIL — OpenShift runs containers with random UIDs by default via the restricted SCC.

📖 Explanation

Fix: Use USER 1001, ensure files are world-readable. Never run as root in production containers.

Q3
What's the difference between a container IMAGE and a running CONTAINER?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

Image = blueprint (read-only template). Container = running instance (writable layer on top of the image). Like a class vs an object in OOP.

📖 EXPLANATION
Image (OCI): Layers read-only    Container: Image + writable layer
podman images                     podman ps
Build once → deploy many          Run instance → ephemeral changes
# Image = class, Container = object (OOP analogy)
Q4
Why does OpenShift use UBI (Universal Base Image) instead of Alpine Linux?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

UBI is Red Hat-supported, security-patched, and certified for OpenShift.

📖 EXPLANATION
UBI (RHEL-based):               Alpine (musl-based):
FROM ubi9/python-311             FROM python:3.11-alpine
✅ Red Hat supported              ❌ No Red Hat support
glibc → numpy/scipy/PyTorch ✅    musl libc → ML libs may fail
Security patches included         Community patches
Q5
What are the 3 key Dockerfile instructions for OpenShift compatibility?
Click
✅

1. Don't use USER root 2. Make files world-readable (chmod -R g+rwX) 3. Use UBI base images for Red Hat support.

📖 EXPLANATION
FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/python-311
USER 1001                    # Random UID (not root)
RUN chmod -R g+rwX /app      # Group read/write
COPY --chown=1001:0 . /app   # Owned by UID 1001, group 0
# OpenShift assigns random UID → must work with any UID
Q6
What is an image registry and how does OpenShift use it?
Click
✅

Image registry stores container images. OpenShift has a built-in registry + can pull from any external registry (Docker Hub, Quay.io, ECR).

📖 EXPLANATION
oc get route -n openshift-image-registry  # Built-in registry URL
podman build -t image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/anihpj/jobpost:v1 .
podman push image-registry.../anihpj/jobpost:v1
# OpenShift auto-pulls from this registry when deploying pods
Q7
What are image stream tags and why are they useful?
Click
✅

ImageStreams track image tags over time. They provide a stable reference even when the underlying image digest changes.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc import-image anihpj/jobpost:v1 --from=quay.io/anihpj/jobpost:v1 --confirm
# ImageStream tag anihpj/jobpost:v1 → always points to the latest v1 image
# DeploymentConfig triggers on tag update → auto-rollout new pods
Q8
How do you layer a Dockerfile efficiently for Python ML projects?
Click
✅

Order by change frequency: base image → system deps → Python deps (requirements.txt) → application code. Cache earlier layers.

📖 EXPLANATION
FROM ubi9/python-311        # Rarely changes → cached
RUN dnf install -y gcc      # System deps → cached
COPY requirements.txt .     # Only changes when deps change
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  # Cached if requirements.txt unchanged
COPY . /app                  # Application code → changes frequently
# Result: code change = only last 2 layers rebuild
Q9
What's the difference between podman build and S2I builds?
Click
✅

podman build: Uses Dockerfile. S2I (Source-to-Image): Uses builder images — no Dockerfile needed. S2I auto-detects language, installs deps, creates runnable image.

📖 EXPLANATION
# podman build (Dockerfile):
podman build -t anihpj-jobpost:v1 .
# S2I (no Dockerfile needed):
oc new-build python:3.11~https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost.git --name=anihpj-jobpost
# S2I auto: detects Python → pip install -r requirements.txt → creates image
Q10
How do you push/pull images to OpenShift's internal registry?
Click
✅

podman login with oc token → podman push to internal registry → oc new-app --docker-image to deploy.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc whoami -t | podman login -u $(oc whoami) --password-stdin \
  image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000
podman tag anihpj-jobpost:v1 image-registry.../anihpj/jobpost:v1
podman push image-registry.../anihpj/jobpost:v1
oc new-app --docker-image=image-registry.../anihpj/jobpost:v1 --name=jobpost

Chapter 3: OpenShift CLI (oc) — Your Primary Tool 🟢 Beginner

Chapter 3: Mastering oc — The OpenShift Command Line

The oc CLI is your primary interface to OpenShift. It wraps kubectl completely but adds OpenShift-specific superpowers. This chapter covers everything from basic commands to the oc Command Universe Map — your quick reference for EX267.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours ⌨️ CLI 🎯 EX267 Essential

3.1 oc vs kubectl — What's the Difference?

📖 Simple Rule

Every kubectl command works with oc. You can literally alias oc to kubectl. But oc adds OpenShift-specific features: new-app, new-build, new-project, start-build, rollback, idle, rsh, debug, and more.

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "When Do I Use oc vs kubectl?"

During the EX267 exam, always use oc. OpenShift-specific resources (Routes, BuildConfigs, DeploymentConfigs, ImageStreams, Projects) cannot be managed with kubectl. oc handles both standard K8s resources AND OpenShift resources. One tool to rule them all.

Mental model: kubectl get pods = oc get pods (they're the same command under the hood). But oc get routes has no kubectl equivalent — Routes are an OpenShift-only resource.

Operationkubectloc (OpenShift)
Create namespacekubectl create nsoc new-project (adds security, quotas)
Deploy from imagekubectl create deployoc new-app (auto-detects everything)
Expose servicekubectl exposeoc expose svc + auto-creates Route
Build image❌ No equivalentoc new-build / oc start-build
Rollback deploykubectl rollout undooc rollback (full deployment history)
Debug podkubectl execoc debug (creates debug pod copy)
SSH-like access❌ No equivalentoc rsh (remote shell into pod)

3.2 Installing and Configuring oc

Terminal — oc Setup
# Download from OpenShift Console (Help → Command Line Tools)
# Or from: https://mirror.openshift.com/pub/openshift-v4/clients/ocp/

# Login to your cluster
oc login https://api.cluster.example.com:6443 -u developer -p password

# Verify
oc whoami                    # Shows current user
oc whoami --show-token       # Shows session token
oc version                   # Client + Server version

# Manage multiple clusters
oc config get-contexts       # List all contexts
oc config use-context dev    # Switch to dev cluster

3.3 The oc new-app Command — The Swiss Army Knife

oc new-app is OpenShift's most powerful command. It auto-detects what you're trying to do and creates ALL necessary resources:

Terminal — 10 Variations of oc new-app
# 1. From a Docker image
oc new-app registry.example.com/anihpj:latest

# 2. From a Git repository (auto-detects Python/Django)
oc new-app https://github.com/anihs/anihpj.git

# 3. From a Dockerfile in Git
oc new-app https://github.com/anihs/anihpj.git --strategy=docker

# 4. From an OpenShift Template
oc new-app --template=python-django -p NAME=anihpj

# 5. With environment variables
oc new-app python:3.11~https://github.com/anihs/anihpj.git \
  -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://... -e DEBUG=False

# 6. Deploy database + app together
oc new-app postgresql-persistent -p DATABASE_SERVICE_NAME=anihpj-db
oc new-app python:3.11~https://github.com/anihs/anihpj.git \
  -e DATABASE_SERVICE_NAME=anihpj-db

3.4 Project Management with oc

Project Lifecycle Commands
oc new-project anihpj-dev --display-name="anihpj Dev"
oc project anihpj-dev                        # Switch to project
oc project                                    # Show current project
oc get projects                               # List all projects
oc status                                     # Dashboard in terminal!
oc describe project anihpj-dev                # Full project details
oc delete project anihpj-dev                  # Delete everything

3.5 Debugging with oc

Essential Debugging Commands
oc logs anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k9m              # Pod logs
oc logs -f anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k9m            # Stream logs (follow)
oc logs --previous anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k9m    # Previous crashed instance
oc rsh anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k9m                # Remote shell into pod
oc exec anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k9m -- ls /app    # Run command in pod
oc debug pod/anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k9m          # Debug copy of pod
oc get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'     # Cluster diary
oc adm top pods                              # Resource usage at a glance

3.6 oc explain — Your In-Exam Documentation

🎓 EX267 GOLD: oc explain is Your Most Powerful Tool

During the exam, you can access OpenShift documentation, but oc explain is faster! It shows the exact YAML structure for any resource:

oc explain route.spec              # Route specification
oc explain deploymentconfig.spec   # DeploymentConfig fields
oc explain buildconfig.spec.strategy  # Build strategies
oc explain dsc.spec.components     # DataScienceCluster components

3.7b Systematic Debugging Checklist for EX267

When something breaks during the exam, follow this checklist IN ORDER:

🔍 The 5-Minute Debug Protocol
  1. Check context: oc whoami, oc project — are you in the right project?
  2. Check pod status: oc get pods -o wide — Running? Pending? CrashLoopBackOff?
  3. Check events: oc get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -20 — cluster diary
  4. Check logs: oc logs <pod> --tail=50 (add --previous if it crashed)
  5. Describe the pod: oc describe pod <pod> — OOM kills, image errors, SCC denials
  6. Check resources: oc adm top pods, oc describe quota — hitting limits?
  7. Debug interactively: oc debug pod/<pod> — creates a debug copy you can explore
🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 3

Must-know commands: oc new-app, oc new-project, oc logs, oc describe, oc debug, oc rsh, oc explain. Speed tip: --dry-run=client -o yaml saves time — generate YAML first, review, then apply. Gotcha: oc new-app creates DeploymentConfig (not Deployment). Use oc get dc not oc get deploy.

📝 Chapter 3 Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between oc new-app and kubectl create deployment?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

oc new-app auto-detects the source type, creates DeploymentConfig + Service + ImageStream in one command. kubectl create deployment only creates a Deployment.

📖 Explanation

EXAM TIP: oc new-app is always the right answer for deploying apps on OpenShift during EX267. It handles routing, builds, image tracking automatically.

Q2
Your pod keeps crashing. What are the first 3 oc commands you run?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

1. oc get pods (check status), 2. oc logs <pod> --previous (see crash logs), 3. oc describe pod <pod> (check events for OOM, image pull errors)

📖 EXPLANATION
oc get pods -o wide                   # Status + node
oc logs pod/crash-pod --previous      # Crash logs
oc describe pod crash-pod | grep -A10 Events  # Root cause
Q3
How do you generate a YAML template without actually creating the resource?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

Use --dry-run=client -o yaml. Example: oc new-app nginx:latest --dry-run=client -o yaml > app.yaml. This is an EX267 essential pattern — generate first, review, then apply.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc create deploy app --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml
oc new-app python~repo.git --dry-run=client -o yaml > app.yaml
# -o yaml outputs YAML; --dry-run validates but doesn't create
Q4
What's the difference between oc rsh and oc exec?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

oc rsh opens an interactive shell (like SSH). oc exec runs a single command.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc rsh pod/anihpj                    # Interactive shell (like SSH)
oc exec pod/anihpj -- ls /app        # Single command, output to stdout
oc rsh pod/anihpj = oc exec pod/anihpj -- /bin/sh  # Equivalent
Q5
How do you switch between projects with oc?
Click
✅

oc project <name>. List all: oc projects. Current: oc project.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc projects                         # List accessible projects
oc project anihpj-prod              # Switch to anihpj-prod
oc project                          # Show current project
# All subsequent oc commands operate in the current project
Q6
How do you view resource usage (CPU/Memory) of pods?
Click
✅

oc adm top pods for pods, oc adm top nodes for nodes. Requires metrics-server.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc adm top pods -n anihpj-prod
# NAME                         CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
# anihpj-jobpost-7d4f8b9c-abc  45m          256Mi
# anihpj-db-5c6d7e8f-def       120m         512Mi
oc adm top nodes  # Node-level: CPU%, MEM% across all pods
Q7
How do you label and select resources with oc?
Click
✅

oc label adds labels. oc get pods -l filters by label. Labels are key=value pairs for grouping.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc label pod anihpj-jobpost-xxx app=jobpost env=prod
oc get pods -l app=jobpost          # Select by label
oc get pods -l 'env in (prod,staging)'  # Multiple values
oc describe pod anihpj-jobpost-xxx | grep Labels  # View labels
Q8
What does oc explain do and when should you use it?
Click
✅

Shows CRD field documentation. CRITICAL for EX267 — you can look up YAML spec fields during the exam. oc explain pod.spec.containers.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc explain deployment.spec          # Top-level Deployment fields
oc explain deployment.spec.template.spec.containers.resources  # Nested
oc explain inferenceservice.spec --api-version=serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
# EXAM TIP: Use oc explain whenever you're unsure about YAML field names
Q9
How do you tail logs from multiple pods matching a label?
Click
✅

oc logs -l app=jobpost --tail=20 --follow. Streams logs from ALL pods matching the label selector.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc logs -l app=jobpost --tail=50 -f  # Stream last 50 lines from all matching pods
oc logs -l app=jobpost --since=5m    # Last 5 minutes
oc logs -l app=jobpost --timestamps  # Include timestamps
oc logs deployment/jobpost --previous  # Previous crashed container logs
Q10
How do you debug a running pod interactively?
Click
✅

oc debug pod/<name> creates a debug pod with troubleshooting tools. Use oc rsh to enter an existing running pod.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc debug pod/anihpj-jobpost-xxx      # Creates debug pod (root access, tools)
oc debug node/worker-1               # Debug node (privileged container on host)
oc rsh pod/anihpj-jobpost-xxx        # Enter running pod (as-is, no extra tools)
oc rsh -c sidecar pod/anihpj-xxx     # Enter specific container in multi-container pod

Chapter 4: OpenShift Web Console — The Visual Control Center 🟢 Beginner

Chapter 4: Navigating the OpenShift Web Console

The OpenShift web console is one of its biggest advantages over vanilla Kubernetes. It provides TWO perspectives — Administrator (cluster management) and Developer (application management) — plus a dedicated AI/ML tab for OpenShift AI. The EX267 exam tests your ability to use BOTH the CLI and the console.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1 hour 🖥️ Console 🎯 EX267 Essential

4.1 Two Views: Administrator vs Developer

🔧
Administrator Perspective

Cluster health, nodes, operators, storage classes, networking, user management, cluster settings. You see: everything in the cluster. Use for: installation, operator management, SCC, resource quotas.

👨‍💻
Developer Perspective

Topology view, Add page, project-scoped resources, monitoring dashboard, pipelines. You see: only your project. Use for: deploying apps, adding services, monitoring workloads.

4.3 Monitoring Dashboard in Console

OpenShift includes built-in Grafana dashboards accessible directly from the console. Per-project dashboards show: CPU usage, memory consumption, network I/O, and pod health — all without installing anything extra.

💡 Monitoring Quick Access

From Developer perspective → Observe tab → Dashboard. You'll see pre-built dashboards for: Kubernetes/Compute Resources (Namespace/Pods), Kubernetes/Networking, and more. For GPU monitoring, the NVIDIA DCGM dashboard appears once the GPU Operator is installed.

4.4 Observability — Logs, Metrics, and Traces

OpenShift ships with a complete observability stack — no external tools needed. This is one of the biggest advantages over vanilla Kubernetes, where you'd have to install and configure Prometheus, Grafana, and logging separately.

🔍 For EX267 — Quick Observability Commands

Metrics: oc adm top pods, oc adm top nodes — instant resource usage. Console → Observe → Metrics for Grafana.

Logs: oc logs deploy/anihpj --tail=50 — last 50 lines. oc logs --previous if pod crashed.

Events: oc get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' — the cluster diary showing everything that happened.

4.5 The Developer Perspective — Your Daily Dashboard

The Developer perspective is where data scientists and developers spend most of their time. It's project-scoped — you only see what's in your current project. Here's a complete tour:

➕
+Add Page

Quick-launch anything: containers from images, databases (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB), Templates, Helm charts, Operator-backed services. The one-stop shop for deploying new things into your project.

🗺️
Topology

Visual graph of every workload in your project. See pods, services, routes, and builds as connected nodes. Health status (green/yellow/red rings). Click any node to see logs, metrics, and details.

🔍
Search

Find ANY resource in your project: pods, configmaps, secrets, PVCs, routes. Type a name, filter by resource type. Much faster than memorizing oc get commands.

📊
Observe

Per-project monitoring: dashboards (CPU, memory, network), metrics explorer, events timeline. See exactly how your anihpj pods are performing without any setup.

📦
Helm

Manage Helm releases from the GUI. Install charts, view release history, rollback with one click. Great for installing complex apps like MLflow or Kubeflow.

🔄
Pipelines

Visualize Tekton pipelines: see each task, its status, logs, and execution time. Debug pipeline failures by clicking on the failed task. For anihpj: see training pipeline stages.

💡 Developer Perspective Quick Tip

From the Topology view, right-click any pod to: view logs, open terminal, edit resource YAML, scale replicas, or delete. This is the fastest way to debug issues during development. No CLI needed for basic operations.

4.6 The Administrator Perspective — Cluster Management

The Administrator perspective gives you cluster-wide visibility — you see ALL projects, ALL nodes, ALL operators. This is where platform engineers and cluster admins manage the entire OpenShift environment.

⚙️
Cluster Settings

View cluster version, update channel, update history. See ALL ClusterOperators and their health. Configure: Console customization, OAuth identity providers, Ingress settings, image registry configuration, and alert receivers.

🖥️
Compute

Manage: Nodes (view health, cordon/drain, edit labels), Machines (VM instances), MachineSets (auto-scaling groups), MachineAutoscalers, and ClusterAutoscaler configuration. For AI: add GPU nodes via MachineSets.

🌐
Networking

Manage: Services (ClusterIP/NodePort/LB), Routes (HTTP/HTTPS/TLS), Ingress Controllers, NetworkPolicies, and Cluster Network configuration. See DNS records, ingress sharding, and router pod placement.

💾
Storage

Manage: PersistentVolumes (cluster-wide), PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, VolumeSnapshots, and VolumeSnapshotClasses. Configure CSI drivers. For AI: check if RWX storage is available for shared datasets.

📦
Operators

Browse OperatorHub (hundreds of operators), manage installed operators, view ClusterServiceVersions (CSVs), check operator health. This is where you install OpenShift AI, GPU Operator, Pipelines, and Serverless.

👥
User Management

Manage: Users, Groups, ServiceAccounts, Roles, RoleBindings, and ClusterRoles. Configure identity providers (LDAP, OIDC, GitHub). Set up project templates with default quotas and network policies.

🔐 Admin Quick Access

From the Administrator perspective, go to Home → Overview for cluster health at a glance: ClusterOperators status, cluster version, and recent alerts. For the EX267 exam, the Administrator perspective is where you install operators (OperatorHub) and configure cluster-wide settings (OAuth, SCC, networking).

4.7 OpenShift AI Console — The AI/ML Tab

When OpenShift AI is installed, a new section appears in the console with dedicated pages for:

📊
Data Science Projects

Create and manage AI/ML projects with data connections, workbenches, and resource quotas.

📓
Notebooks (Workbenches)

Launch Jupyter notebooks with CPU/GPU, custom images, and persistent storage.

🔄
Pipelines

View and manage Elyra/Kubeflow pipeline runs, artifacts, and execution graphs.

🚀
Model Serving

Deploy and monitor KServe/ModelMesh inference endpoints from the UI.

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 4

Console tasks: Some EX267 tasks are FASTER via console (e.g., creating Data Connections, launching notebooks). Speed tip: Use oc get routes -n openshift-console to get console URL if not provided. Gotcha: ClusterOperators page = fastest cluster health check. Any Degraded operator must be fixed first.

📝 Chapter 4 Practice Questions

Q1
Which perspective shows cluster operator health?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

Administrator perspective → Cluster Settings → ClusterOperators.

📖 EXPLANATION

ClusterOperators are the heartbeat of OpenShift — 20+ operators manage everything from authentication to networking. Each shows: Available (is it working?), Progressing (is it updating?), Degraded (is something wrong?). On EX267, if asked to "verify cluster health," always check oc get clusteroperator or Administrator → Cluster Settings → ClusterOperators. A Degraded operator = cluster issue that must be resolved before proceeding.

Q2
Where do AI/ML features appear after installing OpenShift AI?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

A new AI/ML section in the left nav: Data Science Projects, Notebooks, Pipelines, Model Serving.

📖 EXPLANATION

The OpenShift AI Operator adds these menu items by creating CRDs (Custom Resource Definitions). The navigation is dynamic — if KServe is Removed in DSC, "Model Serving" won't appear. For EX267: after installing the AI Operator, verify the menu appears by refreshing the console. If missing → check oc get dsc -o yaml | grep managementState — all components should be Managed.

Q3
How do you access an application's logs from the Developer perspective?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

Navigate to Topology → click the pod → Resources tab → View logs. Or use the Observe tab → Logs.

📖 EXPLANATION

The Developer perspective is designed for app developers and data scientists — it abstracts away infrastructure details. Topology view shows your app as a visual graph. Clicking a pod reveals: Details (status, labels), Resources (PVCs, Services), Logs (live + historical), Terminal (interactive shell). For EX267: if asked to "debug an application," you can use either the web console (Developer → Topology → Logs) or CLI (oc logs deploy/anihpj --tail=50). Both are valid — choose the faster path.

Q4
You need to monitor GPU utilization. Where in the console do you find GPU metrics?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

Observe → Dashboards → NVIDIA DCGM dashboard (appears after installing NVIDIA GPU Operator). Shows GPU utilization, memory, temperature, and power.

📖 EXPLANATION

The DCGM dashboard is auto-deployed by the GPU Operator's dcgmExporter component. It queries Prometheus for DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL, DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED, DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP, and other metrics. If the dashboard doesn't appear: 1) Verify GPU Operator pods are running: oc get pods -n nvidia-gpu-operator. 2) Check Prometheus is scraping DCGM: oc get servicemonitor -n nvidia-gpu-operator. 3) User-workload monitoring must be enabled. On EX267: this dashboard is key for GPU monitoring tasks.

Chapter 5: Installing OpenShift — Your First Cluster

The EX267 exam tests your ability to manage OpenShift AI installation and configuration (35% of the exam). Install AI Operator DataScienceCluster

5.1 Installation Options Overview

OpenShift offers 5 installation methods — from a single-node laptop environment to fully managed cloud services. Choose based on your scale, control needs, and budget.

📊 Installation Decision Tree — Which Method for Which Scenario?
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│           🚀 WHICH OPENSHIFT INSTALLATION DO I NEED?             │
│                                                                  │
│  Q1: Do you need a full production cluster?                     │
│  ├── NO → Are you just learning/dev/testing?                    │
│  │        └── YES → ✅ CRC (OpenShift Local) — laptop, single-node     │
│  │                                                                  │
│  └── YES → Q2: Do you want OpenShift to provision infra?        │
│            ├── YES → ✅ IPI — provisions VMs, networking, LB, DNS     │
│            │         (AWS, Azure, GCP, vSphere, bare metal)     │
│            │                                                    │
│            └── NO → Q3: Do you need full control over infra?    │
│                     ├── YES → ✅ UPI — you create VMs, networking, DNS    │
│                     │         OpenShift installs itself on top   │
│                     │                                           │
│                     └── NO → Q4: Do you want a managed service?  │
│                              ├── YES → ✅ ROSA/ARO/OSD — Red Hat manages it  │
│                              │         ROSA (AWS), ARO (Azure), OSD (GCP)│
│                              └── NO → Re-evaluate. You probably want IPI│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
MethodWhereWho ManagesBest ForNodesEX267?
OpenShift Local (CRC)Your laptopYouLearning & testing1✅ Practice

UPI (User-Provisioned)Any infrastructureYou provision infraCustom / restricted env3+—

Developer SandboxRed Hat cloudRed Hat (free)Quick experimentationShared✅ Free trial

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — What Does "Provisioned Infrastructure" Even Mean?

Installer-Provisioned (IPI): You give OpenShift cloud credentials, it creates EVERYTHING — VMs, load balancers, DNS records, storage, security groups. You just wait 35-45 minutes. This is the "easy button."

User-Provisioned (UPI): You create the VMs, configure DNS, set up load balancers yourself. Then you run openshift-install and it installs OpenShift on your pre-built infrastructure. More work, but you control every detail — required for air-gapped (disconnected) environments and custom networking.

5.2 OpenShift Local (CRC) — Your Practice Environment

CRC (CodeReady Containers, now called OpenShift Local) is your personal OpenShift cluster on a laptop. It's NOT for production — it's for learning, development, and testing. EX267 note: Many candidates use CRC for hands-on practice because it's free and runs anywhere.

🖥️ CRC System Requirements (Non-Negotiable!)

💾 RAM16 GB minimum — the cluster itself uses ~10GB. With less, CRC won't start.
🖥️ CPU4 vCPUs — more cores = faster builds and pod scheduling
💿 Disk35 GB free — SSD required for etcd performance (etcd is very sensitive to disk latency)
🐧 OSLinux (RHEL/Fedora/Ubuntu), macOS 12+, Windows 10/11 Pro+
🌐 NetworkInternet for initial pull secret download (one-time). Offline mode available.

What CRC gives you: A fully functional OpenShift cluster inside a single VM, including: API server, OAuth, Router (Ingress), internal image registry, Operator Lifecycle Manager, monitoring stack (Prometheus), and the OpenShift Console web UI.

What CRC does NOT give you: High availability (single node), production-grade storage, automatic upgrades, or multi-node networking. It's strictly for development and learning.

CRC Installation — Complete Walkthrough
# STEP 1: Download from https://console.redhat.com/openshift/create/local
# (Requires free Red Hat account)

# STEP 2: Set up hypervisor and networking
crc setup
# This configures: Hyper-V (Windows), HyperKit (macOS), or libvirt (Linux)

# STEP 3: Start your cluster (first time downloads ~5GB VM image)
crc start
# ⏱️ First run: ~5-10 minutes (downloads + boots)
# ⏱️ Subsequent runs: ~1-2 minutes

# STEP 4: Get login credentials
crc console --credentials
# Username: developer (non-admin) / kubeadmin (cluster-admin)
# Password: displayed in terminal output

# STEP 5: Login via CLI
crc oc-env | Invoke-Expression   # PowerShell (adds oc to PATH)
eval $(crc oc-env)               # Linux/macOS
oc login -u kubeadmin https://api.crc.testing:6443

# STEP 6: Open web console
crc console
# Opens https://console-openshift-console.apps-crc.testing in browser

# USEFUL CRC COMMANDS:
crc status          # Check if cluster is running
crc stop            # Stop cluster (saves state — can resume later)
crc start           # Resume stopped cluster
crc delete          # 💣 Wipe everything, start fresh
crc ip              # Get cluster IP (usually 192.168.130.11)
crc cleanup         # Remove CRC completely from your machine

5.3 The openshift-install Binary & Bootstrap Process

Production OpenShift clusters are created using the openshift-install binary. The key configuration file is install-config.yaml which defines networking, platform, and cluster details. This single YAML file is everything the installer needs.

install-config.yaml — The Single Configuration File
apiVersion: v1
baseDomain: example.com              # Your DNS domain
metadata:
  name: anihpj-cluster               # Cluster name
platform:
  aws:                               # Cloud provider (aws/azure/gcp/vsphere/none)
    region: us-east-1
pullSecret: '{"auths":{...}}'        # From cloud.redhat.com
sshKey: 'ssh-rsa AAAAB3Nza...'      # SSH key for node access

networking:
  clusterNetwork:
  - cidr: 10.128.0.0/14             # Pod network (CANNOT change later!)
    hostPrefix: 23                   # /23 = 512 pods per node
  serviceNetwork:
  - 172.30.0.0/16                    # Service IP range (CANNOT change!)
  networkType: OVNKubernetes         # Default CNI

compute:
- name: worker
  replicas: 3                        # 3 worker nodes
  platform:
    aws:
      type: m5.xlarge               # 4 vCPU, 16 GB

controlPlane:
  name: master
  replicas: 3                        # 3 control plane nodes
  platform:
    aws:
      type: m5.2xlarge              # 8 vCPU, 32 GB
🔄 Bootstrap Sequence — How a Production Cluster Comes to Life
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    BOOTSTRAP SEQUENCE (IPI)                          │
│                                                                      │
│  Step 1:  openshift-install create install-config                   │
│           ↓  You define: cloud, region, nodes, network CIDRs         │
│                                                                      │
│  Step 2:  openshift-install create cluster                          │
│           ↓  OpenShift provisions VMs, LBs, DNS, security groups    │
│                                                                      │
│  Step 3:  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│           │  🔥 BOOTSTRAP NODE (TEMPORARY — auto-destroyed)│          │
│           │  • Runs single-member etcd                     │          │
│           │  • Runs temporary control plane                │          │
│           │  • Serves Ignition configs to master nodes     │          │
│           │  • Lives ~10-15 minutes, then self-destructs   │          │
│           │  Purpose: Bootstraps the permanent cluster     │          │
│           └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
│           ↓  (bootstrap hands off to masters)                       │
│                                                                      │
│  Step 4:  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│           │  🧠 MASTER/CONTROL PLANE NODES (3 — permanent) │          │
│           │  • etcd cluster (3 members, Raft consensus)    │          │
│           │  • kube-apiserver (load-balanced)              │          │
│           │  • kube-scheduler + kube-controller-manager    │          │
│           │  • OpenShift Cluster Operators kick in:        │          │
│           │    - Cluster Version Operator (CVO)            │          │
│           │    - Authentication Operator                   │          │
│           │    - Console Operator                          │          │
│           │    - Monitoring Operator                       │          │
│           └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
│           ↓                                                          │
│  Step 5:  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│           │  💪 WORKER NODES (N — runs your applications)  │          │
│           │  • CRI-O container runtime (NOT Docker!)       │          │
│           │  • OVN-Kubernetes networking (pod network)     │          │
│           │  • Your pods, Deployments, Routes run here     │          │
│           │  • Auto-scalable via Machine API               │          │
│           └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
│           ↓                                                          │
│  ✅ DONE: ClusterVersion = "Available=True, Progressing=False"      │
│           Bootstrap node destroyed. Cluster is self-hosted.         │
│           All operators manage themselves via the CVO.              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

5.4 Cluster Networking During Installation

The Cluster Network Operator (CNO) deploys OVN-Kubernetes as the default CNI (replacing the older OpenShift SDN). You define these networks in install-config.yaml — they CANNOT be changed after installation!

NetworkDefault CIDRWhat It DoesExample IP
Pod Network10.128.0.0/14Every pod gets a unique IP from this range. All pods can route to all other pods (flat network).10.128.2.15
Service Network172.30.0.0/16Stable virtual IPs for Services (ClusterIP). Pods reach services via kube-proxy or OVN.172.30.0.1 (kubernetes API)
Host Prefix/23Subnet size allocated to EACH node for pod IPs. /23 = 512 IPs per node (~512 pods).10.128.0.0/23 → Node 0
Machine CIDRVaries by cloudThe network where node VMs get their IPs (infrastructure network, not pod network).10.0.0.0/16 (AWS)
⚠️ Cannot Change After Install!

Once you set clusterNetwork, serviceNetwork, and hostPrefix in install-config.yaml, they are permanent for the life of the cluster. Changing them requires a full cluster reinstall. Plan carefully!

5.5 Post-Installation Verification

After installation, you MUST verify cluster health. Here's the complete 15-step checklist used in production environments and expected knowledge for EX267:

✅ 15-Step Post-Install Verification Checklist

  1. oc get nodes — All nodes show Ready status
  2. oc get clusterversion — Shows Available=True, Progressing=False
  3. oc get clusteroperators — ALL operators Available=True, Degraded=False (this is the single most important check!)
  4. oc get co — Short alias, same output as above
  5. oc get pods -n openshift-ingress — Router pods Running (2 replicas minimum)
  6. oc get pods -n openshift-authentication — OAuth pods Running
  7. oc get pods -n openshift-console — Console pods Running (web UI)
  8. oc get pods -n openshift-monitoring — Prometheus + AlertManager Running
  9. oc get pods -n openshift-image-registry — Internal registry pods Running
  10. oc adm top nodes — CPU/Memory usage within expected ranges
  11. oc get csr — No pending Certificate Signing Requests (all Approved)
  12. oc get pv — PersistentVolumes provisioned and Bound
  13. oc get sc — A default StorageClass exists (annotated as default)
  14. oc get routes --all-namespaces — Console route is accessible
  15. oc whoami --show-token — Can authenticate successfully
Quick One-Liner: Are All Cluster Operators Healthy?
oc get co | awk 'NR==1 || $3!="True" || $4!="False" || $5!="False"'
# If this returns ONLY the header row → ALL operators are healthy!
# If any operator appears below the header → investigate it immediately.

5.6 Installing OpenShift AI Operator 🎯

This is the CORE EX267 task. The OpenShift AI Operator is installed via the Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM):

Installing OpenShift AI Operator + DataScienceCluster
# 1. Create namespace for the operator
oc new-project redhat-ods-operator

# 2. Create OperatorGroup
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1
kind: OperatorGroup
metadata:
  name: redhat-ods-operator
  namespace: redhat-ods-operator
spec:
  targetNamespaces: []
EOF

# 3. Create Subscription (installs the operator)
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata:
  name: rhods-operator
  namespace: redhat-ods-operator
spec:
  channel: stable
  name: rhods-operator
  source: redhat-operators
  sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace
EOF

# 4. Wait for operator to be ready
oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator -w

# 5. Create DataScienceCluster (enables AI components!)
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: datasciencecluster.opendatahub.io/v1
kind: DataScienceCluster
metadata:
  name: default-dsc
spec:
  components:
    dashboard: { managementState: Managed }
    workbenches: { managementState: Managed }
    datasciencepipelines: { managementState: Managed }
    kserve: { managementState: Managed, serving: { name: Knative } }
    modelregistry: { managementState: Managed }
EOF
