🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — Understanding the DataScienceCluster YAML

The DataScienceCluster (DSC) is the SINGLE most important YAML in OpenShift AI. It's like a master switchboard — one file controls whether notebooks, pipelines, model serving, and model registry are enabled or disabled.

Each component has a managementState: Managed means "install and maintain this component for me" — the operator handles everything. Removed means "take it away." There's no in-between — a component is either fully managed or not present.

EX267 relevance: Expect to be asked to enable specific components. The exam will give you a scenario like "Enable model serving with Knative for the data science team" — you need to know that means setting kserve: { managementState: Managed, serving: { name: Knative } } in the DSC.

5.8 Configuring GPU Support During Installation

For AI workloads, GPU support is critical. OpenShift uses the NVIDIA GPU Operator to manage the entire GPU software stack — drivers, CUDA, container runtime, and monitoring (DCGM). This is a prerequisite for running GPU-enabled notebooks and model serving.

GPU Installation — Operator + ClusterPolicy + Validation
# Step 1: Install Node Feature Discovery (NFD) first
# NFD auto-detects GPU hardware and labels nodes
# OperatorHub → Node Feature Discovery → Install

# Step 2: Install NVIDIA GPU Operator
# OperatorHub → NVIDIA GPU Operator → Install

# Step 3: Create ClusterPolicy (triggers GPU driver deployment)
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: gpu-cluster-policy
spec:
  operator:
    defaultRuntime: crio          # OpenShift uses CRI-O
  driver:
    enabled: true                 # Auto-install GPU drivers
  toolkit:
    enabled: true                 # NVIDIA container toolkit
  devicePlugin:
    enabled: true                 # Expose GPUs to pods
  dcgm:
    enabled: true                 # GPU monitoring (metrics)
  mig:
    strategy: mixed              # Multi-Instance GPU support
EOF

# Step 4: Wait for GPU driver deployment (2-5 minutes)
oc get pod -n nvidia-gpu-operator -w

# Step 5: Validate GPU availability
oc describe node <gpu-node> | grep nvidia
# Must show: nvidia.com/gpu: 1 (or 2, 4, 8 depending on hardware)

# Step 6: Verify GPU operator health
oc get csv -n nvidia-gpu-operator
# PHASE must be: Succeeded

# Step 7: Test GPU access from a pod
oc run gpu-test --rm -it \
  --image=nvidia/cuda:12.0-base \
  --restart=Never \
  --limits=nvidia.com/gpu=1 \
  -- nvidia-smi
# Should show GPU info: model, memory, CUDA version
🎮 GPU Troubleshooting Quick Check

GPU not showing on node? Check NFD labels: oc get nodes -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, labels: .metadata.labels}' | grep nvidia. Pods can't use GPU? Check the service account has privileged SCC: oc adm policy add-scc-to-user privileged -z default -n my-project. Driver not deploying? Check ClusterPolicy status: oc describe clusterpolicy gpu-cluster-policy.

5.9 Installation Troubleshooting — Common Pitfalls

Installation problems are common. Here's a reference table of the most frequent issues and their fixes:

SymptomLikely CauseFix
CRC won't start — "insufficient memory"Less than 16GB RAM availableClose other apps. CRC needs ~10GB free. Or upgrade RAM.
CRC start fails — "network error"VPN or proxy interferingDisconnect VPN during crc start, then reconnect.
oc login fails — certificate errorExpired CRC certificates (30-day limit)crc delete then crc start (fresh certs)
Operator stuck in PendingNo OperatorGroup or wrong namespaceoc get operatorgroup -n redhat-ods-operator
DataScienceCluster not reconcilingDependency operator missing (Pipelines/Serverless)Check operator logs: oc logs -n redhat-ods-operator deployment/rhods-operator
Pull secret expiredPull secrets expire after 1 yearDownload fresh from console.redhat.com/openshift/downloads
Nodes show NotReadykubelet down, disk pressure, or network issueoc describe node <name> → check Conditions section
ClusterOperators degradedOne or more core operators failingoc describe co <name> → check status.conditions
Cannot pull images from registryImage registry not exposed or no storageoc patch configs.imageregistry cluster -p '{"spec":{"defaultRoute":true}}' --type=merge
🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 5 (35% of exam!)

Core task: Install OpenShift AI Operator → Create DataScienceCluster → Verify oc get dsc. Speed tip: Use console for operator install (faster than CLI YAML). Gotcha: Namespace MUST be redhat-ods-operator. DSC MUST be named default-dsc. GPU Operator requires NFD installed FIRST.

📝 Chapter 5 Practice Questions

Q1
What CRD do you create to enable OpenShift AI components?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

DataScienceCluster (apiVersion: datasciencecluster.opendatahub.io/v1).

📖 EXPLANATION

The DSC is the single YAML manifest that controls ALL AI components. It's like a master switch panel — each managementState: Managed enables a component (dashboard, workbenches, pipelines, kserve, etc.). The operator watches this CR and reconciles the cluster to match. EX267 tip: After creating a DSC, always verify with oc get dsc -o yaml | grep -A2 managementState — every component should show Managed or Removed as intended.

Q2
Which namespace must the OpenShift AI Operator be installed in?
Click to reveal
✅ Answer

redhat-ods-operator — this is the required namespace for the operator.

📖 EXPLANATION

The namespace is hardcoded — using any other namespace will cause the operator to fail. This is a common EX267 gotcha. The operator's components (pods, services) deploy into redhat-ods-applications, redhat-ods-monitoring, and other namespaces. The DSC is cluster-scoped (not namespaced) — it applies globally. Verify: oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator → Phase: Succeeded.

Q3
What happens if you set managementState: Removed on the workbenches component?
Click
✅

Jupyter notebook functionality is disabled. Users cannot create or access notebooks. All notebook pods are terminated.

📖 EXPLANATION

Removed tells the operator to DELETE all resources for that component. This is different from Unmanaged (leaves existing resources but stops managing them). For EX267: if asked to "disable a component," use Removed. If asked to "stop managing" without deleting, use Unmanaged. The operator reconciliation loop will: 1) Remove CRDs, 2) Delete operator pods, 3) Clean up RBAC. Existing user data (PVCs, S3 artifacts) is NOT deleted — only the serving infrastructure.

Q4
How do you verify the OpenShift AI Operator is healthy?
Click
✅

oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator — look for Phase: Succeeded. Also oc get dsc — all components should show Ready.

📖 EXPLANATION

Full health check: 1) oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator → Phase: Succeeded (operator installed correctly). 2) oc get dsc → All components Ready (components reconciled). 3) oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications → All Running (workload pods healthy). 4) oc get route -n redhat-ods-applications → Dashboard URL accessible. Run this 4-step check after every installation task on EX267 — it proves your work is complete and catches dependency issues early. See Appendix B.5 for the full verification script.

Q5
What is a MachineConfig and what does it control?
Click
✅

MachineConfig defines node-level OS configuration (kernel params, files, systemd units). Applied via MachineConfigPool to worker/master nodes.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: machineconfiguration.openshift.io/v1
kind: MachineConfig
metadata: { name: 99-gpu-kernel-params, labels: { machineconfiguration.openshift.io/role: worker } }
spec:
  kernelArguments: [pci=realloc, pcie_aspm=off]
# Applied to all worker nodes via MachineConfigPool
Q6
What is the difference between a ClusterVersion and ClusterOperator?
Click
✅

ClusterVersion: overall OpenShift version + update channel. ClusterOperator: health of individual operators (networking, auth, etc.).

📖 EXPLANATION
oc get clusterversion   # Shows: version, channel, available, progressing
oc get clusteroperator  # Shows: 20+ operators, each showing Available/Progressing/Degraded
# Any Degraded=True → cluster issue that needs investigation
Q7
How does node auto-scaling work in OpenShift?
Click
✅

ClusterAutoscaler watches for pending pods. If no node fits, it provisions a new node via MachineSet. MachineAutoScaler sets min/max per MachineSet.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: autoscaling.openshift.io/v1beta1
kind: MachineAutoscaler
metadata: { name: worker-gpu }
spec:
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  scaleTargetRef: { kind: MachineSet, name: gpu-worker }
Q8
What OAuth identity providers does OpenShift support?
Click
✅

LDAP, GitHub, GitLab, Google, OpenID Connect, Keystone, HTPasswd (dev only), RequestHeader. Configured via OAuth CR.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: config.openshift.io/v1
kind: OAuth
metadata: { name: cluster }
spec:
  identityProviders:
  - name: github
    mappingMethod: claim
    type: GitHub
    github: { clientID: xxx, clientSecret: { name: github-secret }, organizations: [anihpj] }
Q9
What is the OpenShift SDN and how does it handle pod networking?
Click
✅

OVN-Kubernetes is the default SDN. Every pod gets a unique IP from 10.128.0.0/14. All pods can communicate without NAT. NetworkPolicy adds segmentation.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: operator.openshift.io/v1
kind: Network
metadata: { name: cluster }
spec:
  defaultNetwork:
    ovnKubernetesConfig:
      mtu: 1400
    type: OVNKubernetes
# Pod network: 10.128.0.0/14, Service network: 172.30.0.0/16
Q10
How do you configure node labels and taints for GPU nodes?
Click
✅

NFD auto-labels GPU nodes. Add taints to reserve GPUs for AI workloads only. Pods need tolerations to schedule on tainted GPU nodes.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc adm taint nodes gpu-node-1 nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule
# Pod toleration:
tolerations:
- key: nvidia.com/gpu
  operator: Equal
  value: "present"
  effect: NoSchedule
# Auto-labels by NFD: feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-10de.present=true

5.10 Disconnected (Air-Gapped) Installation — Red Hat Docs Essential

🆕 From Official Red Hat Docs — "Installing in a disconnected environment"

Many enterprise and government environments have no internet access. OpenShift AI fully supports disconnected (air-gapped) installations using a local mirror registry. All operators, images, and models must be mirrored locally before installation.

🔌 Disconnected Installation Flow
INTERNET-CONNECTED (JUMP HOST)              AIR-GAPPED CLUSTER
┌──────────────────────────────┐          ┌────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. oc adm catalog mirror     │          │ 4. oc create -f ImageContentSourcePolicy │
│    → copies operators to     │  USB/   │    → redirects pulls to     │
│      local registry          │  DISK   │      local mirror           │
│ 2. oc mirror --config=...    │───────▶ │ 5. oc create -f CatalogSource │
│    → mirrors release images  │  ───▶   │    → uses local catalog     │
│ 3. Build local OperatorHub   │          │ 6. Install OpenShift AI    │
│    catalog                   │          │    from mirrored operators │
└──────────────────────────────┘          └────────────────────────────┘

Key commands: oc adm catalog mirror (mirror OperatorHub operators), oc mirror (mirror release images), ImageContentSourcePolicy (redirect pulls to local registry). For AI workloads: also mirror notebook images, pipeline images, and model serving runtimes (KServe/ModelMesh containers).

Chapter 6: Authentication & User Management🟡 Intermediate · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 6: OpenShift Authentication — Securing Access

OpenShift's built-in OAuth server and RBAC system provide enterprise-grade access control. Essential for EX267 where you configure access for data science teams.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔐 Security

6.1 How Authentication Works in OpenShift

OpenShift has a built-in OAuth server — not a separate deployment. Every cluster ships with its own authentication service. Users authenticate through Identity Providers (IdPs), receive an OAuth token, and use that token for all subsequent API calls.

🔐 Authentication Flow — User → OAuth → IdP → Token → API
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         🔐 OPENSHIFT AUTHENTICATION FLOW                       │
│                                                                │
│  👤 USER (browser or CLI)                                      │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ 1. `oc login` or Console login                         │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                     │
│  │  🔒 OpenShift OAuth Server            │                     │
│  │  (Built-in, runs in openshift-        │                     │
│  │   authentication namespace)           │                     │
│  │                                        │                     │
│  │  2. "Who are you?" → Redirect to IdP │                     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                     │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ 3. Browser redirects to Identity Provider              │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                     │
│  │  🏢 IDENTITY PROVIDER (IdP)           │                     │
│  │  • HTPasswd (file-based, simple)      │                     │
│  │  • LDAP (Active Directory)            │                     │
│  │  • GitHub / Google / GitLab OAuth     │                     │
│  │  • OpenID Connect (OIDC) — Keycloak,  │                     │
│  │    Azure AD, Okta                     │                     │
│  │  • Request Header (proxy-based)       │                     │
│  │                                        │                     │
│  │  4. User provides credentials         │                     │
│  │  5. IdP validates → Returns identity  │                     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                     │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ 6. OAuth server issues access token                    │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                     │
│  │  🎫 OAUTH TOKEN (Bearer Token)        │                     │
│  │  • Stored in ~/.kube/config           │                     │
│  │  • Valid for 24 hours by default      │                     │
│  │  • Sent with EVERY API request        │                     │
│  │    Header: Authorization: Bearer xxx  │                     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                     │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ 7. Every API call carries this token                   │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                     │
│  │  🧠 API SERVER                        │                     │
│  │  • Validates token signature          │                     │
│  │  • Checks RBAC (RoleBindings)         │                     │
│  │  • Checks SCC (Security Context)      │                     │
│  │  • Returns result or 403 Forbidden    │                     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

6.2 Configuring HTPasswd Identity Provider

HTPasswd is the simplest IdP — users and (hashed) passwords stored in a file. Perfect for EX267 practice and small teams. Here's the complete walkthrough for our anihpj data science team:

Adding anihpj Team Users via HTPasswd (Step-by-Step)
# Step 1: Install htpasswd utility (if not present)
yum install -y httpd-tools          # RHEL/Fedora
apt-get install -y apache2-utils    # Ubuntu

# Step 2: Create htpasswd file with 3 anihpj team users
htpasswd -c -B htpasswd anihpj-admin      # -c = create, -B = bcrypt
htpasswd -B htpasswd anihpj-ds            # Data scientist — notebooks & pipelines
htpasswd -B htpasswd anihpj-viewer       # Read-only — view dashboards

# Step 3: Store as a Secret in openshift-config namespace
oc create secret generic htpass-secret \
  --from-file=htpasswd=htpasswd \
  -n openshift-config

# Step 4: Update the OAuth CR to use HTPasswd
oc patch oauth cluster --type=merge -p '
spec:
  identityProviders:
  - name: htpasswd_provider
    mappingMethod: claim
    type: HTPasswd
    htpasswd:
      fileData:
        name: htpass-secret'

# Step 5: Wait for OAuth pods to restart
oc get pods -n openshift-authentication -w

# Step 6: Test login as each user
oc login -u anihpj-admin https://api.crc.testing:6443
oc whoami    # Should show: anihpj-admin

# Step 7: Grant cluster-admin to anihpj-admin
oc adm policy add-cluster-role-to-user cluster-admin anihpj-admin
🔑 Mapping Method Options

mappingMethod: claim — every unique identity gets a unique user (use this). mappingMethod: lookup — maps to existing identities only. mappingMethod: generate — generates a username from the identity (default). For EX267, know that claim is the preferred method.

6.3 RBAC — Who Can Do What?

OpenShift RBAC is additive — you grant permissions, never take them away. A user's effective permissions = union of all roles bound to them. Default cluster roles cover 90% of use cases:

RoleScopeCreate?Delete?RBAC?Best For
cluster-adminCluster✅ All✅ All✅Platform admins
adminProject✅ All✅ All✅Project owners
editProject✅ Most✅ Most❌Data scientists
viewProject❌❌❌Stakeholders

Real-world anihpj RBAC setup: The data scientist gets edit on anihpj-ml (can create notebooks, pipelines, but can't add other users). The project lead gets admin (can manage RBAC). The intern gets view (can see dashboards, can't modify anything).

Hands-On: Configure anihpj RBAC
# Create project for ML work
oc new-project anihpj-ml

# Grant edit to data scientists (can create notebooks, pipelines)
oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit anihpj-ds -n anihpj-ml

# Grant admin to project lead (can manage RBAC + resources)
oc adm policy add-role-to-user admin anihpj-admin -n anihpj-ml

# Grant view to stakeholders (read-only dashboard access)
oc adm policy add-role-to-user view anihpj-viewer -n anihpj-ml

# Verify bindings
oc get rolebindings -n anihpj-ml
oc describe rolebinding admin -n anihpj-ml

6.4 Service Accounts for Machine-to-Machine Auth

When a pod talks to the Kubernetes API (e.g., to list other pods, read ConfigMaps, or update its own status), it authenticates using a Service Account (SA). Every namespace has a default SA — but you should create dedicated SAs for specific workloads.

🤖 Service Account Authentication — Pod → API Server
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         🤖 SERVICE ACCOUNT AUTHENTICATION FLOW                  │
│                                                                │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                     │
│  │  📦 POD (anihpj-ml namespace)         │                     │
│  │  serviceAccountName: anihpj-cicd      │                     │
│  │                                       │                     │
│  │  Mounted at:                          │                     │
│  │  /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/      │                     │
│  │    serviceaccount/                    │                     │
│  │    ├── token       ← JWT token        │                     │
│  │    ├── ca.crt      ← API server CA    │                     │
│  │    └── namespace   ← Namespace name   │                     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                     │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ Pod sends HTTP request with token in header:           │
│       │ Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...                    │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                     │
│  │  🧠 API SERVER                        │                     │
│  │  1. Validates JWT signature           │                     │
│  │  2. Extracts SA username:             │                     │
│  │     system:serviceaccount:anihpj-ml:  │                     │
│  │     anihpj-cicd                       │                     │
│  │  3. Checks RBAC: Does this SA have    │                     │
│  │     permission to do this action?     │                     │
│  │  4. Checks SCC: Which SCC applies?    │                     │
│  │  5. Returns result or 403 Forbidden   │                     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                     │
│                                                                │
│  Key SA facts:                                                 │
│  • SA username format: system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>       │
│  • Token auto-mounted unless automountServiceAccountToken:false│
│  • Token is a JWT — signed by kube-apiserver's signing key     │
│  • SA tokens are time-limited (default 1 hour, configurable)   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Hands-On: Create anihpj CI/CD Service Account
# Step 1: Create SA for CI/CD pipeline
oc create sa anihpj-cicd -n anihpj-ml

# Step 2: Grant it image pull permissions (pull from internal registry)
oc policy add-role-to-user system:image-puller \
  system:serviceaccount:anihpj-ml:anihpj-cicd \
  -n anihpj-ml

# Step 3: Grant edit access (create/delete pods, deployments)
oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit \
  -z anihpj-cicd -n anihpj-ml

# Step 4: Use SA in a pod/deployment
oc set serviceaccount deployment/anihpj anihpj-cicd -n anihpj-ml

# Step 5: Verify SA token (from inside the pod)
oc exec deploy/anihpj -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token

# Step 6: Check SA permissions
oc auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-ml:anihpj-cicd -n anihpj-ml
# Should return: yes

# Step 7: Isolate — Create SA with MINIMAL permissions for safety
oc create sa anihpj-pipeline -n anihpj-ml
# Grant ONLY what it needs — NOT edit or admin!
oc adm policy add-role-to-user view -z anihpj-pipeline -n anihpj-ml
# Pipeline can see resources but cannot modify them
🔐 SA Best Practices for AI Workloads

Least privilege: Create a separate SA for each workload type (notebooks, pipelines, model serving). Never use the default SA for production workloads. GPU workloads: Your SA needs the privileged SCC. Pipeline SAs: Need edit access to create pipeline pods + S3 access for artifacts. Notebook SAs: Need edit in their namespace + PVC mount access.

6.5 Security Context Constraints (SCC) — OpenShift's Security Layer

SCCs are OpenShift's replacement for Kubernetes Pod Security Standards — they control what pods CAN and CANNOT do at the cluster level. They are evaluated at admission time, BEFORE the pod is created.

SCCRun as RootHost NetworkPrivileged ContainerHost FS AccessUse Case
restricted❌❌❌❌Default — all pods
restricted-v2❌❌❌❌Newer, stricter default (4.11+)
nonroot❌❌❌❌Non-root but needs some caps
anyuid✅❌❌❌Legacy apps that need root
hostaccess✅✅❌✅Monitoring/logging agents
hostnetwork✅✅❌❌Pods that need host network
privileged✅✅✅✅GPU workloads, storage drivers
Hands-On: Assign SCC to Service Account
# Check which SCC a pod received (from pod events)
oc describe pod my-pod | grep scc
# Output: openshift.io/scc: restricted

# Grant a more permissive SCC to a service account
oc adm policy add-scc-to-user anyuid -z my-sa -n my-project

# Grant privileged SCC (required for NVIDIA GPU access)
oc adm policy add-scc-to-user privileged -z gpu-workload-sa -n anihpj-ml

# List all SCCs
oc get scc
oc describe scc privileged

6.6 OAuth Deep Dive — Custom Identity Providers

For enterprise deployments, you'll want more than HTPasswd. OpenShift supports multiple IdPs simultaneously — your users can log in via LDAP, GitHub, or OIDC all at once. Each IdP appears as an option on the login page.

IdP TypeBest ForComplexityExample Use
LDAPActive Directory / corporate directory🟡 MediumEnterprise users
GitHubDeveloper teams using GitHub🟢 LowOpen source projects
GoogleGoogle Workspace orgs🟢 LowGoogle-based teams
OIDCSSO (Keycloak, Azure AD, Okta)🔴 HighEnterprise SSO
Request HeaderProxy-based auth (SAML via proxy)🔴 HighLegacy SAML systems
🔑 The oauth.config.openshift.io CR

All IdP configuration lives in a single Custom Resource: oc edit oauth cluster. You add identity providers under spec.identityProviders. Each provider has a name, mappingMethod, and provider-specific configuration. Multiple providers = multiple login buttons on the console.

6.7 Certificates and TLS in OpenShift

OpenShift has a built-in certificate authority (the service-ca) that automatically issues and rotates certificates for internal services. This means your pods get TLS certificates without you doing anything. Here's the lifecycle:

📜 Certificate Lifecycle in OpenShift
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CERTIFICATE LIFECYCLE                             │
│                                                                │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐             │
│  │  🏛️ SERVICE-CA (Internal Certificate Authority)│             │
│  │  • Runs in openshift-service-ca namespace      │             │
│  │  • Auto-issues certs to services               │             │
│  │  • Rotates certs before expiry (auto-renew at  │             │
│  │    80% of validity)                            │             │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘             │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ Annotate Service: service.beta.openshift.io/serving-  │
│       │ cert-secret-name=my-cert                               │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐             │
│  │  📜 ISSUED CERT (stored as Secret)            │             │
│  │  • tls.crt + tls.key                          │             │
│  │  • Valid for 26 months (API server cert)      │             │
│  │  • Auto-mounted to pods                       │             │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘             │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ ~21 months later (80% of validity)                     │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐             │
│  │  🔄 AUTO-RENEW                                │             │
│  │  • New cert issued BEFORE old expires          │             │
│  │  • Secret updated with new tls.crt/tls.key    │             │
│  │  • Pods pick up new cert (may need restart)   │             │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘             │
│       │                                                        │
│  Key customizations:                                           │
│  • API Server cert: Custom in APIServer CR                     │
│  • Ingress (Router) cert: Custom in IngressController CR       │
│  • Service certs: Automatic via service-ca annotation          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

6.8 Multi-Tenancy with Projects and RBAC

Multi-tenancy means multiple teams share the same cluster without seeing or interfering with each other. OpenShift achieves this through the combination of Projects (namespaces with extra isolation), RBAC, NetworkPolicies, and ResourceQuotas.

🏢 Multi-Tenancy Architecture — Team Isolation
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🏢 OPENSHIFT CLUSTER — MULTI-TENANCY                   │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐               │
│  │  📁 anihpj-dev        │  │  📁 anihpj-ml         │               │
│  │  (Development)        │  │  (Machine Learning)   │               │
│  │                       │  │                       │               │
│  │  RBAC:                │  │  RBAC:                │               │
│  │  • anihpj-dev: admin  │  │  • anihpj-ds: edit    │               │
│  │  • developers: edit   │  │  • anihpj-admin:admin │               │
│  │                       │  │                       │               │
│  │  Quota:               │  │  Quota:               │               │
│  │  CPU: 10 cores        │  │  CPU: 20 cores        │               │
│  │  RAM: 20Gi            │  │  RAM: 64Gi            │               │
│  │  GPU: 0               │  │  GPU: 2               │               │
│  │                       │  │                       │               │
│  │  NetworkPolicy:       │  │  NetworkPolicy:       │               │
│  │  → Can reach ml-db    │  │  → Can reach ml-db    │               │
│  │  → Cannot reach prod  │  │  → Cannot reach dev   │               │
│  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘               │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────┐                                          │
│  │  📁 anihpj-prod        │  ┌──────────────────────┐              │
│  │  (Production)          │  │  📁 postgres-db       │              │
│  │                         │  │  (Shared Database)    │              │
│  │  RBAC:                  │  │                       │              │
│  │  • anihpj-admin: admin  │  │  NetworkPolicy:       │              │
│  │  • NO developers        │  │  Allow from: dev, ml  │              │
│  │                         │  │  Deny from: everyone  │              │
│  │  Quota:                 │  │    else               │              │
│  │  CPU: 40 cores          │  │                       │              │
│  │  RAM: 128Gi             │  └──────────────────────┘              │
│  │  GPU: 4                 │                                          │
│  │                         │                                          │
│  │  NetworkPolicy:         │                                          │
│  │  → ISOLATED (default-   │                                          │
│  │    deny all ingress)    │                                          │
│  └──────────────────────┘                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🏗️ Multi-Tenancy Best Practices

1. Use separate projects per environment (dev/ml/prod) — never mix. 2. Apply ResourceQuotas to prevent one team from starving others. 3. Use NetworkPolicies to isolate — default is everything open, so add restrictions. 4. Use oc policy add-role-to-group with Groups, not individual users, for RBAC at scale. 5. For anihpj: dev can talk to ml-db, ml can talk to ml-db, prod is fully isolated.

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — SCC: "Why Does My Pod Keep Failing?"

The #1 reason pods fail on OpenShift when they work fine on vanilla Kubernetes is SCC violations. Here's why:

Vanilla K8s: Pods can run as root by default. Your Dockerfile says USER root — it works.

OpenShift: The restricted SCC is applied to ALL pods by default. It says: "You CANNOT run as root. You CANNOT use host networking. You CANNOT access host filesystem." If your container tries any of these — it's denied at admission time before the pod even starts.

Fix: Either build your image to work as non-root (preferred) OR assign a more permissive SCC like anyuid or privileged to the service account: oc adm policy add-scc-to-user anyuid -z default -n my-project

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 6

Core tasks: Create users, assign roles (edit/admin/view), configure HTPasswd IdP, bind SCC to service accounts. Speed tip: oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit user -n project is the #1 RBAC command. Gotcha: GPU pods need privileged SCC — create a dedicated SA, don't grant it to default.

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 6

Core tasks: Create users, assign edit/admin/view roles, configure HTPasswd IdP, bind SCC to SAs. Speed tip: oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit user -n project. Gotcha: GPU pods need privileged SCC — create dedicated SA, never use default.

📝 Chapter 6 Practice Questions

Q1
Which SCC should GPU workload pods use?
Click
✅

privileged — GPU needs host device access.

📖 EXPLANATION

GPU containers need the privileged SCC because the NVIDIA container runtime must access /dev/nvidia* device nodes and load kernel modules. This is the ONLY legitimate use case for privileged SCC in most OpenShift deployments. Best practice: don't grant privileged to the default SA. Create a dedicated SA: oc create sa gpu-workload → oc adm policy add-scc-to-user privileged -z gpu-workload. Non-GPU pods should use restricted SCC.

Q2
How to give a user edit access to a project?
Click
✅

oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit <user> -n <project>

📖 EXPLANATION

OpenShift RBAC uses roles (permissions) bound to subjects (users/groups/SAs). edit is a cluster role that grants read-write access to most resources except RBAC and quotas. Other roles: admin (edit + manage RBAC within project), view (read-only). For data scientists: give edit to their DS project so they can create notebooks and pipelines. For platform engineers: give admin so they can manage the project's RBAC.

Q3
What's the difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?
Click
✅

Role = scoped to ONE namespace. ClusterRole = cluster-wide (all namespaces). Use ClusterRole for node access, SCC management, and cluster-level resources.

📖 EXPLANATION

RoleBinding (Role + subject + namespace) grants permissions within a single project. ClusterRoleBinding (ClusterRole + subject) grants permissions across ALL projects. Use ClusterRole for: SCC management (oc adm policy add-scc-to-user), node access, PV management, and cluster-level operators. For DS projects: use RoleBindings with the edit ClusterRole — this scopes the cluster-wide edit role to just one namespace.

Q4
How does the service-ca handle certificate rotation?
Click
✅

Service-ca auto-rotates certificates at 80% of their validity period. It issues a new cert BEFORE expiry and updates the Secret. Pods may need a restart: oc rollout restart deploy/<name>.

📖 EXPLANATION

The service-ca operator runs in openshift-service-ca namespace. It watches for Secrets annotated with service.beta.openshift.io/serving-cert-secret-name and auto-generates TLS certificates. Rotation timeline: cert issued → 80% of validity reached → new cert generated → Secret updated → pods must restart to pick up new cert. For anihpj: annotate your service with service.beta.openshift.io/serving-cert-secret-name: anihpj-tls to auto-provision TLS.

Q5
What's the difference between mappingMethod: claim, lookup, and generate?
Click
✅

claim: Every unique identity gets a unique user (preferred). lookup: Maps to existing identities only (fails for new users). generate: Creates username from identity. Use claim for EX267.

📖 EXPLANATION

These are Identity Provider mapping methods in the OAuth CR. claim uses the IdP's unique ID as the OpenShift user identity — most secure, never duplicates. lookup requires the user to already exist in OpenShift's identity database — fails for new users. generate creates a username from the IdP's name claim — but names aren't guaranteed unique. For EX267: always use mappingMethod: claim unless specifically told otherwise.

Q6
How do you configure HTPasswd as an identity provider for development?
Click
✅

Create HTPasswd Secret → add to OAuth CR as identityProvider. Create/update users with htpasswd utility. Dev only — use LDAP/GitHub for production.

📖 EXPLANATION
htpasswd -c -B htpasswd admin
htpasswd -B htpasswd dscientist
oc create secret generic htpass-secret --from-file=htpasswd -n openshift-config
# OAuth CR patch:
spec:
  identityProviders:
  - name: htpasswd-provider
    mappingMethod: claim
    type: HTPasswd
    htpasswd: { fileData: { name: htpass-secret } }
Q7
How do you grant a data scientist access to create notebooks and pipelines?
Click
✅

oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit dscientist -n anihpj-ml. The edit role allows creating pods, notebooks, pipelines, but NOT managing RBAC.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Data scientist access:
oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit dscientist -n anihpj-ml
# MLOps engineer access (can manage project RBAC):
oc adm policy add-role-to-user admin mlops-engineer -n anihpj-ml
# Read-only access (view dashboards, logs):
oc adm policy add-role-to-user view intern -n anihpj-ml
Q8
How do you create a dedicated ServiceAccount for GPU workloads?
Click
✅

oc create sa gpu-workload -n anihpj-ml → bind privileged SCC only to this SA → use in pod spec.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc create sa gpu-workload -n anihpj-ml
oc adm policy add-scc-to-user privileged -z gpu-workload -n anihpj-ml
# Pod spec:
spec:
  serviceAccountName: gpu-workload  # Only this SA gets privileged SCC
  containers:
  - name: train
    resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 1 } }
Q9
What is an OAuth client and how does it relate to the OpenShift console?
Click
✅

OAuth clients are registered applications that use OpenShift OAuth for authentication. The console is the default OAuth client. Custom apps register via OAuthClient CR.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: oauth.openshift.io/v1
kind: OAuthClient
metadata: { name: anihpj-dashboard }
secret: "supersecret123"
redirectURIs: ["https://anihpj.apps.ocp.example.com/oauth/callback"]
grantMethod: prompt  # Always ask user for consent
Q10
How do you troubleshoot authentication failures in OpenShift?
Click
✅

Check oc get authentication cluster -o yaml, OAuth pod logs, identity provider config, and user identity mapping.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc get authentication cluster -o yaml     # OAuth config
oc get pods -n openshift-authentication   # OAuth pods
oc logs -n openshift-authentication deployment/oauth-openshift --tail=20
oc get identities                         # User→Identity mappings
oc describe oauth cluster | grep -A20 identityProviders

Chapter 7: Networking — Routes, Services & Ingress🟡 Intermediate · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 7: OpenShift Networking

OVN-Kubernetes SDN + HAProxy Router. Services, Routes (with TLS), NetworkPolicies, and Service Mesh — everything to securely expose anihpj and AI model endpoints.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🌐 Networking

7.1 Networking Fundamentals

OpenShift uses OVN-Kubernetes as its Software-Defined Network (SDN). Every pod gets its own IP address from the pod network (10.128.0.0/14). Services provide stable endpoints. Routes expose services to the outside world.

🌐 Network Topology — Pod → Service → Route → External User
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🌐 OPENSHIFT NETWORKING TOPOLOGY                   │
│                                                                │
│  EXTERNAL USER 🌍                                               │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ HTTPS (TLS)                                            │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                     │
│  │  🔒 ROUTE (HAProxy Router)            │                     │
│  │  • anihpj.apps.cluster.example.com   │                     │
│  │  • TLS termination (Edge/Passthrough) │                     │
│  │  • Path-based routing: /api → svc A  │                     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                     │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ Routes to Service by name                              │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                     │
│  │  🔄 SERVICE (ClusterIP: 172.30.x.x)   │                     │
│  │  • Stable virtual IP                  │                     │
│  │  • Load balances across pod replicas  │                     │
│  │  • Service type: ClusterIP (internal) │                     │
│  │    NodePort (node IP + port)          │                     │
│  │    LoadBalancer (cloud LB provisioned)│                     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                     │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ iptables/OVN rules → randomly to one pod               │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                     │
│  │  📦 PODS (Pod Network: 10.128.x.x)    │                     │
│  │  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐   │                     │
│  │  │ Pod 1  │ │ Pod 2  │ │ Pod 3  │   │                     │
│  │  │ 10.128 │ │ 10.128 │ │ 10.128 │   │                     │
│  │  │ .2.10  │ │ .2.11  │ │ .2.12  │   │                     │
│  │  └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘   │                     │
│  │  All pods can reach all other pods    │                     │
│  │  by default (unless NetworkPolicy)    │                     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                     │
│                                                                │
│  Service Types:                                                │
│  • ClusterIP: Internal only (default, stable IP)               │
│  • NodePort: Exposes on each Node's IP at a static port        │
│  • LoadBalancer: Provisions cloud load balancer (AWS ELB, etc) │
│  • ExternalName: DNS CNAME alias (maps to external service)    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

7.2 Routes — OpenShift's Ingress Superpower

A Route is OpenShift's native way to expose services to the outside world. It's more powerful than Kubernetes Ingress — Routes natively handle TLS termination, path-based routing, load balancing, and even A/B testing (via weighted routing). The HAProxy-based Router runs as pods in openshift-ingress and watches all Routes across the entire cluster.

🛣️ How Routes Work — HAProxy Router Internals
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🛣️ ROUTE — OPENSHIFT'S INGRESS SUPERPOWER              │
│                                                                     │
│  🌐 External Traffic                                                │
│  https://anihpj.apps.cluster.example.com                           │
│       │                                                             │
│       │ DNS: *.apps.cluster.example.com → Router's external IP     │
│       ▼                                                             │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  🔒 HAProxy ROUTER (Runs as pods in openshift-ingress)        │  │
│  │                                                                │  │
│  │  Step 1: Match hostname → "anihpj.apps.cluster.example.com"  │  │
│  │  Step 2: Match path → "/" or "/api/*" or "/admin/*"         │  │
│  │  Step 3: TLS termination:                                     │  │
│  │    • EDGE: Decrypt TLS → send HTTP to pod                     │  │
│  │    • PASSTHROUGH: Pass TLS through → pod handles it           │  │
│  │    • RE-ENCRYPT: Decrypt → re-encrypt for pod                 │  │
│  │  Step 4: Load balance → pick one healthy pod endpoint         │  │
│  │  Step 5: Forward request to pod IP:port                       │  │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│       │                                                             │
│       │ Route resolves Service name → gets pod endpoints            │
│       ▼                                                             │
│  ┌────────────────┐                                                │
│  │ 📦 Pod (anihpj) │  ← HTTP request received                      │
│  │  10.128.2.15   │  ← Pod sees original Host header               │
│  └────────────────┘                                                │
│                                                                     │
│  Route Features Beyond K8s Ingress:                                │
│  ✅ Built-in TLS (no cert-manager needed for basics)               │
│  ✅ Path-based routing: /api → backend-A, /jobs → backend-B        │
│  ✅ Weighted routing: 90% → v1, 10% → v2 (canary deployments)     │
│  ✅ Sticky sessions (for stateful apps)                            │
│  ✅ Wildcard routes (*.example.com → single Route)                 │
│  ✅ Route annotations for custom timeouts, CORS, rate limiting     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Route TypeTLS Where?What HappensUse Caseanihpj?
EdgeRouter decryptsBrowser→Router (TLS), Router→Pod (HTTP)Most web apps✅ Default
PassthroughPod decryptsBrowser→Router→Pod (TLS end-to-end)Model serving with mTLS🟡 Prod
Re-encryptRouter decrypts+re-encryptsBrowser→Router (TLS1), Router→Pod (TLS2)Different internal/external certs🔴 High Sec
SimpleNo TLSBrowser→Router→Pod (HTTP only)Internal dev only❌ NEVER
Creating Routes — Essential Commands
# Expose a service as a Route (auto-detects service port)
oc expose svc anihpj -n anihpj-ml
# Creates: anihpj.apps.cluster.example.com (Edge by default)

# Create an HTTPS Edge route (most common)
oc create route edge anihpj --service=anihpj -n anihpj-ml

# Create with custom hostname
oc create route edge anihpj \
  --service=anihpj \
  --hostname=jobs.example.com

# Create Passthrough (end-to-end TLS)
oc create route passthrough anihpj-secure \
  --service=anihpj \
  --hostname=secure.anihpj.example.com

# Path-based routing (different paths → different services)
oc create route edge api-route \
  --service=api-backend \
  --path=/api

# List all routes
oc get routes -n anihpj-ml
oc get routes --all-namespaces

# Check route details
oc describe route anihpj -n anihpj-ml

7.3 TLS Certificates — Securing Routes

OpenShift provides a default wildcard certificate (*.apps.cluster.example.com) for Routes. For production, you'll want custom certificates — either uploaded manually or automated via cert-manager with Let's Encrypt.

Hands-On: Create HTTPS Route for anihpj with Custom Certificate
# Step 1: Create TLS secret with your certificate
oc create secret tls anihpj-tls \
  --cert=anihpj.crt \
  --key=anihpj.key \
  -n anihpj-ml

# Step 2: Create Edge Route with custom TLS
oc create route edge anihpj-https \
  --service=anihpj \
  --hostname=anihpj.example.com \
  --key=anihpj.key \
  --cert=anihpj.crt

# Step 3: Verify the route is serving HTTPS
curl -v https://anihpj.example.com
# Should show: TLS 1.3, certificate CN=anihpj.example.com

# Step 4: Create Passthrough route (end-to-end TLS)
oc create route passthrough anihpj-e2e \
  --service=anihpj \
  --hostname=secure.anihpj.example.com
# Passthrough: Router does NOT decrypt — pod handles TLS

7.4 Network Policies — Micro-Segmentation

By default, ALL pods can communicate with ALL other pods across the entire cluster — even across different projects! NetworkPolicies let you restrict this to only approved traffic patterns.

🔒 NetworkPolicy — Securing anihpj Components
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BEFORE NetworkPolicy (Default: EVERYTHING OPEN)                   │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐          │
│  │ anihpj-ml   │────▶│ anihpj-dev  │────▶│ anihpj-prod │          │
│  │  (Pod A)    │◀────│  (Pod B)    │◀────│  (Pod C)    │          │
│  └─────────────┘     └─────────────┘     └─────────────┘          │
│       │                   │                   │                    │
│       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘                    │
│                           │ All pods can talk to all pods!         │
│                           ▼ (even across projects)                 │
│                    ┌─────────────┐                                  │
│                    │  postgres   │                                  │
│                    │  (database) │                                  │
│                    └─────────────┘                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AFTER NetworkPolicy (Only Approved Traffic)                       │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐          │
│  │ anihpj-ml   │────▶│ anihpj-dev  │     │ anihpj-prod │          │
│  │  (Pod A)    │     │  (Pod B)    │     │  (ISOLATED) │          │
│  └──────┬──────┘     └──────┬──────┘     └─────────────┘          │
│         │                   │                                       │
│         │     ALLOWED       │  ALLOWED                              │
│         ▼                   ▼                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐                       │
│  │          postgres (database)             │                       │
│  │  Ingress: from ml-dev namespace ONLY     │                       │
│  │  Egress: none (database doesn't call out)│                       │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘                       │
│                                                                     │
│  Policy: default-deny-all (block everything not explicitly allowed)│
│  Policy: allow-from-ml (allow anihpj-ml → postgres)                 │
│  Policy: allow-from-dev (allow anihpj-dev → postgres)               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Creating NetworkPolicy for anihpj
# Allow only anihpj-ml namespace to reach postgres
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ml-to-postgres
  namespace: postgres-db
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: anihpj-ml
    ports:
    - port: 5432
      protocol: TCP
EOF

7.5 Service Mesh (Istio) — Advanced Networking

OpenShift Service Mesh is based on Istio and adds an entirely new layer of traffic management, security, and observability on top of basic networking. It's optional but powerful for complex microservice and AI architectures.

🕸️ Istio Service Mesh Architecture on OpenShift
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│               🕸️ ISTIO SERVICE MESH ON OPENSHIFT               │
│                                                                │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                     │
│  │  🧠 CONTROL PLANE (istio-system ns)   │                     │
│  │  • istiod — manages all proxies       │                     │
│  │  • Injects Envoy sidecar into pods    │                     │
│  │  • Distributes routing rules          │                     │
│  │  • Manages mTLS certificates          │                     │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                     │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ Configures sidecar proxies via xDS protocol            │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐             │
│  │  📊 DATA PLANE (Your Application Pods)        │             │
│  │                                                │             │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐ │             │
│  │  │ anihpj Pod           │  │  model-server    │ │             │
│  │  │ ┌─────────┐         │  │  ┌─────────────┐ │ │             │
│  │  │ │  Envoy   │◄──mTLS──►│  │ │   Envoy     │ │ │             │
│  │  │ │ Sidecar  │         │  │ │   Sidecar   │ │ │             │
│  │  │ └─────────┘         │  │  └─────────────┘ │ │             │
│  │  │    App Container    │  │   App Container  │ │             │
│  │  └─────────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘ │             │
│  │                                                │             │
│  │  What Envoy gives you:                         │             │
│  │  ✅ mTLS between all services (automatic)      │             │
│  │  ✅ Traffic splitting (canary: 90% v1, 10% v2) │             │
│  │  ✅ Circuit breaking (stop cascading failures)  │             │

│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘             │
│                                                                │

7.7 Route Types Decision Matrix

Choosing the right Route type depends on your TLS requirements. Here's when to use each:

🧭 Route TLS Termination Decision Matrix
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Route Type    │ TLS Where?      │ When to Use          │ anihpj?│
│  ──────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────│
│  Edge          │ Router decrypts │ Public-facing apps   │ ✅ YES │
│                │ (HTTP to pod)   │ that need HTTPS but  │        │
│                │                 │ use HTTP internally  │        │
│  ──────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────│
│  Passthrough   │ Pod decrypts    │ End-to-end TLS       │ 🟡 Prod│
│                │ (TLS through)   │ Router passes TLS    │        │
│                │                 │ straight to pod      │        │
│  ──────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────│
│  Re-encrypt    │ Router decrypts │ Mutual TLS between   │ 🔴 High│
│                │ + re-encrypts   │ router and pod       │  Sec   │
│                │ (TLS to pod)    │ (different certs)    │        │
│  ──────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────────┼────────│
│  Simple        │ No TLS          │ Internal dev only    │ ❌ NO  │
│                │ (HTTP only)     │ NEVER for production │        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚡ Quick Decision: Which Route Type?

Edge — you want HTTPS but your app doesn't handle TLS (this is 80% of cases). Passthrough — your app handles its own TLS and you need end-to-end encryption (model serving endpoints). Re-encrypt — you want different certificates for external vs internal traffic (enterprise security policies).

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 7

Core tasks: Create Routes (edge/passthrough/re-encrypt), expose services, configure NetworkPolicy. Speed tip: oc expose svc/name creates a Route instantly. Gotcha: Route hostname auto-generated unless you specify --hostname. Model serving endpoints need passthrough for end-to-end TLS.

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 7

Core tasks: Create Routes (edge/passthrough/re-encrypt), expose services. Speed tip: oc expose svc/name creates a Route instantly. Gotcha: Model serving endpoints need passthrough for end-to-end TLS.

📝 Chapter 7 Practice Questions

Q1
How to create TLS-secured Route?
Click
✅

oc create route edge anihpj --service=anihpj

📖 EXPLANATION

Edge termination means the HAProxy Router handles TLS → decrypts → forwards HTTP to your pod. This is the simplest TLS setup — your pod doesn't need TLS configured. The router uses the cluster's default wildcard certificate (*.apps.cluster.example.com). For custom certs: oc create route edge --service=anihpj --key=priv.key --cert=cert.pem. EX267: Edge routes are the most commonly tested TLS type.

Q2
Default pod-to-pod communication across projects?
Click
✅

ALL pods can talk to ALL pods — unless NetworkPolicy restricts.

📖 EXPLANATION

OpenShift's OVN-Kubernetes SDN creates a flat network — every pod gets a unique IP from 10.128.0.0/14. By default, there are NO firewall rules between pods. Any pod in `project-a` can reach any pod in `project-b` by IP. This is why NetworkPolicy is critical for multi-tenant AI platforms — without it, team A could access team B's model server. Use NetworkPolicy with podSelector and ingress/egress rules to isolate DS projects.

Q3
Which Route type keeps TLS encrypted end-to-end through the router?
Click
✅

Passthrough — the router does NOT decrypt; it passes the TLS connection directly to the pod.

📖 EXPLANATION

Passthrough uses SNI (Server Name Indication) to route TLS traffic without decrypting it. The router reads the TLS ClientHello to determine the destination, then forwards the encrypted stream. Use when: 1) Pod handles its own TLS termination. 2) You need end-to-end encryption with no router in the trust chain. 3) Using mutual TLS (mTLS). Trade-off: router can't do path-based routing or inject headers — it's purely a TCP proxy.

Q4
How does an Edge Route differ from a Re-encrypt Route?
Click
✅

Edge: Browser→Router (TLS), Router→Pod (HTTP). Re-encrypt: Browser→Router (TLS cert A), Router→Pod (TLS cert B). Re-encrypt uses DIFFERENT certs — the internal connection is also encrypted.

📖 EXPLANATION

Re-encrypt provides defense-in-depth — even if an attacker compromises the cluster network, traffic between router and pod is encrypted. The router uses one certificate for external clients and re-encrypts with the pod's certificate for internal. Use for production AI model serving where data in transit must be protected at all hops. The pod's certificate can be auto-provisioned by service-ca.

Q5
What service type for internal microservice-to-model-server communication?
Click
✅

ClusterIP — internal-only, stable virtual IP from the service network (172.30.0.0/16). This is the default and correct choice for pod-to-pod communication within the cluster.

📖 EXPLANATION

ClusterIP creates a virtual IP (VIP) backed by iptables/OVN rules — traffic is load-balanced across all pods matching the selector. The service name also creates a DNS entry: anihpj-inference.anihpj-prod.svc.cluster.local. For anihpj: Django uses postgres.anihpj-prod.svc.cluster.local:5432 to reach PostgreSQL. No Route needed — this is purely internal. The service network (172.30.0.0/16) is separate from the pod network (10.128.0.0/14).

Q6
How do you restrict model endpoint access with NetworkPolicy?
Click
✅

Create NetworkPolicy with podSelector matching the model pod, ingress from only the frontend namespace. Default-deny all other traffic.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: model-endpoint-access, namespace: anihpj-ml }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: anihpj-classifier } }
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { name: anihpj-frontend } }
    ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
Q7
How do you expose a model endpoint externally with a custom hostname?
Click
✅

oc create route edge classifier --service=anihpj-classifier --hostname=ml.anihpj.com. DNS must point to the router's external IP.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc create route edge classifier \
  --service=anihpj-classifier \
  --hostname=ml.anihpj.com \
  --port=8080
# Verify: curl https://ml.anihpj.com/v1/models/classifier:predict
# DNS: ml.anihpj.com → router canonical hostname (CNAME) or IP (A record)
Q8
How does canary routing work with OpenShift Routes?
Click
✅

Route supports multiple backends with weights. Set 90% to v1 service, 10% to v2 service. Monitor, then promote to 100% v2.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc set route-backends classifier \
  anihpj-classifier-v1=90 anihpj-classifier-v2=10
# Route auto-load-balances: 90% → v1, 10% → v2
# Monitor v2 errors → if OK: oc set route-backends classifier v2=100
Q9
How does internal DNS work for services in OpenShift?
Click
✅

Every Service gets a DNS A record: svc-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Pods use this instead of IPs. CoreDNS handles resolution.

📖 EXPLANATION
# DNS hierarchy:
anihpj-classifier.anihpj-ml.svc.cluster.local → 172.30.15.100 (ClusterIP)
# Resolves from any pod in any namespace
# Short form (same namespace): anihpj-classifier
# Cross-namespace: anihpj-classifier.anihpj-ml.svc
Q10
How do you expose multiple ports on a single service?
Click
✅

Define multiple ports in the Service spec with unique names. Common for model serving: REST (8080) + gRPC (9000) + metrics (8000).

📖 EXPLANATION
spec:
  ports:
  - { name: rest, protocol: TCP, port: 8080, targetPort: 8080 }
  - { name: grpc, protocol: TCP, port: 9000, targetPort: 9000 }
  - { name: metrics, protocol: TCP, port: 8000, targetPort: 8000 }
  selector: { app: anihpj-classifier }

Chapter 8: Storage for AI Workloads🟡 Intermediate · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 8: Storage — Persistent Data for AI/ML Workloads

AI workloads need storage: notebooks need PVCs for workspaces, pipelines need S3 for artifacts, model serving needs model storage. This chapter covers PVs, PVCs, StorageClasses, and S3-compatible object storage with NooBaa.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1 hour💾 Storage

8.1 Storage Fundamentals

In Kubernetes/OpenShift, storage is abstracted away from pods. When a pod is deleted, its local files are GONE. For persistent data (databases, ML models, notebook workspaces), you use Persistent Volumes.

💾 Storage Flow — PVC → StorageClass → PV → Pod Mount
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              💾 STORAGE PROVISIONING FLOW                       │
│                                                                │
│  👤 User creates PVC:                                          │
│     oc create pvc notebook-workspace --size=50Gi              │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ 1. PVC is created in namespace (status: Pending)       │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐         │
│  │  📋 PERSISTENT VOLUME CLAIM (PVC)                  │         │
│  │  • Name: notebook-workspace                        │         │
│  │  • Size: 50Gi                                      │         │
│  │  • Access: ReadWriteOnce                           │         │
│  │  • StorageClass: gp3 (default)                     │         │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ 2. StorageClass provisions the volume                  │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐         │
│  │  🏭 STORAGE CLASS (Provisioner)                    │         │
│  │  • gp3 → AWS EBS (kubernetes.io/aws-ebs)          │         │
│  │  • standard → GCE PD                               │         │
│  │  • managed-premium → Azure Disk                    │         │
│  │  • ocs-storage → OpenShift Data Foundation (Ceph) │         │
│  │  • noobaa → S3 object storage                      │         │
│  │                                                     │         │
│  │  3. Storage provisioner creates actual volume       │         │
│  │  (e.g., AWS creates 50Gi EBS volume)               │         │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ 4. PV is created and Bound to PVC                      │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐         │
│  │  💿 PERSISTENT VOLUME (PV)                         │         │
│  │  • Name: pvc-abc123 (auto-generated)               │         │
│  │  • Capacity: 50Gi                                  │         │
│  │  • Reclaim: Delete (default) / Retain              │         │
│  │  • Status: Bound → notebook-workspace              │         │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
│       │                                                        │
│       │ 5. Pod references PVC, volume mounted                  │
│       ▼                                                        │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐         │
│  │  📦 POD (Notebook / anihpj)                        │         │
│  │  • Mount: /opt/app-root/src (notebook workspace)  │         │
│  │  • Mount: /data (datasets)                        │         │
│  │  • Data persists even if pod is deleted!          │         │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

8.2 AI/ML Storage Options — What to Use When

AI workloads have diverse storage needs. A single ML pipeline might use all three storage types: Block for the notebook workspace, File for shared training datasets, and Object/S3 for pipeline artifacts and final model storage. Understanding when to use each is critical for EX267.

💾 Three Storage Types — How They Fit Into an AI Pipeline
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         💾 THREE STORAGE TYPES IN AN AI/ML PIPELINE                │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  1️⃣ BLOCK STORAGE (RWO — ReadWriteOnce)                       │ │
│  │  ┌──────────┐                                                 │ │
│  │  │ Notebook  │──▶ /opt/app-root/src (50Gi PVC)                │ │
│  │  │   Pod     │    Personal workspace, code, small datasets     │ │
│  │  └──────────┘                                                 │ │
│  │  Examples: AWS EBS, GCE PD, Azure Disk, vSphere Disk          │ │
│  │  Speed: ⚡ FASTEST (low latency, high IOPS)                    │ │
│  │  Limitation: ONE pod can mount at a time (RWO)                │ │
│  │  AI Use: Notebook workspaces, database storage                │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  2️⃣ FILE STORAGE (RWX — ReadWriteMany)                        │ │
│  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐                    │ │
│  │  │ Notebook │  │ Training │  │  Model   │                     │ │
│  │  │  Pod A   │  │  Pod B   │  │ Eval Pod │                     │ │
│  │  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘                    │ │
│  │       └──────────────┼──────────────┘                          │ │
│  │                      │ ALL mount /shared-data (200Gi PVC)     │ │
│  │                      ▼                                         │ │
│  │               ┌────────────┐                                   │ │
│  │               │ NFS / EFS  │  Shared filesystem                │ │
│  │               └────────────┘                                   │ │
│  │  Examples: NFS, AWS EFS, GlusterFS, ODF (CephFS)              │ │
│  │  Speed: 🟡 MEDIUM (network-attached adds some latency)        │ │
│  │  Advantage: MULTIPLE pods mount simultaneously                │ │
│  │  AI Use: Shared training datasets, distributed training       │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  3️⃣ OBJECT STORAGE (S3 API — Unlimited Scale)                 │ │
│  │  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐              │ │
│  │  │ Pipeline │────▶│   S3     │◀────│  Model   │              │ │
│  │  │  Step 1  │ PUT │  Bucket  │ GET │  Serving │              │ │
│  │  └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘              │ │
│  │                         │                                      │ │
│  │                         │ HTTP/HTTPS (S3 API — boto3, awscli) │ │
│  │                         ▼                                      │ │
│  │               ┌──────────────────┐                             │ │
│  │               │ NooBaa / MinIO   │  S3-compatible endpoint     │ │
│  │               │ / AWS S3         │                             │ │
│  │               └──────────────────┘                             │ │
│  │  Examples: NooBaa (built-in), MinIO, AWS S3, Ceph RGW         │ │
│  │  Speed: 📊 SCALABLE (throughput over latency)                 │ │
│  │  Advantage: Unlimited scale, accessible via HTTP/S3 API       │ │
│  │  AI Use: Pipeline artifacts, trained models, data versioning  │ │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
TypeExamplesSpeedSharingAccess ModeAI Use
BlockAWS EBS, GCE PD, Azure Disk⚡ FastestSingle-nodeRWONotebook PVCs, databases
FileNFS, AWS EFS, GlusterFS, ODF🟡 MediumMulti-nodeRWXShared datasets, distributed training
ObjectNooBaa, MinIO, AWS S3, Ceph RGW📊 ScalableUnlimited (HTTP)N/A (S3 API)Pipeline artifacts, model storage
🧠 How to Choose: The AI Storage Decision Framework

"Does it need a POSIX filesystem?" (files, directories, permissions like a normal disk)

  • YES, single user → Block (RWO) — notebook workspace, database
  • YES, multiple users → File (RWX) — shared datasets, distributed training
  • NO, accessed via API → Object (S3) — pipeline artifacts, model files

"Is it the final model artifact?" → Object (S3) — version it like code, serve it via S3 endpoint or OCI container registry.

"Does it need to survive pod restarts?" → Any PVC or S3 — NOT emptyDir (ephemeral), NOT container filesystem (lost on restart).

8.3 PVCs for Notebooks — Hands-On

Jupyter notebooks in OpenShift AI need persistent storage for their workspace. Without a PVC, all your notebooks and data disappear when the pod restarts!

Hands-On: Create PVCs for anihpj ML Workspace
# Create PVC for notebook workspace (personal notebooks)
oc create pvc notebook-workspace \
  --size=50Gi \
  --access-mode=ReadWriteOnce \
  -n anihpj-ml

# Create PVC for shared datasets (larger, shared)
oc create pvc shared-datasets \
  --size=200Gi \
  --access-mode=ReadWriteMany \
  --storage-class=nfs-storage \
  -n anihpj-ml

# Create PVC for model artifacts
oc create pvc model-artifacts \
  --size=100Gi \
  --access-mode=ReadWriteMany \
  -n anihpj-ml

# Verify PVCs are bound
oc get pvc -n anihpj-ml
# Look for STATUS: Bound (if Pending → StorageClass issue!)

# Sizing Guidelines for ML workloads:
# 20Gi  = Small ML (tabular data, scikit-learn)
# 50Gi  = Medium ML (image datasets, notebooks)
# 200Gi+ = Large ML (video, NLP, large datasets)
# 500Gi+ = LLM training (terabytes of text data)

8.4 NooBaa S3 Object Storage — Built-in S3 for OpenShift

NooBaa (pronounced "no-bah") is OpenShift's built-in S3-compatible object storage. It's deployed via an operator and provides an S3 API that works with any S3-compatible tool (boto3, awscli, s3cmd, MinIO client).

NooBaa Configuration Walkthrough for anihpj Training Data
# Step 1: Install NooBaa Operator (from OperatorHub)
# Go to: Operators → OperatorHub → Search "NooBaa" → Install

# Step 2: Create NooBaa instance
oc create -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: noobaa.io/v1
kind: NooBaa
metadata:
  name: noobaa
  namespace: openshift-storage
spec: {}
EOF

# Step 3: Wait for NooBaa to be ready
oc get noobaa -n openshift-storage -w

# Step 4: Create an ObjectBucketClaim (like a PVC, but for S3)
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: objectbucket.io/v1alpha1
kind: ObjectBucketClaim
metadata:
  name: anihpj-training-data
  namespace: anihpj-ml
spec:
  generateBucketName: anihpj-training-
  storageClassName: openshift-storage.noobaa.io
EOF

# Step 5: Get S3 credentials (auto-created as Secret + ConfigMap)
oc get secret anihpj-training-data -n anihpj-ml -o jsonpath='{.data.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}' | base64 -d
oc get secret anihpj-training-data -n anihpj-ml -o jsonpath='{.data.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}' | base64 -d

# Step 6: Use in Python (boto3) to access training data
# The S3 endpoint is: https://s3.openshift-storage.svc
# Works exactly like AWS S3!
🗂️ When to Use NooBaa vs PVC

Use NooBaa (S3): Pipeline artifacts, model files, training datasets shared across teams, anything that needs S3 API compatibility. Use PVC: Notebook workspaces (personal), databases, anything that needs a filesystem. NooBaa = object storage (PUT/GET objects), PVC = block/filesystem storage (mount as directory).

8.5 Storage Best Practices for Production AI

✅ 10 Storage Rules for AI Workloads

  1. Data locality: Keep data near compute (same availability zone). Cross-AZ data transfer = latency + $$$
  2. storage = dataset × 3: Plan capacity for raw data + processed data + trained models. A 50Gi dataset needs ~150Gi.
  3. Notebook workspace = PVC (RWO): Each notebook gets its own workspace PVC. Don't share notebook workspaces.
  4. Shared datasets = PVC (RWX) or S3: Use ReadWriteMany (NFS/EFS) or S3 for data accessed by multiple pods.
  5. Pipeline artifacts = S3 (NooBaa): Pipelines pass data between steps via S3. Never use local pod storage.
  6. Model storage = S3 or OCI registry: Trained models are artifacts — version them like code. Store in S3 buckets or OCI container registry.
  7. Cache frequently accessed datasets: Use local SSD storage for hot data. Offload cold data to S3.
  8. Backup PVCs regularly: Use CSI snapshots or Velero for backup. PVCs are NOT backed up by default.
  9. Set Reclaim Policy: Retain: Change from default Delete to Retain for production PVCs — prevents accidental data loss.
  10. Monitor storage usage: Use oc describe pvc and Prometheus alerts. Running out of storage = pod eviction.
Access ModeAbbreviationConcurrencyTypical Use
ReadWriteOnceRWOSingle node mounts as read/writeNotebook workspaces
ReadWriteManyRWXMany nodes mount as read/writeShared datasets, NFS
ReadOnlyManyROXMany nodes mount as read-onlyReference data, model files
ReadWriteOncePodRWOPSingle pod mounts as read/writeKubernetes 1.22+ CSI
🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 8

Core tasks: Create PVCs for notebooks, configure Data Connections (S3 secrets), understand RWO vs RWX. Speed tip: oc create pvc name --size=50Gi — one command, done. Gotcha: PVC status Pending = no default StorageClass or no available capacity. Verify with oc get sc.

📝 Chapter 8 Practice Questions

Q1
What storage type is best for pipeline artifacts?
Click
✅

Object storage (S3/NooBaa) — scalable, accessible from any pod.

📖 EXPLANATION

Object storage (S3 API) is ideal for ML artifacts because: 1) Accessible from any pod in any project (no node affinity). 2) Scales to petabytes without manual resizing. 3) Built-in versioning. 4) Standard API — works with boto3, s3fs, minio client. On OpenShift AI, Data Connections wire S3 credentials to notebooks and pipelines. NooBaa (built-in) provides S3-compatible storage using the cluster's PVs. For anihpj: train models store output in s3://anihpj-models/job-classifier/v2/model.joblib.

Q2
How do you create a 50Gi PVC for a notebook?
Click
✅

oc create pvc notebook-workspace --size=50Gi --access-mode=ReadWriteOnce

📖 EXPLANATION

This creates a PVC that the StorageClass provisioner fulfills by creating a PV (e.g., 50GB EBS volume on AWS, or Ceph RBD on-prem). The PVC remains bound even if the pod is deleted — your data persists. For EX267: always verify PVC status with oc get pvc before launching notebooks. If PVC is Pending, check: 1) Is there a default StorageClass? 2) Does the StorageClass support the requested size? 3) Is there available capacity?

Q3
What's the difference between RWO, RWX, and ROX access modes?
Click
✅

RWO=ReadWriteOnce (single node), RWX=ReadWriteMany (multiple nodes, shared), ROX=ReadOnlyMany. Notebooks use RWO. Shared datasets need RWX.

📖 EXPLANATION

RWO — volume can only be mounted by pods on a SINGLE node. Most block storage (EBS, GCE PD). OK for notebooks (single pod). RWX — volume can be mounted by pods on MULTIPLE nodes simultaneously. Requires shared filesystem (NFS, CephFS, GlusterFS). Use for shared datasets accessed by multiple training jobs. ROX — read-only across nodes. Use for reference datasets that don't change. EX267 tip: if a notebook can't mount a PVC, check the access mode — RWO can't be shared across nodes.

Q4
What happens to a PVC when the pod using it is deleted?
Click
✅

Nothing! PVCs have an independent lifecycle from pods. Your data persists. You must explicitly delete the PVC to free storage.

📖 EXPLANATION

PVCs and Pods have independent lifecycles. When a notebook pod is deleted (e.g., idle culling), the PVC remains bound with ALL data intact. When the notebook is restarted, it reconnects to the same PVC — your work is still there. This is why OpenShift AI workbenches survive pod restarts. To free storage: you must explicitly oc delete pvc <name>. The reclaim policy then determines what happens to the underlying PV (Delete = destroy, Retain = keep for manual recovery).

Q5
What's the default PV reclaim policy and why change it for production?
Click
✅

Default is Delete — deleting PVC also deletes PV and underlying cloud storage. For production, use Retain to prevent accidental data loss.

📖 EXPLANATION

Reclaim policies: Delete (default) = PVC delete → PV + cloud disk deleted immediately. Retain = PVC delete → PV preserved, but requires manual admin cleanup. Recycle = PV wiped (rm -rf) and made available (deprecated). For production AI workloads: ALWAYS set persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain on StorageClass. This prevents accidental deletion of training data and model checkpoints if someone runs oc delete pvc --all. Use CSI snapshots as an additional safety layer.

Q6
What is NooBaa and how does it provide S3 for AI workloads?
Click
✅

NooBaa is OpenShift's built-in object storage operator. Creates S3-compatible buckets backed by cluster PVs. Auto-installed with OpenShift Data Foundation.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: noobaa.io/v1alpha1
kind: NooBaa
metadata: { name: noobaa, namespace: openshift-storage }
# Creates S3 endpoint: https://s3.openshift-storage.svc
# Use with Data Connection → auto-injected into notebooks/pipelines
Q7
How do StorageClasses enable dynamic volume provisioning?
Click
✅

StorageClass defines the provisioner (EBS, Ceph, etc.) and parameters. When a PVC references it, the provisioner auto-creates a PV. No manual PV creation needed.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata: { name: fast-ssd, annotations: { storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true" } }
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters: { type: gp3, iopsPerGB: "10" }
reclaimPolicy: Retain
# PVC referencing this SC → AWS EBS gp3 volume auto-created
Q8
How do CSI volume snapshots protect ML data?
Click
✅

CSI snapshots create point-in-time copies of PVCs at the storage driver level. Fast, storage-efficient. Restore to new PVC for recovery or cloning.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshot
metadata: { name: notebook-snap-20250609 }
spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: csi-snapshotclass
  source: { persistentVolumeClaimName: notebook-workspace }
# Restore: oc create pvc restore-pvc --dataSource name=notebook-snap-20250609
Q9
How do you mount a ConfigMap or Secret as a file in a pod?
Click
✅

Use volumes + volumeMounts. ConfigMaps mount as individual files (keys = filenames). Secrets mount similarly but with tmpfs (in-memory).

📖 EXPLANATION
volumes:
- name: model-config
  configMap: { name: classifier-config }
- name: s3-creds
  secret: { secretName: aws-connection-anihpj }
volumeMounts:
- { name: model-config, mountPath: /etc/config }
- { name: s3-creds, mountPath: /etc/creds, readOnly: true }
Q10
What storage strategy should anihpj use for its ML workflow?
Click
✅

RWO PVC for notebooks (50Gi), S3 (NooBaa) for pipeline artifacts/datasets/models, RWX PVC for shared reference data, CSI snapshots for backups.

📖 EXPLANATION
Notebook workspace: PVC RWO 50Gi (per data scientist)
Pipeline artifacts: S3 NooBaa (shared, scalable)
Trained models: S3 NooBaa → Model Registry → KServe
Shared datasets: PVC RWX 500Gi (all team members)
Backups: CSI snapshots (daily) + S3 replication (continuous)

📋 Part 2 Summary — Installation & Configuration
