9.1 Understanding Deployments and DeploymentConfigs

OpenShift supports BOTH Kubernetes-native Deployments and OpenShift-specific DeploymentConfigs. The key difference: DeploymentConfigs add triggers, lifecycle hooks, and rollback capabilities that vanilla Deployments lack.

FeatureKubernetes DeploymentOpenShift DeploymentConfig
Rolling update✅ (maxSurge/maxUnavailable)✅ + Custom strategy params
Triggers❌ Manual / external only✅ Image change + Config change auto-triggers
Lifecycle Hooks❌ Pod-level hooks only✅ Pre, Mid, Post deployment hooks
Rollbackkubectl rollout undooc rollback — full history + auto-revert
Recreate Strategy✅ Kill all → Create new✅ + Custom strategy support
Custom Strategy❌✅ Write your own deployment logic
Recommended forStateless apps, new projectsOpenShift-native apps, CI/CD pipelines, anihpj
🔄 Deployment Strategies — Rolling vs Recreate
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🔄 DEPLOYMENT STRATEGIES                              │
│                                                                     │
│  ROLLING (Default — Zero Downtime):                                │
│  ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐  ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐   │
│  │ v1 ✅ │→│ v1 ✅ │→│ v1 ✅ │→│ v2 🆕│→│ v2 ✅ │→│ v2 ✅ │   │
│  │ v1 ✅ │ │ v2 🆕│ │ v2 ✅ │ │ v2 ✅ │ │       │ │       │   │
│  │ v1 ✅ │ │ v1 ✅ │ │ v2 🆕│ │ v2 ✅ │ │       │ │       │   │
│  └───────┘ └───────┘ └───────┘  └───────┘ └───────┘ └───────┘   │
│  Old pods gradually replaced. Traffic always served.              │
│                                                                     │
│  RECREATE (Downtime — Stateful Apps):                              │
│  ┌───────┐     ┌───────┐     ┌───────┐                            │
│  │ v1 ❌ │ ──▶ │       │ ──▶ │ v2 ✅ │                            │
│  │ v1 ❌ │     │       │     │ v2 ✅ │                            │
│  │ v1 ❌ │     │  💀   │     │ v2 ✅ │  ← ALL old killed first    │
│  └───────┘     └───────┘     └───────┘                            │
│  All old pods killed. Then new pods created. DOWNTIME!            │
│                                                                     │
│  CUSTOM: You write the deployment logic (e.g., canary, blue-green)│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

9.2 Deploying anihpj — The Complete Walkthrough 🎯

This is the most important hands-on section in Part 3. Follow these 6 steps to deploy the full anihpj stack — Django app + PostgreSQL database — on OpenShift:

│  │  │ Gunicorn │ │ Gunicorn │ │ Gunicorn │         │             │
│  │  │ :8080    │ │ :8080    │ │ :8080    │         │             │
│  │  └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘         │             │
│  │       └──────────────┼──────────────┘              │             │

│  │  │  :5432   │                                     │             │

Step-by-Step: Deploy anihpj on OpenShift
# ===== STEP 1: Create Project =====
oc new-project anihpj-prod --display-name="anihpj Production"

# ===== STEP 2: Deploy PostgreSQL (with persistent storage) =====
oc new-app postgresql-persistent \
  -p DATABASE_SERVICE_NAME=anihpj-db \
  -p POSTGRESQL_USER=anihpj \
  -p POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD=SecurePass123! \
  -p POSTGRESQL_DATABASE=anihpj \
  -p VOLUME_CAPACITY=50Gi
# Wait for postgres to be ready
oc wait --for=condition=Available deploy/anihpj-db --timeout=120s

# ===== STEP 3: Create ConfigMap for Django settings =====
oc create configmap django-settings \
  --from-literal=DEBUG=False \
  --from-literal=ALLOWED_HOSTS=anihpj.apps.cluster.example.com \
  --from-literal=DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings

# ===== STEP 4: Create Secret for Database credentials =====
oc create secret generic db-credentials \
  --from-literal=DATABASE_URL=postgresql://anihpj:SecurePass123!@anihpj-db:5432/anihpj \
  --from-literal=SECRET_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32)

# ===== STEP 5: Deploy the Django app =====
oc new-app https://github.com/anihs/anihpj.git \
  --name=anihpj \
  --strategy=python \
  -e DATABASE_URL=postgresql://anihpj:SecurePass123!@anihpj-db:5432/anihpj

# Mount ConfigMap as environment variables
oc set env deploy/anihpj --from=configmap/django-settings

# ===== STEP 6: Expose via HTTPS Route =====
oc create route edge anihpj --service=anihpj

# ===== VERIFY EVERYTHING =====
oc status                    # Dashboard overview
oc get pods                  # All pods Running?
oc get routes                # Route created with TLS?
oc get svc,pvc,configmap,secret  # All resources present?
curl -k https://$(oc get route anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.host}')/jobs/
🧠 What Just Happened — Step by Step

Step 2: oc new-app postgresql-persistent auto-created: Deployment, Service, PVC (50Gi), and Secret (with generated password). That's 4 resources from ONE command. Step 5: oc new-app detected Python source code, used the Python S2I builder, built the image, pushed it to the internal registry, and created a DeploymentConfig + Service + ImageStream — all automatically. This is the magic of OpenShift.

Quick Verification: oc status shows a dashboard-like overview in your terminal — which services are running, routes exposed, build status, and any warnings. oc get pods,svc,route,pvc lists all resources. curl -k https://$(oc get route anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.host}')/jobs/ does a live smoke test.

9.3 Source-to-Image (S2I) — Build Without a Dockerfile

S2I is OpenShift's secret weapon for building container images. Instead of writing a Dockerfile, you just point S2I at your source code — it detects the language, injects a builder image, and produces a runnable container. For anihpj (Python/Django), S2I is the recommended approach.

🏭 How S2I Works — Source Code → Runnable Image
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  🏭 S2I BUILD PROCESS                              │
│                                                                     │
│  Step 1:          Step 2:           Step 3:         Step 4:        │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐   │
│  │ Builder  │    │ Inject   │     │ Assemble │     │ Commit   │   │
│  │ Image    │ +  │ Source   │ →   │ & Build  │ →   │ Image    │   │
│  │ (Python) │    │ Code     │     │          │     │          │   │
│  └──────────┘    └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘   │
│       │              │                 │                 │          │
│       ▼              ▼                 ▼                 ▼          │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Python 3.11    anihpj/         pip install -r           │    │
│  │  + Gunicorn     manage.py       requirements.txt         │    │
│  │  + pip          models.py       collectstatic            │    │
│  │  + virtualenv   views.py        set up gunicorn          │    │
│  │                 urls.py                                  │    │
│  │  ~800MB         ~50KB           ~2 minutes               │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                     │
│  Final Image: Python 3.11 + your code + all deps = ~350MB          │
│  Entrypoint: gunicorn anihpj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8080│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
S2I Commands — Build and Deploy anihpj from Source
# Create a BuildConfig using S2I (auto-detects Python)
oc new-build python:3.11~https://github.com/anihs/anihpj.git \
  --name=anihpj

# Start the build
oc start-build anihpj --follow
# Watch logs: pip install → collectstatic → image commit → push

# Check build status
oc get builds
oc logs build/anihpj-1

# Deploy from the built image
oc new-app anihpj --name=anihpj

# Alternative: One command for everything
oc new-app python:3.11~https://github.com/anihs/anihpj.git \
  --name=anihpj
# This does: new-build + start-build + new-app — ALL in one!

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "Why S2I Instead of a Dockerfile?"

You already have a Dockerfile for anihpj — why use S2I? S2I builder images are maintained by Red Hat — they include security patches, best-practice configurations, and are optimized for OpenShift. When a critical Python vulnerability is patched, Red Hat updates the builder image, and you just rebuild — no Dockerfile changes needed.

When to use Dockerfile instead: You have custom system dependencies (like CUDA for GPU, or complex C libraries), or you need very specific build logic that S2I can't express. For most Python/Django apps, S2I is faster and safer.

Customizing S2I: You can add .s2i/bin/assemble (custom build script) and .s2i/bin/run (custom startup script) in your repo. S2I runs these instead of the default — giving you full control while keeping the builder image maintained by Red Hat.

9.4 Environment Variables, ConfigMaps, and Secrets

Never hardcode configuration in your code or Dockerfile. OpenShift provides three ways to inject configuration into pods:

MethodWhat It HoldsEncrypted?Size LimitUse For
Environment VariablesKey=value pairs❌ Plain text in pod specN/ASimple settings
ConfigMapKey=value, files, JSON/YAML❌ Plain text (base64 in etcd)1MBApp config, Django settings
SecretKey=value, files, TLS certs✅ etcd encryption + RBAC1MBPasswords, API keys, tokens
Hands-On: Configure anihpj with ConfigMap + Secret
# === CONFIGMAP: Non-sensitive Django settings ===
oc create configmap django-config \
  --from-literal=DEBUG=False \
  --from-literal=ALLOWED_HOSTS=anihpj.apps.cluster.example.com,localhost \
  --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=INFO \
  --from-literal=WORKERS=4 \
  --from-file=settings_overrides.py

# Mount ConfigMap as environment variables
oc set env deploy/anihpj --from=configmap/django-config

# Mount ConfigMap as files (for settings_overrides.py)
oc set volume deploy/anihpj \
  --add -t configmap -m /app/anihpj/overrides \
  --name django-overrides \
  --configmap-name=django-config

# === SECRET: Database credentials (BASE64 ≠ ENCRYPTED!) ===
oc create secret generic db-secret \
  --from-literal=DATABASE_URL='postgresql://anihpj:SecurePass123!@anihpj-db:5432/anihpj' \
  --from-literal=SECRET_KEY='django-insecure-abc123xyz' \
  --from-literal=EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD='smtp-password'

# Mount Secret as environment variables
oc set env deploy/anihpj --from=secret/db-secret

# === VERIFY ===
oc get configmap django-config -o yaml
oc get secret db-secret -o yaml   # Values are base64-encoded
oc set env deploy/anihpj --list   # See all env vars on deployment
⚠️ Secrets Are Base64, NOT Encrypted!

Kubernetes Secrets are stored as base64-encoded strings in etcd — this is encoding, not encryption. Anyone with oc get secret -o yaml access can decode them. For production: use etcd encryption at rest, restrict RBAC to secrets, and consider external secret stores like HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager via the External Secrets Operator.

9.5 Resource Management — Requests, Limits, and Quotas

OpenShift lets you control exactly how much CPU and memory each pod can use. This prevents a single misbehaving pod from starving other workloads — critical in shared clusters.

📊 Requests vs Limits — The Gas Pedal Analogy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              📊 CPU/MEMORY REQUESTS vs LIMITS                       │
│                                                                     │
│  REQUEST = Guaranteed Minimum (Your reservation)                   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐         │
│  │  Pod requests 500m CPU (0.5 core)                    │         │
│  │  Scheduler RESERVES 500m on the node                 │         │
│  │  Pod ALWAYS gets at least 500m                       │         │
│  │  If node has no 500m free → pod stays Pending        │         │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
│                                                                     │
│  LIMIT = Hard Ceiling (Cannot exceed)                               │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐         │
│  │  Pod limit 1000m CPU (1 core)                        │         │
│  │  Pod can burst up to 1000m if available              │         │
│  │  If pod exceeds 1000m → CPU THROTTLED (slowed)       │         │
│  │  If pod exceeds memory limit → OOMKilled (terminated)│         │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
│                                                                     │
│  🚗 Analogy:                                                        │
│  • Request = Your lane on the highway (always available)           │
│  • Limit = Speed governor (can't exceed this)                      │
│  • CPU limit exceeded = Slowed down (throttled)                    │
│  • Memory limit exceeded = Car explodes (OOMKilled) 💥             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
ComponentCPU RequestCPU LimitMemory RequestMemory Limit
anihpj Django250m1000m (1 core)256Mi512Mi
PostgreSQL500m2000m (2 cores)512Mi2Gi
Redis (cache)100m500m128Mi256Mi
Celery Worker250m2000m256Mi1Gi
Setting Resources + Quotas
# Set resource requests/limits on deployment
oc set resources deploy/anihpj \
  --requests=cpu=250m,memory=256Mi \
  --limits=cpu=1000m,memory=512Mi

# Create ResourceQuota for the project (prevents runaway usage)
oc create quota anihpj-quota \
  --hard=cpu=10,memory=20Gi,pods=20,persistentvolumeclaims=10

# Create LimitRange (defaults for pods without explicit resources)
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: anihpj-defaults
spec:
  limits:
  - default: { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
    defaultRequest: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
    type: Container
EOF

# Check current usage vs quota
oc describe quota anihpj-quota

9.6 Health Checks — Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes

Kubernetes doesn't know if your app is actually working — it only knows if the process is running. Probes tell Kubernetes when to restart, when to send traffic, and when to wait for initialization.

🏥 Three Types of Health Probes
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    🏥 KUBERNETES HEALTH PROBES                      │
│                                                                     │
│  STARTUP PROBE (Is it still booting?)                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Pod starts → Startup probe checks every 10s             │    │
│  │  Django migrate runs → takes 30s → probe fails x3        │    │
│  │  "It's still starting — give it time"                    │    │
│  │  PROBE SUCCEEDS → Liveness + Readiness probes take over   │    │
│  │  ❌ If startup probe NEVER succeeds → pod is killed       │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                     │
│  LIVENESS PROBE (Should we restart it?)                            │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Pod running → Liveness probe checks /healthz every 15s  │    │
│  │  App deadlocked → /healthz returns 500                   │    │
│  │  "App is alive but broken → RESTART IT"                  │    │
│  │  Kubelet kills pod → new pod starts                      │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                     │
│  READINESS PROBE (Should it receive traffic?)                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  Pod running → Readiness probe checks /ready every 10s   │    │
│  │  Database connection lost → /ready returns 503           │    │
│  │  "App is alive but can't serve → REMOVE FROM SERVICE"    │    │
│  │  Pod removed from Service endpoints → no traffic          │    │
│  │  Pod stays running (not killed!) — waits for DB to return │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Probe Configuration for anihpj (Django) + PostgreSQL
# === DJANGO PROBES (HTTP) ===
oc set probe deploy/anihpj --liveness \
  --get-url=http://:8080/healthz \
  --initial-delay-seconds=30 \
  --period-seconds=15 \
  --timeout-seconds=5 \
  --failure-threshold=3

oc set probe deploy/anihpj --readiness \
  --get-url=http://:8080/ready \
  --initial-delay-seconds=10 \
  --period-seconds=10 \
  --timeout-seconds=3 \
  --failure-threshold=2

oc set probe deploy/anihpj --startup \
  --get-url=http://:8080/healthz \
  --initial-delay-seconds=0 \
  --period-seconds=10 \
  --failure-threshold=30   # 30 x 10s = 5 min for migrations

# === POSTGRES PROBES (TCP + Command) ===
oc set probe deploy/anihpj-db --liveness \
  --tcp-socket=5432 \
  --initial-delay-seconds=60 \
  --period-seconds=30

oc set probe deploy/anihpj-db --readiness \
  -- /bin/sh -c "pg_isready -U anihpj -d anihpj"

9.7 Scaling Applications — Manual and Automatic

Scaling means running more (or fewer) copies of your application. OpenShift supports manual scaling, CPU/memory-based autoscaling (HPA), and event-driven autoscaling (KEDA).

MethodHow It WorksBest ForExample
Manualoc scale sets exact replicasKnown traffic patternsoc scale deploy/anihpj --replicas=5
HPACPU/Memory triggers scalingVariable web trafficScale 3→10 when CPU > 70%
KEDAEvents trigger scaling (Kafka, Redis, Prometheus)Event-driven AI pipelinesScale Celery workers by queue length
Scaling Commands
# Manual scaling
oc scale deploy/anihpj --replicas=5
oc scale deploy/anihpj --replicas=10  # Job posting season!

# Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (CPU-based)
oc autoscale deploy/anihpj \
  --min=3 --max=10 \
  --cpu-percent=70

# Check HPA status
oc get hpa
oc describe hpa anihpj
# Watch: TARGETS column shows current CPU% / target%

# Pod Disruption Budget (prevents too many pods going down at once)
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: anihpj-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2   # At least 2 pods must always be running
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      deployment: anihpj
EOF
⚡ KEDA — Event-Driven Autoscaling for AI Pipelines

KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) scales pods based on external events — not just CPU/memory. For AI workloads: scale Celery workers by Redis queue length, scale inference pods by Prometheus metrics, or scale pipeline workers by Kafka lag. Install from OperatorHub, create a ScaledObject CR:

# Scale Celery workers by Redis queue length
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: anihpj-celery-scaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: anihpj-celery
  minReplicaCount: 1
  maxReplicaCount: 20
  triggers:
  - type: redis
    metadata:
      address: redis-service:6379
      listName: celery
      listLength: "10"    # Scale up when 10+ tasks queued

9.8 Canary and Blue-Green Deployments

Updating your app without downtime and with the ability to instantly roll back is critical for production AI services. OpenShift Routes support traffic splitting natively.

🔵🟢 Blue-Green vs Canary Deployment Strategies
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  BLUE-GREEN (Instant Switch):                                      │
│  ┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────┐                      │
│  │  🔵 BLUE     │  100%    │  🟢 GREEN    │                      │
│  │  anihpj v1   │  traffic │  anihpj v2   │                      │
│  │  Pods: 3     │─────────▶│  Pods: 3     │                      │
│  └──────────────┘          └──────────────┘                      │
│  Route switches service: anihpj-blue → anihpj-green              │
│  Instant rollback: switch service back                           │
│  Cost: 2x resources during deployment                            │
│                                                                     │
│  CANARY (Gradual Shift):                                           │
│  ┌──────────────┐  90%    ┌──────────────┐                      │
│  │  🔵 v1 (old) │◀────────│              │                      │
│  │  Pods: 9     │         │   ROUTER     │                      │
│  └──────────────┘         │              │                      │
│                           │              │                      │
│  ┌──────────────┐  10%    │              │                      │
│  │  🟡 v2 (new) │────────▶│              │                      │
│  │  Pods: 1     │         └──────────────┘                      │
│  └──────────────┘                                                │
│  Gradually: 10% → 25% → 50% → 75% → 100%                       │
│  Monitor errors at each step → auto-rollback if needed           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Canary Deployment with Route Weighting
# Deploy v2 alongside v1
oc new-app anihpj:v2 --name=anihpj-v2

# Create weighted Route (90% v1, 10% v2)
oc create route edge anihpj-canary \
  --service=anihpj-v1 \
  --weight=90

# Add alternate backend (v2 gets 10%)
oc set route-backend anihpj-canary \
  anihpj-v2 --weight=10

# Gradually increase v2 weight
oc set route-backend anihpj-canary anihpj-v2 --weight=25
oc set route-backend anihpj-canary anihpj-v1 --weight=75

# Gradually increase v2 weight
oc set route-backend anihpj-canary anihpj-v2 --weight=25
oc set route-backend anihpj-canary anihpj-v1 --weight=75

# Check route configuration
oc describe route anihpj-canary
🔄 Rollback Strategies — Getting Back to Safety

DeploymentConfig rollback: oc rollback dc/anihpj reverts to the last successful deployment. OpenShift keeps a full deployment history — use oc rollout history dc/anihpj to see all versions. Route-level rollback: If doing canary with route weights, just set v2 weight to 0: oc set route-backend anihpj-canary anihpj-v2 --weight=0. ImageStream rollback: Re-tag the old image: oc tag anihpj:old-version anihpj:latest — ImageChange trigger auto-redeploys the old version.

9.9 Pod Scheduling — Controlling Where Pods Run

For AI workloads, pod placement matters. You need GPU pods on GPU nodes, training jobs near data, and critical services spread across availability zones. OpenShift gives you four tools for pod placement:

📍 Pod Scheduling Decision Tree — "Where Should My Pod Run?"
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│          📍 POD SCHEDULING — "HOW DO I GET MY POD ON THE RIGHT NODE?"│
│                                                                     │
│  START: I need my pod on a specific node...                         │
│       │                                                             │
│       ├── "Just a simple label match"                               │
│       │    └── ✅ nodeSelector: { gpu: nvidia }                     │
│       │                                                             │
│       ├── "Must run on GPU node, prefer SSD nodes"                  │
│       │    └── ✅ Node Affinity: requiredDuringScheduling +          │
│       │         preferredDuringScheduling                           │
│       │                                                             │
│       ├── "Keep pods spread across zones"                           │
│       │    └── ✅ Topology Spread Constraints:                      │
│       │         maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone│
│       │                                                             │
│       ├── "Keep related pods together (ML training + data cache)"   │
│       │    └── ✅ Pod Affinity: labelSelector + topologyKey         │
│       │                                                             │
│       ├── "Keep competing pods apart (two GPU training jobs)"       │
│       │    └── ✅ Pod Anti-Affinity: labelSelector + topologyKey    │
│       │                                                             │
│       └── "This node is special — only specific pods can run here"  │
│            └── ✅ Taints & Tolerations:                              │
│                 Node: taint gpu=true:NoSchedule                     │
│                 Pod: toleration gpu=true                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Scheduling Examples for anihpj
# 1. NODE SELECTOR — Simple: Django on SSD nodes
oc patch deploy/anihpj -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"disktype":"ssd"}}}}}'

# 2. NODE AFFINITY — Django MUST be on SSD, PREFER zone-a
oc patch deploy/anihpj -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"affinity":{"nodeAffinity":{"requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution":{"nodeSelectorTerms":[{"matchExpressions":[{"key":"disktype","operator":"In","values":["ssd"]}]}]},"preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution":[{"weight":1,"preference":{"matchExpressions":[{"key":"topology.kubernetes.io/zone","operator":"In","values":["us-east-1a"]}]}}]}}}}}}'

# 3. TAINT + TOLERATION — GPU training on dedicated GPU nodes
# Admin taints the GPU node:
oc adm taint nodes gpu-node-1 nvidia.com/gpu=true:NoSchedule
# Pod needs toleration to run there:
oc patch deploy/gpu-training -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"tolerations":[{"key":"nvidia.com/gpu","operator":"Equal","value":"true","effect":"NoSchedule"}]}}}}'
📍 Quick Scheduling Reference

nodeSelector: Simplest — just key=value. Affinity: Complex rules — required vs preferred, In/NotIn/Exists operators. Taints/Tolerations: Node says "stay away unless you have this toleration" — great for dedicated GPU or high-memory nodes. Topology Spread: Balance pods across zones/hosts — critical for HA deployments.

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 9

Core task: Deploy apps with oc new-app, set resources, configure probes, scale with HPA. Speed tip: oc set probe deploy/name --liveness --get-url=http://:8080/healthz sets probes in one command. Gotcha: Deployment vs DeploymentConfig — the exam may ask for either. DC adds triggers + rollback.

📝 Chapter 9 Practice Questions

Q1
What's the key difference between a Deployment and a DeploymentConfig?
Click
✅

DeploymentConfig adds: triggers (image change, config change), lifecycle hooks (pre/mid/post), and oc rollback with full deployment history.

📖 EXPLANATION
OpenShift DeploymentConfig adds to K8s Deployment:
spec:
  triggers:                          # Auto-deploy on changes
  - type: ConfigChange                # Deploy when ConfigMap/Secret changes
  - type: ImageChange                 # Deploy when ImageStream tag updates
    imageChangeParams:
      automatic: true
      from: { kind: ImageStreamTag, name: "anihpj:latest" }
  strategy:
    type: Rolling                     # Rolling, Recreate, or Custom
    rollingParams:
      pre:                            # Lifecycle hooks!
        failurePolicy: Abort
        execNewPod: { command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"] }
      post:
        failurePolicy: Retry
        execNewPod: { command: ["python", "manage.py", "clearcache"] }
# EX267: DeploymentConfig = OpenShift's enhanced Deployment

Key advantage: auto-deploy when ImageStream tag updates (common in CI/CD). DeploymentConfigs are OpenShift-only — for cross-platform compatibility, use Deployments with external CI/CD triggers.

Q2
How does S2I build an image without a Dockerfile?
Click
✅

S2I uses a builder image (e.g., Python 3.11) that knows how to assemble applications. It injects your source code, runs assemble (pip install, collectstatic), and commits the result as a runnable image.

📖 EXPLANATION
S2I Build Flow:
1. Builder image (registry.redhat.io/ubi9/python-311)
   ├── Contains: Python + pip + gunicorn + S2I scripts
   └── Scripts: /usr/libexec/s2i/assemble, run, save-artifacts

2. Source code injected (git clone → /tmp/src)
   └── requirements.txt, manage.py, anihpj/

3. assemble script runs:
   ├── pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
   ├── python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
   └── chown -R 1001:0 /opt/app-root

4. Commit: source layers + builder = runnable image
   └── CMD: /usr/libexec/s2i/run → gunicorn

# Writes zero Dockerfiles — the builder IS the Dockerfile

For anihpj: oc new-app python:3.11~https://github.com/anihpj/anihpj.git triggers the full S2I pipeline — clone, assemble, push, deploy — in one command.

Q6
How do you mount ConfigMap values as environment variables?
Click
✅

oc set env deploy/anihpj --from=configmap/django-config. Each ConfigMap key becomes an env var.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc create configmap django-config --from-literal=DEBUG=False --from-literal=WORKERS=4
oc set env deploy/anihpj --from=configmap/django-config
# Result: DEBUG=False, WORKERS=4 injected as env vars in all pods
Q7
How do you set resource requests and limits on a deployment?
Click
✅

oc set resources deploy/anihpj --requests=cpu=250m,memory=256Mi --limits=cpu=1000m,memory=512Mi

📖 EXPLANATION
spec:
  containers:
  - resources:
      requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }  # Guaranteed minimum
      limits: { cpu: 1000m, memory: 512Mi }     # Hard ceiling
# Requests=guarantee, Limits=ceiling. Memory limit exceeded = OOMKilled
Q8
How does pod anti-affinity improve availability?
Click
✅

Anti-affinity spreads pods across nodes/zones. If one node fails, other pods survive. Uses podAntiAffinity with topologyKey.

📖 EXPLANATION
affinity:
  podAntiAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
    - labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: anihpj } }
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname  # Max 1 pod per node
Q9
What is the difference between oc rollout and oc rollback?
Click
✅

oc rollout manages deployment progress/history. oc rollback reverts a DeploymentConfig to its previous version — OpenShift-specific feature.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc rollout history dc/anihpj       # See all revisions
oc rollout status dc/anihpj         # Watch rollout progress
oc rollback dc/anihpj               # Revert to previous (DC only!)
oc rollout undo deploy/anihpj        # Revert Deployment (K8s native)
Q10
How do you configure a pod to restart on failure vs never?
Click
✅

Use restartPolicy: Always (default for Deployments), OnFailure (for Jobs), Never (run once, don't restart).

📖 EXPLANATION
spec:
  restartPolicy: Always      # Deployment: always restart crashed pods
  restartPolicy: OnFailure    # Job/CronJob: restart only on error
  restartPolicy: Never        # Run once, exit, never restart
# For AI training jobs: use OnFailure (retry on error, stop on success)
Q3
Your Django pod keeps getting OOMKilled. What do you check?
Click
✅

1. oc describe pod — look for OOMKilled. 2. Check memory limits: oc get deploy -o yaml | grep memory. 3. Increase memory limit or fix memory leak.

📖 EXPLANATION

OOMKilled diagnostic chain: 1) oc describe pod <pod> → State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled. 2) oc adm top pod <pod> — is memory near the limit? 3) oc get deploy anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 resources — what are the limits? 4) Fix: increase memory: 512Mi to memory: 2Gi in the deployment. OR: profile the app for memory leaks (Django DEBUG=False can help). OR: add HPA to spread load. If training job OOM: reduce batch size or use gradient accumulation.

Q4
Liveness vs Readiness probe — what's the difference?
Click
✅

Liveness: "Should we RESTART this pod?" (deadlocked app). Readiness: "Should we SEND TRAFFIC to this pod?" (temporary issue like DB reconnect).

📖 EXPLANATION
livenessProbe:                               readinessProbe:
  httpGet:                                     httpGet:
    path: /healthz    ← "Am I alive?"            path: /ready    ← "Can I serve?"
    port: 8080                                   port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 30                      initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10                            periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3                          failureThreshold: 3
  → RESTART pod if fails 3x                    → STOP traffic if fails 3x

Liveness: catches deadlocks, infinite loops, crashed processes
Readiness: catches DB unavailable, cache warming, large model loading
# ALWAYS configure BOTH for production AI workloads!

For AI inference: readiness should check model loaded (/v1/models/<name>/ready). Liveness should be simple (process alive). Cold start: readiness fails → no traffic sent, pod stays alive to finish loading.

Q5
How do you send 10% of traffic to a new version (canary)?
Click
✅

oc set route-backend myroute new-service --weight=10 and adjust old service weight accordingly.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Deploy v2 alongside v1
oc new-app --image=anihpj:v2 --name=anihpj-v2

# Create service for v2
oc expose deploy/anihpj-v2 --port=8080

# Split traffic: 90% v1, 10% v2
oc set route-backend anihpj anihpj-v2 --weight=10
oc set route-backend anihpj anihpj    --weight=90

# Verify: watch traffic distribution
oc describe route anihpj

# Gradual promotion: 10% → 50% → 100% over hours
# If v2 shows errors: oc set route-backend anihpj anihpj-v2 --weight=0

OpenShift Routes support native weighted traffic splitting — no service mesh needed. For model serving canary: deploy InferenceService v3 with canaryTrafficPercent: 10 for KServe-native canary.

Chapter 10: Build Strategies & Image Management🟡 Intermediate · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 10: Mastering OpenShift Builds

Images are the foundation of every workload on OpenShift. This chapter dives deep into BuildConfigs, ImageStreams, build optimization, and image promotion across environments — everything you need to manage the anihpj container lifecycle.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🏗️ Builds

10.1 BuildConfig Deep Dive

A BuildConfig defines HOW to build your container image — source location, build strategy, output destination, and triggers that kick off builds automatically.

🏗️ BuildConfig Anatomy — Every Field Explained
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🏗️ BUILDCONFIG ANATOMY                                 │
│                                                                     │
│  apiVersion: build.openshift.io/v1                                  │
│  kind: BuildConfig                                                  │
│  metadata:                                                          │
│    name: anihpj                       ← BuildConfig name            │
│  spec:                                                              │
│    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│    │  📂 SOURCE (Where is the code?)                          │     │
│    │  • git: { uri: https://github.com/anihs/anihpj.git }    │     │
│    │  • contextDir: /                    ← Subdirectory       │     │
│    │  • sourceSecret: github-credentials ← Private repo auth  │     │
│    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│    │  🏭 STRATEGY (How to build?)                             │     │
│    │  • sourceStrategy: { from: python:3.11 }  ← S2I         │     │
│    │  • dockerStrategy: { dockerfilePath: Dockerfile } ← Docker│    │
│    │  • customStrategy: { from: my-builder }  ← Custom       │     │
│    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│    │  📤 OUTPUT (Where does the image go?)                    │     │
│    │  • to: { kind: ImageStreamTag, name: anihpj:latest }    │     │
│    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│    │  ⚡ TRIGGERS (When to build?)                            │     │
│    │  • type: GitHub (webhook on push)                        │     │
│    │  • type: ConfigChange (BuildConfig changed)              │     │
│    │  • type: ImageChange (base image updated)                │     │
│    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Creating & Managing Builds
# Create BuildConfig from source
oc new-build python:3.11~https://github.com/anihs/anihpj.git \
  --name=anihpj

# Start a build manually
oc start-build anihpj

# Start with environment variables
oc start-build anihpj -e PIP_INDEX_URL=https://pypi.org/simple

# Stream build logs
oc start-build anihpj --follow

# Cancel a stuck build
oc cancel-build anihpj-4

# Add build hooks (pre-build and post-build scripts)
oc patch bc anihpj -p '{"spec":{"postCommit":{"script":"echo Build complete!"}}}'

# List builds and their status
oc get builds
oc describe build anihpj-1

# View BuildConfig details
oc describe bc anihpj
oc get bc anihpj -o yaml

# Webhook URL for GitHub integration
oc describe bc anihpj | grep Webhook
# Copy Generic Webhook URL → Add to GitHub repo Settings → Webhooks
🔧 Build Hooks — Pre and Post Build Automation

Pre-build hooks: Run before the build starts — e.g., run tests, validate dependencies. Post-commit hooks: Run after the image is committed — e.g., tag the image, send notifications. Hooks run inside the builder pod and can use any command available in the builder image.

10.2 ImageStreams — Smart Image Tracking

An ImageStream is a virtual view of container images — it tracks image tags across registries and automatically triggers deployments when images change. Think of it as a "smart pointer" to container images.

🖼️ ImageStream Flow — Build → Tag → Deploy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🖼️ IMAGESTREAM — SMART IMAGE TRACKING                  │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────┐           │
│  │  Build   │────▶│  ImageStream      │────▶│ Deploy   │           │
│  │ anihpj-1 │     │  anihpj:latest    │     │ auto-    │           │
│  └──────────┘     │  ┌────────────┐   │     │ trigger  │           │
│                   │  │ tag: latest │───┼────▶│          │           │
│  ┌──────────┐     │  │ → sha256:   │   │     └──────────┘           │
│  │  Build   │────▶│  │   abc123... │   │                            │
│  │ anihpj-2 │     │  └────────────┘   │                            │
│  └──────────┘     │  ┌────────────┐   │                            │
│                   │  │ tag: stable │   │  ← Points to tested ver    │
│  ┌──────────┐     │  │ → sha256:   │   │                            │
│  │  Build   │────▶│  │   def456... │   │                            │
│  │ anihpj-3 │     │  └────────────┘   │                            │
│  └──────────┘     └──────────────────┘                            │
│                                                                     │
│  Key Insight: When Build pushes a new image, ImageStream updates   │
│  the tag. If DeploymentConfig has an ImageChange trigger, it       │
│  AUTOMATICALLY rolls out the new version. Zero manual steps!       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
ImageStream Commands
# Create ImageStream
oc create imagestream anihpj

# Tag an image into the stream
oc tag anihpj:latest anihpj:stable
oc tag anihpj:latest anihpj:canary

# Import an external image into an ImageStream
oc import-image anihpj --from=quay.io/anihs/anihpj:latest --confirm

# Check ImageStream tags and their digests
oc describe is anihpj
oc get is anihpj -o yaml

# Check which deployments use this ImageStream
oc get deploy -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.template.spec.containers[].image | contains("anihpj")) | .metadata.name'

# Set ImageChange trigger on DeploymentConfig
oc set triggers dc/anihpj --from-image=anihpj:latest -c anihpj

10.3 Optimizing Builds for Speed

Slow builds kill developer productivity. Here's how to dramatically speed up your OpenShift builds:

TechniqueHow It WorksSpeed BoostExample
Layer CachingDocker/S2I caches unchanged layers5-10xrequirements.txt → pip install cached
Incremental S2IS2I reuses previous build artifacts3-5xOnly reinstall changed packages
Multi-stage BuildsSeparate build deps from runtimeImage size: 60-70% smallerBuilder stage → Runtime stage
Parallel BuildsRun multiple builds simultaneouslyWall-clock: 2-4xTekton parallel pipeline tasks
Build PruningDelete old builds to free resourcesResource savingsoc adm prune builds
Build Optimization Commands
# Enable incremental builds (S2I only)
oc patch bc anihpj -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"sourceStrategy":{"incremental":true}}}}'

# Set build resource limits (give builds more power)
oc patch bc anihpj -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"limits":{"cpu":"2","memory":"4Gi"}}}}'

# Prune old completed builds (keep last 5)
oc adm prune builds --keep-complete=5 --confirm

# Set build history limit on BuildConfig
oc patch bc anihpj -p '{"spec":{"successfulBuildsHistoryLimit":5,"failedBuildsHistoryLimit":3}}'

10.4 Managing Images Across Environments

Production images shouldn't come directly from developer laptops. Use an image promotion pipeline: dev → staging → production, with ImageStream tags tracking which version is where.

Registry Authentication & Pull Secrets
# Create a pull secret for external registry (e.g., quay.io)
oc create secret docker-registry quay-pull-secret \
  --docker-server=quay.io \
  --docker-username=anihs \
  --docker-password=my-token \
  --docker-email=anihs@example.com

# Link pull secret to service account (so pods can pull images)
oc secrets link default quay-pull-secret --for=pull

# Link pull secret to builder SA (so builds can push images)
oc secrets link builder quay-pull-secret

# Use a private image in a deployment
oc new-app --docker-image=quay.io/anihs/anihpj:latest \
  --name=anihpj
# Pods will use the linked pull secret automatically

# For cross-namespace image access:
oc policy add-role-to-group system:image-puller \
  system:serviceaccounts:anihpj-prod \
  -n anihpj-dev
# Allows anihpj-prod SAs to pull images from anihpj-dev registry
📤 Image Promotion Pipeline — Dev → Staging → Prod
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              📤 IMAGE PROMOTION WORKFLOW                            │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐         │
│  │  anihpj-dev  │    │ anihpj-staging│   │ anihpj-prod  │         │
│  │              │    │              │    │              │         │
│  │ ImageStream: │    │ ImageStream: │    │ ImageStream: │         │
│  │ anihpj:dev   │───▶│ anihpj:test  │───▶│ anihpj:prod  │         │
│  │              │    │              │    │              │         │
│  │ Build auto-  │    │ Tag promoted │    │ Tag promoted │         │
│  │ pushes here  │    │ after tests  │    │ after staging│         │
│  │              │    │ pass         │    │ validation   │         │
│  └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘         │
│                                                                     │
│  Promotion command:                                                 │
│  oc tag anihpj-dev/anihpj:latest anihpj-staging/anihpj:test        │
│  oc tag anihpj-staging/anihpj:test anihpj-prod/anihpj:prod         │
│                                                                     │
│  Each tag promotion creates an ImageStreamTag pointing to the      │
│  specific image digest (immutable). Rollback = re-tag old digest.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

10.5 Build Strategy Decision Tree — Which Method for anihpj?

🏗️ Build Strategy Decision Flowchart
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🏗️ BUILD STRATEGY DECISION TREE                       │
│                                                                    │
│                        START                                       │
│                          │                                         │
│              ┌───────────┴───────────┐                            │
│              │  Have a Dockerfile?    │                            │
│              └───────┬───────┬───────┘                            │
│                  YES │       │ NO                                  │
│                      ▼       ▼                                    │
│              ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐               │
│              │ Want to  │ │ Is it Python/Django? │               │
│              │ customize│ │ (like anihpj?)       │               │
│              │ deeply?  │ └──────────┬───────────┘               │
│              └──┬───┬───┘         YES │       │ NO                │
│             YES │   │ NO              ▼       ▼                   │
│                 ▼   ▼          ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐         │
│          ┌────────┐┌────────┐  │ Python   │ │ Custom   │         │
│          │ Docker ││ Docker │  │ S2I      │ │ Builder  │         │
│          │ Build  ││ Build  │  │ Builder  │ │ Image    │         │
│          │(Custom ││ (Std)  │  │(Easiest) │ │(Advanced)│         │
│          │Strategy││        │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘         │
│          └────────┘└────────┘                                      │
│                                                                    │

│     for custom dependencies (like ML libraries)                   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚡ Quick Decision Guide

S2I: Standard frameworks (Django, Flask, Express, Spring Boot). No Dockerfile needed. Red Hat maintains the builder. Docker Build: Custom dependencies, ML libraries, any Dockerfile-based project. Custom Build: You provide a builder image with specialized logic — rarely needed.

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 10

Core tasks: Create BuildConfig, start builds, promote images between environments. Speed tip: oc new-build python~repo.git --name=app then oc start-build app --follow. Gotcha: ImageStream tags are pointers — oc tag src:tag dest:tag copies the digest, not the image bytes.

📝 Chapter 10 Practice Questions

Q1
What triggers can automatically start a build?
Click
✅

GitHub/GitLab webhook (code push), ImageChange (base image updated), ConfigChange (BuildConfig modified). Configured in spec.triggers.

📖 EXPLANATION
spec:
  triggers:
  - type: GitHub                        # Webhook on git push
    github:
      secretReference: { name: github-secret }
  - type: ImageChange                   # When base image updates
    imageChange:
      from:
        kind: ImageStreamTag
        name: "python:3.11"
  - type: ConfigChange                  # When BuildConfig YAML changes
  - type: Generic                       # Generic webhook (custom CI)
    generic:
      secretReference: { name: generic-secret }
      allowEnv: true
# EX267: GitHub + ImageChange are the most tested triggers
Q2
How does an ImageStream trigger a deployment?
Click
✅

When a new image is pushed to an ImageStream tag, the DeploymentConfig's ImageChange trigger fires and automatically rolls out the new image.

📖 EXPLANATION
# ImageStream tracks image versions:
apiVersion: image.openshift.io/v1
kind: ImageStream
metadata: { name: anihpj }
spec:
  tags:
  - name: latest
    from: { kind: DockerImage, name: "quay.io/anihpj/anihpj:latest" }

# DeploymentConfig auto-deploys on tag update:
spec:
  triggers:
  - type: ImageChange
    imageChangeParams:
      automatic: true                          # Auto-rollout!
      containerNames: ["django"]
      from:
        kind: ImageStreamTag
        name: "anihpj:latest"
# Flow: Image pushed → IS tag updated → DC trigger fires → Rolling deploy
Q3
How do you promote an image from dev to prod?
Click
✅

oc tag anihpj-dev/anihpj:latest anihpj-prod/anihpj:prod

📖 EXPLANATION
# Image promotion pipeline (dev → staging → prod):
# 1. Dev builds and tags:
oc tag anihpj-dev/anihpj:latest anihpj-staging/anihpj:candidate

# 2. Staging validates, then promotes:
oc tag anihpj-staging/anihpj:candidate anihpj-prod/anihpj:prod

# 3. ImageStreamTag copies the digest pointer — NOT re-upload:
# anihpj-dev/anihpj@sha256:abc123...
#   └── anihpj-staging/anihpj@sha256:abc123...
#       └── anihpj-prod/anihpj@sha256:abc123...
# Same image, different tags across namespaces

# Verify promotion chain:
oc get istag -n anihpj-prod
Q4
How do you enable incremental S2I builds and why?
Click
✅

oc patch bc anihpj -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"sourceStrategy":{"incremental":true}}}}'. Reuses previous build artifacts — 3-5x faster.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Incremental build flow:
# Build 1 (full):   pip install → 200 packages → 5 min
# Build 2 (incr):   pip install → 1 changed pkg → 30 sec
# Build 3 (incr):   pip install → 0 changed → 5 sec (no-op)

# Enable via CLI:
oc patch bc anihpj --type merge -p '
{"spec": {"strategy": {"sourceStrategy": {"incremental": true}}}}'

# Or in BuildConfig YAML:
spec:
  strategy:
    sourceStrategy:
      from: { kind: ImageStreamTag, name: "python:3.11" }
      incremental: true    # ← Reuses /opt/app-root/.local from previous build

# Caveat: only works with S2I builder images that support save-artifacts
Q5
How do you allow pods in project-B to pull images from project-A's registry?
Click
✅

oc policy add-role-to-group system:image-puller system:serviceaccounts:project-B -n project-A

📖 EXPLANATION
# Grant image pull access across projects:
oc policy add-role-to-group \
  system:image-puller \                          # Role: pull images
  system:serviceaccounts:anihpj-prod \             # Subject: project's SAs
  -n anihpj-ml                                     # Namespace: where images live

# Now anihpj-prod pods can:
# image: image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/anihpj-ml/anihpj:latest

# Check who has pull access:
oc policy who-can get imagestreams/layers -n anihpj-ml

# For production: grant system:image-puller to CI/CD namespace
# to allow Tekton pipeline to deploy from registry
Q6
How do you change a BuildConfig from S2I to Docker strategy?
Click
✅

oc patch bc anihpj -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Docker","dockerStrategy":{"dockerfilePath":"Dockerfile"}}}}'

📖 EXPLANATION
spec:
  strategy:
    type: Docker                    # Changed from Source to Docker
    dockerStrategy:
      dockerfilePath: Dockerfile    # Path to Dockerfile in repo
# After patching: oc start-build anihpj --follow
Q7
What happens to old images when you prune builds?
Click
✅

oc adm prune builds --keep-complete=5 deletes build objects but NOT the images. Images are pruned separately with oc adm prune images.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc adm prune builds --keep-complete=5 --confirm    # Keep last 5 builds
oc adm prune images --keep-younger-than=48h --confirm  # Delete unused images
# Build pruning ≠ image pruning. Builds are metadata, images are data.
Q8
How do you trigger a build from a GitHub webhook?
Click
✅

Get the webhook URL from oc describe bc anihpj | grep Webhook. Add to GitHub repo Settings → Webhooks. Secret validates the payload.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Get webhook URL:
oc describe bc anihpj | grep -A1 "Webhook GitHub"
# URL: https://api.ocp.example.com:6443/apis/build.openshift.io/v1/.../webhook//github
# Add to GitHub: Repo → Settings → Webhooks → Add webhook → paste URL → Content type: application/json
Q9
What is the difference between BuildConfig and Build?
Click
✅

BuildConfig = template (HOW to build). Build = one execution instance (like a PipelineRun). BuildConfig:Build::Class:Object.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc get bc              # BuildConfigs (templates)
oc get builds           # Individual builds (instances)
oc describe build anihpj-1  # Shows: status, duration, logs URL, output image
Q10
How do you build multi-architecture images for OpenShift?
Click
✅

Use podman build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --manifest anihpj:multi. Or use Tekton to build per-architecture.

📖 EXPLANATION
podman build --platform linux/amd64 -t anihpj:amd64 .
podman build --platform linux/arm64 -t anihpj:arm64 .
podman manifest create anihpj:multi
podman manifest add anihpj:multi anihpj:amd64
podman manifest add anihpj:multi anihpj:arm64
podman manifest push anihpj:multi quay.io/anihpj/anihpj:latest

Chapter 11: Operators — The Heart of OpenShift🟡 Intermediate · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 11: Operators — Automated Operations at Scale

Operators are what make OpenShift special. They encode human operator knowledge into software — handling installation, configuration, updates, backups, and failure recovery automatically. The entire OpenShift AI stack runs on operators.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🤖 Operators🎯 EX267 35%

11.1 What is an Operator? (The Simple Explanation)

An Operator is a Kubernetes controller that manages a complex application's entire lifecycle. It watches a Custom Resource (CR), compares the desired state to the actual state, and takes action to reconcile them.

🤖 How an Operator Works — The Reconciliation Loop
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🤖 OPERATOR RECONCILIATION LOOP                        │
│                                                                     │
│                    ┌──────────────────┐                            │
│                    │  Custom Resource  │                            │
│                    │  (Desired State)  │                            │
│                    │  ──────────────── │                            │
│                    │  DataScienceClust│                            │
│                    │  er: {           │                            │
│                    │    workbenches:  │                            │
│                    │    Managed       │                            │
│                    │  }               │                            │
│                    └────────┬─────────┘                            │
│                             │                                      │
│                             │ 1. Operator watches CR               │
│                             ▼                                      │
│                    ┌──────────────────┐                            │
│                    │    🤖 OPERATOR    │                            │
│                    │  ──────────────── │                            │
│                    │  "Desired state   │                            │
│                    │   says workbenches│                            │
│                    │   should be       │                            │
│                    │   Managed.        │                            │
│                    │   Are they?"      │                            │
│                    └──┬───────────┬────┘                            │
│                       │           │                                 │
│          2. Check     │           │ 3. Reconcile                    │
│          actual state │           │ (create/update/delete)          │
│                       ▼           ▼                                 │
│              ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐                         │
│              │ Actual     │ │ Action:    │                         │
│              │ State:     │ │ Create     │                         │
│              │ No notebook│ │ notebook   │                         │
│              │ pods       │ │ deployment │                         │
│              └────────────┘ └────────────┘                         │
│                                                                     │
│  🔄 This loop runs CONTINUOUSLY — every few seconds                │
│  If someone deletes the notebook deployment, the operator          │
│  notices and recreates it. This is self-healing at the app level.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Maturity PhaseCapabilitiesExample
Phase I (Basic Install)Automated installation, configurationSimple DB operator
Phase II (Seamless Upgrades)+ Automated upgrades, patch managementMost community operators
Phase III (Full Lifecycle)+ Backup, restore, failover, scalingPostgreSQL Operator
Phase IV (Deep Insights)+ Metrics, alerts, auto-scaling, tuningOpenShift AI Operator
Phase V (Auto-Pilot)+ Predictive scaling, auto-healing, self-optimizingFuture state

11.2 Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM)

The Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) manages the full lifecycle of operators — discovery, installation, updates, and dependency resolution. It's like an "app store" for cluster extensions.

🏬 OLM Architecture — From Catalog to Running Operator
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🏬 OLM ARCHITECTURE                                    │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────┐                                              │
│  │  CatalogSource   │  ← Where operators are listed               │
│  │  (OperatorHub)   │    redhat-operators, certified-operators,   │
│  │                  │    community-operators                       │
│  └────────┬────────┘                                              │
│           │ OLM reads available operators                          │
│           ▼                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────┐                                              │
│  │  Subscription    │  ← "I want THIS operator from THAT catalog" │
│  │  name: rhods     │    Tells OLM: channel, version, approval    │
│  │  channel: stable │    strategy (Automatic vs Manual)           │
│  └────────┬────────┘                                              │
│           │ OLM resolves dependencies                              │
│           ▼                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────┐                                              │
│  │  InstallPlan     │  ← "Here's what I'm going to install"       │
│  │  (auto-generated)│    Lists: CRDs, RBAC, Deployments, CSVs     │
│  │  approval: Auto  │    You approve (or it's auto-approved)       │
│  └────────┬────────┘                                              │
│           │ OLM applies InstallPlan                                 │
│           ▼                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────┐                                              │
│  │  ClusterService  │  ← The actual operator deployment           │
│  │  Version (CSV)   │    Shows: version, status, requiress        │
│  │  phase: Succeeded│    Check CSV health for operator status!    │
│  └────────┬────────┘                                              │
│           │                                                        │
│           ▼                                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────┐                                              │
│  │  🤖 OPERATOR     │  ← Now running and watching CRs              │
│  │  (Pod)           │    Ready to manage your application          │
│  └─────────────────┘                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

11.3 Installing the OpenShift AI Operator via OLM 🎯

This is the EX267 core task. You need to install the Red Hat OpenShift AI operator and verify it's running correctly:

Complete: Install OpenShift AI Operator (Console + CLI)
# === METHOD 1: Console (OperatorHub) ===
# Administrator → Operators → OperatorHub
# Search: "Red Hat OpenShift AI" → Install
# Update channel: stable
# Installation mode: All namespaces (recommended)
# Installed namespace: openshift-operators
# Approval strategy: Automatic
# → Click Install → Wait for CSV: Succeeded

# === METHOD 2: CLI ===
# Create namespace + OperatorGroup
oc create ns redhat-ods-operator
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1
kind: OperatorGroup
metadata:
  name: rhods-operator-group
  namespace: redhat-ods-operator
spec:
  targetNamespaces: []
EOF

# Create Subscription
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata:
  name: rhods-operator
  namespace: redhat-ods-operator
spec:
  channel: stable
  name: rhods-operator
  source: redhat-operators
  sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace
  installPlanApproval: Automatic
EOF

# === VERIFY ===
oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator
# PHASE must be: Succeeded
oc get pods -n redhat-ods-operator
# Operator pod must be Running
🔑 CSV Status Is Your Health Check

Always check oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator. PHASE must be Succeeded. If it's Pending, Installing, or Failed — check: oc describe csv for the reason. Common failures: wrong namespace, missing OperatorGroup, or dependency not met.

11.4 Creating a DataScienceCluster Instance 🎯

The DataScienceCluster (DSC) is the Custom Resource that tells the OpenShift AI operator WHAT to deploy. Creating it is the critical EX267 task.

DataScienceCluster — Complete YAML with All Components
apiVersion: datasciencecluster.opendatahub.io/v1
kind: DataScienceCluster
metadata:
  name: default-dsc
spec:
  components:
    # Dashboard — the OpenShift AI Console UI
    dashboard:
      managementState: Managed

    # Workbenches — Jupyter notebooks
    workbenches:
      managementState: Managed

    # Data Science Pipelines — Tekton-based ML pipelines
    datasciencepipelines:
      managementState: Managed

    # Model Serving — KServe for inference
    kserve:
      managementState: Managed
      serving:
        name: Knative          # or: OpenVINO, vLLM
        managementState: Managed

    # Model Registry — version, track, deploy models
    modelregistry:
      managementState: Managed

    # Training Operators — distributed training (PyTorch, TF)
    trainingoperator:
      managementState: Managed

    # TrustyAI — model bias and drift monitoring
    trustyai:
      managementState: Managed

    # Ray — distributed computing for ML
    ray:
      managementState: Managed

    # Feast — feature store
    feast:
      managementState: Removed   # Disabled by default

    # CodeFlare — multi-cluster job scheduling
    codeflare:
      managementState: Removed

# Apply:
# oc apply -f dsc.yaml
# Verify: oc get dsc default-dsc -o yaml

11.5 Other Essential Operators for AI Workloads

🔍
Node Feature Discovery (NFD)

Auto-detects hardware capabilities (GPU, CPU features, kernel version) and labels nodes. Critical for: scheduling GPU workloads to the right nodes. oc describe node gpu-node | grep feature shows NFD labels.

🎮
NVIDIA GPU Operator

Manages the full GPU software stack: drivers, CUDA toolkit, container runtime, monitoring (DCGM). Creates ClusterPolicy CR to auto-deploy drivers. Verify: oc get pod -n nvidia-gpu-operator

🔄
Pipelines Operator (Tekton)

Kubernetes-native CI/CD and ML pipelines. Defines pipelines as code (YAML). Each step runs in its own pod. Required dependency for OpenShift AI pipelines. oc get pipelines

📉
Serverless Operator (Knative)

Scale-to-zero for model serving. Idle models consume ZERO resources. Scales up in milliseconds on first request. Required for KServe model serving. oc get knativeserving

11.6 Building Your Own Operator — The Operator SDK

The Operator SDK provides tools to build operators using Helm, Ansible, or Go. For simple automation, Ansible-based operators are the quickest path.

🛠️ Operator SDK Workflow — Create → Build → Deploy → Publish
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🛠️ OPERATOR SDK WORKFLOW                               │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    │
│  │  CREATE  │───▶│  BUILD   │───▶│  DEPLOY  │───▶│ PUBLISH  │    │
│  │          │    │          │    │          │    │          │    │
│  │ operator │    │ make      │    │ make      │    │ Operator │    │
│  │ sdk init │    │ docker-   │    │ deploy    │    │ Hub PR   │    │
│  │ --plugins│    │ build     │    │ (OLM)     │    │          │    │
│  │ =ansible │    │ docker-   │    │           │    │          │    │
│  │          │    │ push      │    │           │    │          │    │
│  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    │
│                                                                     │
│  Operator Types:                                                    │
│  • Helm: Wrap existing Helm charts (easiest, limited logic)        │
│  • Ansible: Use Ansible playbooks (medium complexity)              │
│  • Go: Full control, best performance (hardest, most powerful)     │
│                                                                     │
│  When to write one: App needs Day-2 operations (backup, scaling,   │
│  upgrade). When NOT to: Simple stateless app, existing Helm chart  │
│  is sufficient, or an operator already exists in OperatorHub.      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

11.7 Operator Best Practices and Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely CauseDiagnostic Command
Operator not showing in OperatorHubCatalogSource not configuredoc get catalogsource -n openshift-marketplace
CSV stuck in PendingDependency not met, insufficient permissionsoc describe csv <name> → check conditions
Subscription not creating InstallPlanChannel doesn't exist, version conflictoc get subscription -o yaml → check status
InstallPlan not applyingManual approval requiredoc patch installplan <name> --type merge -p '{"spec":{"approved":true}}'
Operator pod CrashLoopBackOffRBAC too restrictive, OOMoc logs deploy/<operator>
Operator Troubleshooting Quick Reference
# Check all operators
oc get csv -A
oc get subscriptions -A
oc get installplans -A

# Check operator pod logs
oc logs -n openshift-operators deploy/<operator-name> --tail=50

# Force operator to re-reconcile
oc delete pod -n openshift-operators -l app=<operator-name>

# Check custom resource status
oc get dsc default-dsc -o yaml | grep -A5 status
