Chapter 19: Training Pipelines — End-to-End Automation🔴 Advanced

Chapter 19: From Notebook Experiment to Automated Training Pipeline

Training a model in a Jupyter notebook is the "hello world" of ML. Production ML requires automated, repeatable, scheduled training pipelines that ingest fresh data, preprocess, train, evaluate against quality gates, and register models to the Model Registry — all without human intervention. This chapter connects pipeline design principles with OpenShift's Data Science Pipelines (Kubeflow Pipelines + Tekton under the hood) to build end-to-end training automation for anihpj's job recommendation models.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔄 PipelinesEX267

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "Why Can't I Just Run Training in a Notebook?"

You absolutely can — for initial experiments. But production training needs five things notebooks can't provide: 1) Reproducibility (same code + same data = same model, every time — notebooks have hidden execution state that makes this nearly impossible). 2) Scheduling (retrain every Monday at 2 AM with last week's new data — you're asleep, but the pipeline isn't). 3) Resource isolation (training jobs need dedicated GPUs for hours — you don't want to tie up your notebook environment for 8 hours). 4) Artifact lineage (which data version produced which model? Pipelines capture this automatically via artifact passing between steps). 5) Quality gates (automatically reject models with accuracy below 85% — no human judgment needed at 2 AM). The pipeline is the bridge between "I trained something" and "we have a production ML system that retrains itself."

19.1 End-to-End Pipeline Design

A production training pipeline connects: Data Validation → Feature Engineering → Model Training → Evaluation → Model Registration. Each stage has pass/fail gates — if data validation fails, the pipeline stops; if model accuracy drops below threshold, the model is NOT registered.

🔄 Training Pipeline with Pass/Fail Gates
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         🔄 PRODUCTION TRAINING PIPELINE — PASS/FAIL GATES          │
│  📥 Data → ✅ Validate → 🔧 Features → 🧠 Train → 📊 Eval → 📦 Register
│              │                          │            │              │
│              │ Schema fail?              │            │ Acc < 0.85? │
│              ▼ STOP 🛑                  │            ▼ STOP 🛑    │
│                                       ▼ Acc ≥ 0.85 → Register    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

19.2 Incremental Training & Updates

Instead of retraining from scratch every time, incremental training loads the previous checkpoint and trains only on NEW data. GPU costs drop 80%+.

Incremental Training — sklearn + PyTorch
# scikit-learn warm_start (updates existing trees)
model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, warm_start=True)
model.fit(new_data)  # Doesn't rebuild — adds trees to existing forest

# PyTorch checkpoint resume
checkpoint = torch.load('model_ckpt.pt')
model.load_state_dict(checkpoint['model_state'])
optimizer.load_state_dict(checkpoint['optimizer_state'])
# Train only on new batch → save new checkpoint

19.3 Multi-Model Training

anihpj needs multiple models trained in parallel: job classifier, skill extractor (NER), salary predictor, and recommendation ranker. Use DAG pipelines to express parallelism.

Parallel Multi-Model Pipeline (kfp DAG)
@dsl.pipeline(name='anihpj-multi-model')
def pipeline():
    ingest = load_data()
    # All three run in PARALLEL — independent pods
    classifier = train_classifier(ingest.outputs['data'])
    skill_ner = train_skill_extractor(ingest.outputs['data'])
    salary = train_salary_predictor(ingest.outputs['data'])
    # Merge: ranker waits for ALL to complete
    ranker = train_ranker(classifier.out, skill_ner.out, salary.out)

19.4 Pipeline Optimization

TechniqueSavesHow
Cache Features⏱️ 50-80% timeSkip recompute if input hash unchanged
Spot Instances💰 60-80% costPreemptible VMs + checkpointing
Parallel Steps⏱️ 2-4x fasterIndependent tasks run simultaneously
Compress Artifacts📦 70-90% smallerParquet (vs CSV), model quantization

def evaluate_and_gate(metrics, threshold=0.85):
    if metrics["accuracy"] < threshold:
        raise ValueError(f"Model rejected: acc {metrics['accuracy']} < {threshold}")
    return metrics  # Pass → continue to Model Registration

Click

# kfp caching:
@dsl.component(base_image="python:3.11")
def preprocess_data(input_uri: str) -> str:
    # Output hash = fn(input_uri) — if same URI, skip this step
    ...
# Enable: set enable_caching=True in pipeline config
# Cache stored in S3/MinIO; keyed by component + input hash
Q7
How do you handle pipeline failures gracefully?
Click
✅

Use retry policies, onError handlers, and notifications. Critical: never leave partial artifacts — use finally/cleanup steps.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Pipeline retry + notification:
spec:
  tasks:
  - name: train
    retries: 2  # Retry failed step twice
    taskRef: { name: train-model }
  finally:
  - name: cleanup
    taskRef: { name: cleanup-artifacts }  # Always runs
  - name: notify
    when: [{ input: $(tasks.train.status), operator: in, values: [Failed] }]
    taskRef: { name: slack-alert }

PipelineRun = one-time execution. RecurringRun = cron-based schedule that auto-creates PipelineRuns on a timer.

apiVersion: kubeflow.org/v1beta1
kind: RecurringRun
spec:

  pipelineRef: { name: anihpj-training }
# Equivalent to: cron triggers → creates PipelineRun → executes pipeline

Via pipeline params, step outputs (outputPath), or S3 artifact URIs. Small values as params; large outputs as S3 artifacts.

train_output.output  # dataset path, metrics dict

19.5 AutoML & AutoRAG — Automating ML & RAG Pipelines (Red Hat v3.4)

🆕 From Official Red Hat Docs — "Working with AutoML" & "Working with AutoRAG"

Red Hat OpenShift AI includes AutoML (automated model selection + hyperparameter tuning via Katib) and AutoRAG (automated RAG pipeline optimization). These automate the tedious trial-and-error work of finding optimal ML configurations.

🧪
AutoML (Katib)

Automated hyperparameter tuning: define search space (learning_rate: 0.0001–0.1, batch_size: 16–256), set objective (maximize accuracy), specify algorithm (Bayesian, random, grid), and Katib runs dozens of trials in parallel on your GPU cluster. Finds optimal config in hours vs days of manual tuning.

🔍
AutoRAG

Automates RAG pipeline optimization: tests different chunk sizes, embedding models, retrieval strategies (sparse BM25 vs dense vector), and reranking approaches. Finds the best combination for YOUR specific document corpus and query patterns — critical for anihpj job search accuracy.

Chapter 20: GPU-Accelerated Training 🎯🔴 Advanced · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 20: GPU-Accelerated Training — From Single GPU to Distributed

GPUs are the engines of modern AI, but using them effectively requires understanding the training stack: from single-GPU mixed precision to multi-node distributed training with NCCL. This chapter covers the complete GPU training pipeline — how to request GPUs in OpenShift, configure distributed training with PyTorch DDP/FSDP, optimize memory with gradient checkpointing and LoRA, and avoid the common pitfalls that waste expensive GPU cycles. Every concept maps directly to EX267 GPU management tasks and NCP-AII infrastructure domains.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🎮 GPU Training🎯 EX267🔺 NCP-AII

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "How Does GPU Training Actually Work?"

At its core, training a neural network is just matrix multiplication repeated billions of times. A GPU has thousands of tiny cores designed for exactly this — while a CPU has 64 powerful cores for diverse tasks. Here's the training loop on GPU: 1) Load a batch of data from RAM to GPU VRAM. 2) Forward pass: multiply input × weights through every layer (tensor cores accelerate this 10× via FP16 matrix math). 3) Compute loss (how wrong the prediction was). 4) Backward pass: compute gradients (how much each weight contributed to the error). 5) Optimizer step: adjust weights to reduce error. 6) Repeat for thousands of batches. The key insight: if the GPU is waiting for data from RAM, you're wasting money. This is why DataLoader workers, pinned memory, and fast storage matter — they keep the GPU fed. An idle GPU waiting for data costs exactly as much as a busy one.

20.1 GPU Architecture Refresher

ComponentWhat It DoesKey SpecAI Relevance
CUDA CoresGeneral parallel processingA100: 6,912 coresGeneral ML ops
Tensor CoresMatrix multiply-accumulateH100: 528 (4th Gen, FP8)99% of deep learning
VRAMGPU memory (model + data)A100: 80GB HBM2eLimiting factor for model size
NVLinkGPU-to-GPU interconnect600 GB/s (vs 64 PCIe)Multi-GPU gradient sync
MIGPartition GPU into instancesUp to 7 isolated slicesMulti-tenant GPU sharing
🎯 anihpj GPU Sizing

BERT fine-tuning: 1× A100 (40GB). Llama-7B fine-tuning: 4× A100 (160GB needed). Inference: 1× L40S (48GB) with FP8 quantization.

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 20

Core tasks: Request GPUs in pod spec (nvidia.com/gpu: 1), choose MIG vs time-slicing. Gotcha: GPU Operator + NFD must be installed before any GPU pod runs. Mixed precision = 2× speed, half VRAM.

📝 Chapter 20 Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between MIG and time-slicing for GPU sharing?
Click
✅

MIG: Hardware-level partitioning — dedicated memory+compute. Time-slicing: Software-level — alternating workloads.

📖 EXPLANATION
MIG: 1 A100 → 7 instances, each with dedicated 5-40GB VRAM, hardware isolated
Time-slicing: 1 GPU shared via time multiplexing, all pods share same VRAM pool
Q2
When would you use model parallelism vs data parallelism?
Click
✅

Data parallelism: Model fits on GPU, just slow. Model parallelism: Model too big for 1 GPU.

📖 EXPLANATION
Data parallel: 4 GPUs × 64 batch each = effective batch 256, 4× speed
Model parallel: Llama-70B → GPU 0: layers 0-20, GPU 1: layers 21-40, etc.
Q3
How does NVLink improve multi-GPU training performance?
Click
✅

NVLink provides 600 GB/s GPU-to-GPU (vs 64 GB/s PCIe), speeding up gradient sync in distributed training.

📖 EXPLANATION
PCIe Gen5: 64 GB/s     NVLink 4.0: 900 GB/s (14× faster!)
# Gradient sync (all-reduce) with NVLink: ~1ms, without: ~14ms
# Verify: nvidia-smi topo -m → NVLink connections between GPUs
Q4
How do you request GPUs in a pod spec for distributed training?
Click
✅

Set resources.limits.nvidia.com/gpu: N. For multi-GPU training, request 4-8 GPUs per pod.

📖 EXPLANATION
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 4       # 4 GPUs in one pod
# PyTorch DDP then uses all 4:
torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 train.py
# Each process sees 1 GPU (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES auto-set)
Q5
What is mixed precision training and why use it?
Click
✅

Uses FP16 for forward passes and FP32 for weight updates. 2× faster, half the VRAM, near-identical accuracy.

📖 EXPLANATION
# PyTorch mixed precision:
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, GradScaler
scaler = GradScaler()
with autocast():  # FP16 forward pass
    output = model(input)
    loss = criterion(output, target)
scaler.scale(loss).backward()  # FP32 gradient accumulation
scaler.step(optimizer)
# VRAM: 7B model FP32=28GB → FP16=14GB, speed: 1.8-2× faster on Tensor Cores
Q6
What is gradient accumulation and when do you use it?
Click
✅

Accumulate gradients over multiple micro-batches before updating weights. Simulates large batch sizes on limited GPU memory.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Effective batch = micro_batch × accumulation_steps
accumulation_steps = 4  # Simulate batch 128 with GPU that fits only 32
for i, batch in enumerate(dataloader):
    loss = model(batch) / accumulation_steps  # Scale loss
    loss.backward()  # Accumulate gradients (don't zero!)
    if (i+1) % accumulation_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()  # Update weights
        optimizer.zero_grad()
# Trains like batch=128 but uses only 32 samples in GPU memory simultaneously
Q7
How does GPU Operator handle driver updates on running nodes?
Click
✅

Rolling update: cordon node → drain GPU pods → uninstall old driver → install new → reboot → uncordon. One node at a time.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Update ClusterPolicy driver version:
spec:
  driver:
    version: "550.54.15"  # New driver
# GPU Operator auto-rolls: Node1(cordon→drain→update→reboot)→Node2→...
# Verify: nvidia-smi shows new driver version after each node completes
# Non-GPU pods unaffected — only nvidia.com/gpu pods evicted
Q8
What is pipeline parallelism and when is it preferred over data parallelism?
Click
✅

Split model layers across GPUs sequentially. GPU 0 does layers 0-10, GPU 1 does layers 11-20. For models that fit on one GPU but have sequential bottlenecks.

📖 EXPLANATION
Data Parallel:              Pipeline Parallel:
  GPU0: full_model(batch1)    GPU0: layers[0:12](batch)
  GPU1: full_model(batch2)    GPU1: layers[12:24](GPU0_output)
  GPU2: full_model(batch3)    GPU2: layers[24:36](GPU1_output)
  Good: batches independent   Good: sequential layers, no sync needed
  Bad: full_model RAM each    Bad: pipeline bubbles (GPU idle between stages)
# Pipeline parallel used in DeepSpeed/Megatron for very deep models
Q9
How do you monitor GPU usage during training in real-time?
Click
✅

nvidia-smi dmon for live metrics, DCGM for Prometheus dashboards, oc adm top pods for resource usage.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Live monitoring:
nvidia-smi dmon -s pucvmet -d 1  # 1-second refresh
# Columns: pwr gpu_util mem_util enc dec temp
# Prometheus:
DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL{exported_pod="train-pod"}  # % GPU busy
DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED                             # VRAM used
# If GPU_UTIL < 80%: bottleneck is CPU/data loading, not GPU
Q10
What happens when a training pod is evicted due to node pressure?
Click
✅

Pod receives SIGTERM → 30s to save checkpoint → pod terminated → rescheduled on another node. Must implement checkpoint save in signal handler.

📖 EXPLANATION
import signal, sys
def save_checkpoint(sig, frame):
    torch.save({'epoch': epoch, 'model': model.state_dict(),
                'optimizer': optimizer.state_dict()}, 'checkpoint.pt')
    sys.exit(0)
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, save_checkpoint)
# On resume: new pod loads checkpoint → continues from saved epoch
# Use terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60 (extra time to save)

20.5 Distributed Workloads — CodeFlare, Kueue & Ray (Red Hat v3.4)

🆕 From Official Red Hat Docs — "Working with distributed workloads"

Distributed workloads enable data scientists to use multiple cluster nodes in parallel for faster data processing and model training. The CodeFlare operator manages job queuing and scheduling, Kueue provides resource fairness and quota management, and Ray frameworks simplify distributed task orchestration with GPU-aware auto-scaling.

⚡
CodeFlare

Multi-cluster job orchestration. Manages distributed job lifecycle across OpenShift clusters. Integrates with Kueue for fair queuing. Auto-scales Ray clusters based on workload demand.

📋
Kueue

Resource fairness and quota management for batch/ML jobs. Queue, prioritize, and preempt workloads. Prevents resource hogging by single user/team. Cohort scheduling for shared GPU pools.

☀️
Ray + RayJob

Ray provides distributed Python APIs for data processing, training, and serving. RayJob CR on OpenShift orchestrates Ray clusters. GPU-aware scheduling with auto-scaling based on queue depth.

Chapter 21: Introduction to Model Serving 🎯🔴 Advanced · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 21: Serving Models in Production

Model serving turns your trained model into a production API — accepting requests, running inference, and returning predictions. OpenShift AI supports both single-model (KServe) and multi-model (ModelMesh) serving with autoscaling, GPU acceleration, and monitoring.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🚀 Serving🎯 EX267 25%

21.1 What is Model Serving?

Model serving is the process of making your trained ML model available as an API endpoint for real-time predictions. Instead of running inference manually in a notebook, you deploy the model to a server that handles requests 24/7 — scaling up for traffic spikes and down to zero when idle.

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "I trained a model. Now what?"

Training a model in a notebook is like baking one cake in your kitchen. Model serving is like opening a bakery — you need to handle multiple customers simultaneously, keep the cakes fresh, and never run out. KServe is your bakery manager: it takes your cake recipe (model), sets up the display case (API endpoint), hires staff as needed (autoscaling), and closes when there are no customers (scale to zero).

Batch vs Real-time: Batch inference = process 10,000 job postings overnight (cheap, slow). Real-time inference = user clicks "Find Jobs" → model responds in <100ms (expensive, fast). OpenShift AI supports both — batch via pipelines, real-time via KServe.

🚀 Model Serving Architecture — Training vs Inference
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         🚀 MODEL LIFECYCLE — TRAINING → SERVING → MONITORING       │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────────┐       │
│  │  🧠 TRAINING             │    │  🚀 SERVING             │       │
│  │  (Batch, Offline)        │    │  (Real-time, Online)     │       │
│  │                          │    │                          │       │
│  │  • Notebook/Pipeline     │───▶│  • KServe InferenceService│      │
│  │  • Hours to train        │    │  • Millisecond latency   │       │
│  │  • GPU for training      │    │  • GPU optional (CPU OK) │       │
│  │  • Output: model.pkl     │    │  • Autoscaling 0→N      │       │
│  │  • Register in Registry  │    │  • REST/gRPC API        │       │
│  └─────────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────────┘       │
│                                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  📊 MONITORING (Continuous)                                   │  │
│  │  • Prediction accuracy drift                                  │  │
│  │  • Feature distribution drift                                 │  │
│  │  • Request latency (p50/p95/p99)                              │  │
│  │  • Error rates, throughput                                     │  │
│  │  • Trigger retraining if metrics degrade                      │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

21.2 Serving Options on OpenShift AI

OptionBest ForModels Per ServerAutoscalingGPU
KServe (Single-Model)Production — one model per endpoint1✅ KPA (scale to zero)✅
ModelMesh (Multi-Model)Many small models, cost-efficient10-100+✅ HPA (pod-level)✅
Custom (FastAPI/Flask)Complex preprocessing, custom logicAnyManual or KEDA✅
Triton Inference ServerMaximum throughput, multi-frameworkMultipleVia K8s HPA✅

21.3 Inference Endpoint Lifecycle

An inference endpoint goes through: Create (deploy InferenceService CR) → Ready (pod running, health check passing) → Serving (accepting requests via Route) → Scaling (KPA/HPA adjusts replicas based on load) → Idle (scale to zero if no requests for N minutes) → Delete (remove CR, pods terminated). With KServe + Knative, cold starts from zero take ~200-500ms.

Inference Endpoint URL Patterns & Authentication
# KServe generates a Route automatically:
# https://{inferenceservice-name}-{namespace}.apps.{cluster}.com

# Standard prediction endpoint:
# POST /v1/models/{model-name}:predict
curl -k https://anihpj-classifier-anihpj-ml.apps.crc.testing/v1/models/anihpj-classifier:predict \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(oc whoami -t)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"instances": [...]}'

# Health check endpoint:
# GET /v1/models/{model-name}
curl -k https://anihpj-classifier-anihpj-ml.apps.crc.testing/v1/models/anihpj-classifier

# Authentication options for inference endpoints:
# 1. Service Account token (machine-to-machine):
#    curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)"
# 2. OAuth token (user-level):
#    curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(oc whoami -t)"
# 3. API Key (external clients): Create a ServiceAccount, get its token
# 4. No auth (dev only): Set Route annotation to disable TLS verify

21.4 Serving Architecture Map

Single-Model (KServe)

One InferenceService = one model endpoint. Best isolation, dedicated resources. Predictable latency. Recommended for anihpj production models.

Multi-Model (ModelMesh)

Many models share a pool of serving pods. Cost-efficient for models with low/irregular traffic. Models loaded/unloaded on demand.

Model Storage Options

Models can come from: S3 bucket (via NooBaa/MinIO), OCI container registry, PVC, or HuggingFace Hub. KServe auto-downloads from the specified URI.

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 21

Core concepts: KServe vs ModelMesh vs Custom vs Triton — 4 serving options. Gotcha: Model files stored in S3/OCI/PVC/HuggingFace — storageUri format varies. Choose based on model count + traffic pattern.

📝 Chapter 21 Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between KServe and ModelMesh serving?
Click
✅

KServe: One model per InferenceService — best isolation, scale-to-zero via Knative. ModelMesh: Many models share serving pods — cost-efficient for 10+ models with sporadic traffic.

📖 EXPLANATION
# KServe (Serverless):
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata: { name: anihpj-classifier }
spec:
  predictor:
    minReplicas: 0      # Scale to ZERO when idle
    maxReplicas: 5
    model:
      storageUri: s3://anihpj-models/classifier/v2

# ModelMesh (Multi-model):
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1alpha1
kind: ServingRuntime              # Define server (once)
metadata: { name: triton-runtime }
# Then 50+ InferenceServices → same runtime
# Models paged in/out via LRU cache

# Decision: KServe for 1-5 models, ModelMesh for 20+
Q2
Where can models be stored for serving?
Click
✅

S3 bucket, OCI container registry, PVC, or HuggingFace Hub. Specified via storageUri.

📖 EXPLANATION
# storageUri formats supported:
storageUri: "s3://anihpj-models/classifier/v2"          # S3 (NooBaa/MinIO/AWS)
storageUri: "oci://quay.io/anihpj/models:classifier-v2" # OCI registry
storageUri: "pvc://workspace/models/classifier/v2"      # PVC mount
storageUri: "hf://bert-base-uncased"                     # HuggingFace Hub

# S3 is recommended — scalable, accessible from any node
# OCI is portable — push to any registry, deploy anywhere
# PVC is simple — already in your notebook workspace
# HuggingFace is convenient — 100K+ pre-trained models
Q3
What's the difference between batch inference and real-time inference?
Click
✅

Batch: Process thousands at once (pipeline). Real-time: One request → one prediction, sub-100ms (KServe).

📖 EXPLANATION
# Batch inference (pipeline step):
# Input: 100,000 job postings
# Process: all at once (Triton dynamic batching)
# Latency: minutes (ok — overnight run)
# Output: predictions written to S3/PostgreSQL
# Scale: CronJob → single run, no autoscaling needed

# Real-time inference (KServe):
# Input: 1 job posting (user types in search bar)
# Process: single request → predict → respond
# Latency: <100ms (must be fast — user waiting)
# Output: prediction returned in HTTP response
# Scale: KPA auto-scales 0→5 pods based on traffic
Q4
What is the model serving lifecycle from training to production?
Click
✅

Train → Register (Model Registry) → Deploy (InferenceService) → Monitor (Prometheus) → Retrain (pipeline). Each stage is observable and reversible.

📖 EXPLANATION
Train (Notebook/Pipeline) → Model Registry (OCI artifact + metadata)
  → KServe InferenceService (staging, 10% canary)
  → Monitor (accuracy, latency, drift) → Promote to 100% traffic
  → Detect drift → Pipeline retrain → New version → Repeat
# Each transition observable: oc get inferenceservice → READY=True
Q5
What 4 serving options does OpenShift AI support?
Click
✅

KServe (single model, scale-to-zero), ModelMesh (multi-model, shared pool), Custom (FastAPI/Flask), Triton (max throughput, dynamic batching).

📖 EXPLANATION
KServe:       deploymentMode: Serverless  → 1-5 models, autoscale, scale→0
ModelMesh:    deploymentMode: ModelMesh   → 20+ models, shared GPU pool
Custom:       oc new-app python:3.11~repo → full control, no KServe magic
Triton:       ServingRuntime CR            → max throughput, NVIDIA optimized
# Choose based on: model count, traffic pattern, latency requirements
Q6
How do Data Connections wire S3 credentials to serving pods?
Click
✅

Data Connection creates a labeled Secret. KServe auto-mounts it as env vars (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY) in the predictor pod.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: aws-connection-anihpj
  labels:
    opendatahub.io/dashboard: "true"
    opendatahub.io/managed: "true"
stringData:
  AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: AKIA...
  AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: wJalr...
  AWS_S3_ENDPOINT: https://s3.openshift-storage.svc
# All InferenceServices in the namespace auto-inherit these env vars
Q7
What storage backends are available for model artifacts?
Click
✅

S3 (NooBaa/MinIO/AWS), OCI registry, PVC, HuggingFace Hub, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob.

📖 EXPLANATION
S3/NooBaa:  s3://bucket/model → Data Connection Secret → auto-mounted
OCI:        oci://quay.io/org/model:v1 → same registry as containers
PVC:        pvc://claim-name/path → mount in pod, no network needed
HuggingFace: hf://model-id → auto-download, no storage needed
# S3 recommended for production — scalable, HA, standard API
Q8
How does the serving endpoint get exposed externally?
Click
✅

KServe auto-creates a Service (ClusterIP) + OpenShift Route (external URL). The URL format is: https://is-name-namespace.apps.cluster.example.com.

📖 EXPLANATION
oc get inferenceservice anihpj-classifier
# URL: https://anihpj-classifier-anihpj-ml.apps.ocp.example.com
# Auto-created: Service (internal) + Route (external TLS)
# Test: curl -k https://anihpj-classifier-anihpj-ml.apps.ocp.example.com/v1/models/classifier:predict -d '{"inputs":[...]}'
Q9
What determines whether to use KServe KPA or HPA for autoscaling?
Click
✅

KPA (Knative) = scale-to-zero, concurrency-based. HPA = min replicas always, CPU/memory-based. Use KPA for sporadic traffic; HPA for always-on services.

📖 EXPLANATION
KPA (Serverless):               HPA (RawDeployment):
  minReplicas: 0                  minReplicas: 2
  scaleDownDelay: 60s             metrics: cpu 70%
  Scale-to-zero after 60s idle    Never scales to zero
  Cold start: 5-30s               No cold start (always warm)
  Best: dev/staging, sporadic     Best: production, steady traffic
# anihpj user-facing: HPA (minReplicas=1+), internal batch: KPA (scale→0)
Q10
How does model versioning work across the serving lifecycle?
Click
✅

Model Registry version → OCI tag → InferenceService storageUri reference. Update the tag to switch versions without changing the InferenceService spec.

📖 EXPLANATION
Model v1: oci://quay.io/anihpj/job-classifier:v1 (stage:archived)
Model v2: oci://quay.io/anihpj/job-classifier:v2 (stage:prod)
# InferenceService uses:
storageUri: oci://quay.io/anihpj/job-classifier:prod
# Promote v3: tag v3 as prod → InferenceService auto-switches
# No YAML change, no pod restart — just OCI tag update

Chapter 22: Single-Model Serving — KServe 🎯🔴 Advanced · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 22: Production Model Serving with KServe

KServe is the standard for serving individual models on OpenShift AI. It provides GPU acceleration, autoscaling (scale-to-zero), canary deployments, and explainability — all configured through a single InferenceService YAML. This is the EX267 core serving chapter.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2.5 hours🚀 KServe🎯 EX267 25%

22.1 KServe Fundamentals

KServe (formerly KFServing) is a Kubernetes CRD-based model serving framework. One InferenceService YAML defines everything — KServe handles model download, server startup, endpoint exposure, and autoscaling.

🚀 KServe Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🚀 KSERVE — SINGLE MODEL SERVING                       │
│  👤 Client → 🌐 Route → 📦 Predictor Pod → 🤖 Model              │
│                              │  Optional: 🔄 Transformer + 🔍 Explainer
│  Autoscaling: KPA (scale→0) or HPA (min replicas)                │
│  Model: S3 / OCI registry / PVC / HuggingFace Hub                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

22.2 Deploying an Inference Service

Deploy anihpj Job Classifier with KServe
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-job-classifier
  namespace: anihpj-ml
  annotations:
    serving.kserve.io/enable-prometheus-scraping: "true"
spec:
  predictor:
    minReplicas: 1
    maxReplicas: 5
    scaleTarget: 10          # Scale based on concurrent requests
    scaleMetric: concurrency
    model:
      modelFormat:
        name: sklearn         # sklearn, pytorch, tensorflow, xgboost...
      storageUri: s3://anihpj-models/job-classifier/v1
      resources:
        requests: { cpu: "1", memory: "2Gi" }
        limits: { cpu: "2", memory: "4Gi", "nvidia.com/gpu": 1 }
    # S3 credentials auto-injected from Data Connection!

# Deploy and check:
oc apply -f inference-service.yaml
oc get inferenceservice -n anihpj-ml
# NAME                    URL                                              READY
# anihpj-job-classifier  https://anihpj-job-classifier-anihpj-ml.apps...  True

# Test the endpoint:
curl -k https://anihpj-job-classifier-anihpj-ml.apps.cluster.example.com/v1/models/anihpj-job-classifier:predict \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"instances": [{"description": "Python developer AWS...", "skills": "python,aws"}]}'

22.3 InferenceService Configuration

FieldExamplePurpose
storageUris3://bucket/modelModel location (S3/OCI/PVC/hf://)
modelFormatsklearn, pytorch, xgboostAuto-detects serving runtime
minReplicas0 (scale-to-zero)Minimum pods running
canaryTrafficPercent10Traffic split for canary

22.4 Transformer & Explainer

🔄 KServe InferenceService — Predictor vs Transformer vs Explainer
Client Request (JSON)
     │
     ▼
┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
│ Transformer  │────▶│  Predictor   │────▶│  Explainer   │
│ (optional)   │     │  (required)  │     │  (optional)   │
│              │     │              │     │              │
│ • Preprocess │     │ • Model      │     │ • SHAP/LIME  │
│ • PII filter │     │   inference  │     │ • Feature    │
│ • Tokenize   │     │ • Scoring    │     │   importance │
└──────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘
                                                     │
                                                     ▼
                                          Explanation Response
                                          "Job ranked high because:
                                           skill_match=0.92, salary_fit=0.87"

Transformer: Pre/post-processing container. Example: convert JSON input to model-specific format, filter PII from requests. Explainer: Optional container providing model explanations (SHAP, LIME) — accessible via a separate endpoint for debugging and compliance.

22.5 GPU-Accelerated Inference

YAML — KServe InferenceService with GPU📋
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-job-classifier
  annotations:
    serving.kserve.io/deploymentMode: Serverless
spec:
  predictor:
    model:
      modelFormat: { name: sklearn }
      storageUri: s3://anihpj-models/job-classifier/v2
    resources:
      limits:
        nvidia.com/gpu: 1        # Request 1 GPU
        memory: 8Gi
      requests:
        nvidia.com/gpu: 1
        memory: 4Gi

KServe auto-schedules on GPU nodes. For LLMs: vLLM/TGI runtimes use PagedAttention for 20× faster token generation vs vanilla HuggingFace. GPU time-slicing (not MIG) works for inference — multiple replicas share one GPU.

22.6 Monitoring & Debugging

IS statusoc get isREADY=True, URL populated
IS conditionsoc describe is anihpj-job-classifierLatestDeploymentReady, RoutesReady

22.7 KPA vs HPA Autoscaling

FeatureKPA (Knative)HPA (Kubernetes)
Scale to zero?✅ Yes❌ No
MetricConcurrency (requests in-flight)CPU/Memory %

22.8 Model Explainability

YAML — KServe InferenceService with Explainer📋
spec:
  predictor: ...
  explainer:
    alibi:
      type: AnchorTabular       # SHAP-style explanations
      storageUri: s3://anihpj-models/explainer/
      config:
        threshold: 0.95         # Confidence threshold
    resources:
      requests: { memory: 1Gi }
# Access explanations at:
# POST /v1/models/anihpj-job-classifier:explain

For anihpj: TrustyAI/SHAP shows WHY a job was recommended ("skill_match=0.92 weighted highest"). Critical for user trust and regulatory compliance (GDPR "right to explanation").

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 22 (25% of exam!)

📝 Chapter 22 Practice Questions

Q1
What YAML resource do you create to deploy a model with KServe?
Click
✅

InferenceService. One CR = one model endpoint with predictor, optional transformer, and optional explainer.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1

metadata:
  name: anihpj-job-classifier

    serving.kserve.io/deploymentMode: Serverless

Q2
How do you deploy a model from S3 using KServe?
Click
✅

Set storageUri: s3://bucket/model-path. KServe auto-downloads from S3 using Data Connection credentials.

📖 EXPLANATION
# KServe init container handles model download:
# 1. Reads storageUri
# 2. Reads Data Connection Secret for S3 credentials
# 3. Downloads model files to /mnt/models
# 4. Predictor container starts → loads model

# Verify model loaded:
oc logs deploy/anihpj-classifier-predictor | grep "model loaded"
# Or curl the endpoint:
curl -H "Host: anihpj-classifier.apps.example.com" \
  https://anihpj-classifier.apps.example.com/v1/models/anihpj-classifier
Q3
What's the advantage of KPA over HPA for model serving?
Click
✅

KPA scales to ZERO — no pods, no cost when idle. KPA uses concurrency (requests in-flight) rather than CPU %.

📖 EXPLANATION
# KPA (Knative Pod Autoscaler):
annotations:
  autoscaling.knative.dev/minScale: "0"     # Scale to zero
  autoscaling.knative.dev/maxScale: "5"     # Max 5 pods
  autoscaling.knative.dev/target: "10"      # 10 concurrent req/pod
  autoscaling.knative.dev/scaleDownDelay: "60s"  # Stay warm 60s

# HPA (Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler):
spec:
  minReplicas: 1    # Always running (costs $)
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: cpu, targetAverageUtilization: 70 }
# KPA = inference-native, HPA = generic resource-based
Q4
How do you deploy a model from a PVC using KServe?
Click
✅

Use storageUri: pvc://claim-name/path. The PVC must exist in the same namespace and be readable. KServe mounts the PVC automatically.

📖 EXPLANATION
spec:
  predictor:
    model:
      storageUri: pvc://notebook-workspace/models/anihpj-classifier
# PVC created by notebook workspace — direct access to trained model
# No S3 upload needed — faster iteration for development
# Not recommended for production (PVC tied to node, no HA)
Q5
What is a KServe Transformer and when do you need one?
Click
✅

A Transformer pre/post-processes requests before the predictor. Use when your model expects different input format than what clients send.

📖 EXPLANATION
spec:
  predictor:
    model:
      storageUri: s3://models/anihpj-classifier
  transformer:                        # Runs BEFORE predictor
    containers:
    - image: quay.io/anihpj/preprocess:latest
    env:
    - { name: MODEL_INPUT_FORMAT, value: "array" }
# Client sends raw JSON → Transformer normalizes → Predictor scores → Response
# Use when: feature engineering, tokenization, format conversion needed at serving time
Q6
How do you implement canary deployment with KServe?
Click
✅

Create two InferenceServices (v1 + v2) with traffic split via canaryTrafficPercent on the new version.

📖 EXPLANATION
# v1 (stable, 90% traffic):
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata: { name: anihpj-classifier }
spec:
  predictor:
    model:
      storageUri: s3://models/classifier/v1
# v2 (canary, 10% traffic):
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata: { name: anihpj-classifier-v2 }
spec:
  canaryTrafficPercent: 10  # 10% → v2, 90% → v1 (same base name)
  predictor:
    model:
      storageUri: s3://models/classifier/v2

Click

Add resources.limits.nvidia.com/gpu: 1 in the predictor spec. The GPU Operator must be installed first.

spec:

    containers:
    - name: kserve-container
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 1         # Request 1 GPU
          memory: "8Gi"
        requests:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 1

Q8

Click
✅

Add an explainer section to InferenceService. It runs alongside the predictor and provides LIME/SHAP explanations via a separate endpoint.

spec:

    containers:
    - image: quay.io/trustyai/explainer:latest
      args: ["--model_name", "classifier", "--explainer_type", "Lime"]

Q9
What happens to InferenceService pods when no requests are received?
Click
✅

With KPA Serverless and minReplicas=0, pods terminate after scaleDownDelay seconds. The InferenceService stays Ready (URL still resolves). Next request triggers cold start.

📖 EXPLANATION
minReplicas: 0, scaleDownDelay: 60s
t=0: request → pod created (cold start 5-30s)
t=30: response returned
t=90: last request was at t=30, 60s elapsed → pod terminated
t=300: new request → cold start again
# URL always resolves → Knative activator proxies while pod starts
# Cost: $0 when idle (no GPU), cold start latency on first request
Q10
How do you verify a KServe InferenceService is Ready and serving?
Click
✅

oc get inferenceservice → READY: True, URL populated. Then curl the predict endpoint with a sample request.

📖 EXPLANATION

oc get isvc anihpj-classifier
# NAME                   URL                                                              READY
# anihpj-classifier      https://anihpj-classifier-anihpj.apps.ocp.example.com           True
# Test:
curl -k https://anihpj-classifier-anihpj.apps.ocp.example.com/v1/models/classifier:predict \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"instances": [[5.1,3.5,1.4,0.2]]}'

22.9 KServe Deployment Modes — Serverless vs RawDeployment (Red Hat v3.4)

🆕 From Official Red Hat Docs — "Deploy models with KServe"

KServe supports two deployment modes: Serverless (Knative-based, scale-to-zero) and RawDeployment (Kubernetes-native Deployments, no Knative dependency). Choose based on your scaling and networking requirements.

FeatureServerless (Knative)RawDeployment
Scale-to-zero✅ Yes — pods terminate when idle❌ Min replicas always running
Cold start5-30s (pod startup)None (always warm)
Traffic routingKnative KPA + revision-basedKubernetes Service + Ingress/Route
DependencyRequires OpenShift Serverless operatorNo extra operator needed
Best forDev/test, sporadic traffic, cost-sensitiveProduction with SLA, stable traffic

Chapter 23: Multi-Model Serving — ModelMesh 🎯🔴 Advanced · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 23: Serving Many Models Efficiently — The ModelMesh Story

ModelMesh solves a real problem: what happens when your organization has 50, 100, or 500 models? Deploying one pod per model means 500 pods idling on expensive GPUs. ModelMesh lets dozens of models share a single pool of serving pods, loading and unloading models on demand — think of it as "swap space for AI models." This chapter explains the architecture, deployment, scaling, and decision framework.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🕸️ ModelMeshEX267

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "How Does ModelMesh Actually Share GPUs?"

Imagine a library with 2 reading tables (GPU pods) and 50 books (models). In KServe, each book gets its own dedicated reading room — wasteful when most books sit unread. In ModelMesh, books are stored on a shelf (S3) and fetched to a table only when someone wants to read them. When the table is full, the book nobody has touched in the longest time goes back to the shelf (LRU eviction). The reader just experiences a 2-10 second wait while the book is fetched — after that, reading is just as fast as a dedicated room. This is how ModelMesh achieves 10-50× GPU efficiency: it exploits the fact that most models are idle most of the time, and only a few are "hot" at any given moment.

23.1 What is ModelMesh?

🕸️ ModelMesh — Multi-Model Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 🕸️ MODELMESH: 3 models share 2 serving pods → 50% resource savings│
│  👤 → Route → Pod1: [v1📦 v2📦]  Pod2: [v2📦 v3📦]               │
│  Models paged in/out on demand. Inactive = zero memory.          │
│  Cache eviction: LRU policy auto-unloads unused models.          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

23.2 Deploying to ModelMesh

YAML — ModelMesh: ServingRuntime + InferenceService📋
# Step 1: Define the runtime (once per server type)
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1alpha1
kind: ServingRuntime
metadata: { name: triton-runtime }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: triton
    image: nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.01-py3
    args: ["tritonserver", "--model-repository=s3://anihpj-models/"]

# Step 2: Deploy a model to it (many models → same runtime)
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata: { name: anihpj-skill-rank, annotations: { serving.kserve.io/deploymentMode: ModelMesh } }
spec:
  predictor:
    model:
      modelFormat: { name: xgboost }
      storageUri: s3://anihpj-models/skill-ranker/

ModelMesh auto-routes requests to whichever pod has the requested model cached in memory. Cold start: 2-10s when model loads from S3.

23.3 Scaling & Performance

FeatureKServe Single ModelModelMesh Multi-Model
ScalerKPA (scale-to-zero)HPA (always warm)
GPU sharing1 model per GPU (or time-slicing)50+ models per GPU
Model pinningN/APin hot models to specific pods
Cache evictionN/ALRU — inactive models auto-unloaded
Cold start5-30s (scale-from-zero)2-10s (model load from S3)
Best for1-3 models, scale-to-zero, low traffic10-50+ models, always-on, GPU efficient

23.4 ModelMesh vs KServe — Decision Guide

ScenarioUse KServeUse ModelMesh
1-5 production models✅ Best isolationWorks, but overkill
50+ models, sporadic trafficToo costly✅ Cost-efficient
Strict latency SLO per model✅ Dedicated resourcesPossible with pinning
🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 23

Core concepts: ModelMesh = many models share pods (cost-efficient). ServingRuntime + InferenceService. Gotcha: ModelMesh uses LRU cache eviction — unused models unloaded. Pin critical models with annotation.

📝 Chapter 23 Practice Questions

Q1
When would you choose ModelMesh over KServe?
Click
✅

When you have 20+ models with low/sporadic traffic. ModelMesh shares serving pods across models.

📖 EXPLANATION
KServe: 20 models × 1 pod each = 20 pods ($200/hr GPU)
ModelMesh: 20 models on 2 pods = 2 pods ($20/hr GPU)
annotation: serving.kserve.io/deploymentMode: ModelMesh
Q2
How does ModelMesh handle an inactive model that hasn't been used for hours?
Click
✅

ModelMesh unloads the model from memory (cache eviction) to free resources for active models.

📖 EXPLANATION
LRU Eviction: model_timestamp sorted, oldest evicted first
Model unloaded → metadata stays in etcd → reload on request (2-10s)
# Pin critical model to prevent eviction:
metadata:
  annotations:
    serving.kserve.io/pinned: "true"
Q3
What two CRs do you need to deploy a model with ModelMesh, and what does each define?
Click
✅

ServingRuntime + InferenceService. Runtime defines server; InferenceService points model to runtime.

📖 EXPLANATION
# CR1: ServingRuntime (once per server type)
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1alpha1
kind: ServingRuntime
metadata: { name: triton-runtime }
spec:
  containers:
  - image: nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:23.12
    resources: { limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 2 } }
# CR2: InferenceService (per model) — many can share one runtime
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata:
  annotations:
    serving.kserve.io/deploymentMode: ModelMesh
    serving.kserve.io/servingRuntime: triton-runtime
spec:
  predictor:
    model: { storageUri: s3://models/anihpj-classifier, modelFormat: { name: onnx } }
Q4
How does ModelMesh scale differently from KServe single-model serving?
Click
✅

ModelMesh uses HPA at pod level (total CPU/memory across all models). KServe uses KPA per model (scale-to-zero).

📖 EXPLANATION
ModelMesh HPA:                   KServe KPA:
spec:                           spec:
  scaleTargetRef:                 minReplicas: 0
    name: modelmesh-serving       maxReplicas: 5
  minReplicas: 2                 scaleDownDelay: 60s
  maxReplicas: 10               # Scale-to-zero after 60s idle
  metrics:                       # ModelMesh: pods always warm
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: cpu, target: { averageUtilization: 70 } }
Q5
What is model pinning in ModelMesh and when would you use it?
Click
✅

Model pinning reserves dedicated capacity for critical models. Pinned models stay loaded regardless of traffic.

📖 EXPLANATION
annotations:
  serving.kserve.io/pinned: "true"
# Pinned models: never evicted, always in memory, guaranteed capacity
# Trade-off: reduces flexibility for other models in the pool
Q6
How does the LRU cache eviction work in ModelMesh and what triggers it?
Click
✅

LRU (Least Recently Used) evicts the model that hasn't been accessed for the longest time when memory pressure occurs.

📖 EXPLANATION
Triggers:
1. Pod memory > threshold (model pod OOM imminent)
2. New model loaded, no free VRAM
3. Explicit: oc annotate is  serving.kserve.io/unload=true
Eviction order: timestamp list → unpin → evict oldest → reload when needed
Q7
Can ModelMesh and KServe single-model serving coexist in the same OpenShift AI cluster?
Click
✅

Yes. Different deployment mode annotations route to different infrastructure.

📖 EXPLANATION
# KServe Serverless (dedicated per model):
serving.kserve.io/deploymentMode: Serverless
# ModelMesh (shared pool):
serving.kserve.io/deploymentMode: ModelMesh
# Both managed by same KServe controller, routed to different runtimes
Q8
What happens when ModelMesh runs out of GPU memory for loading a new model?
Click
✅

ModelMesh attempts LRU eviction, then HPA scaling, then refuses with Pending status.

📖 EXPLANATION
Flow: New model → LRU eviction check → Free memory? Yes→load
  No→HPA can scale? Yes→new pod→load there
  No→Event: InsufficientModelMeshMemory → model stays "Pending"
Fix: Increase maxReplicas, add GPU nodes, or reduce model count
Q9
You're deploying 50 anihpj skill-classifier model variants (one per job category). Each gets ~1 request/minute. KServe or ModelMesh?
Click
✅

ModelMesh. 50 models × 1 req/min = 50 req/min total — very low traffic.

📖 EXPLANATION
KServe: 50 pods × 1 GPU = 50 GPUs ($500/hr) ← absurd
ModelMesh: 50 models ÷ 2 pods = 2 GPUs ($20/hr) ← correct
# 25× cost reduction! ModelMesh is purpose-built for this scenario
Q10
Design a hybrid serving architecture for anihpj: 3 critical models (high traffic) + 30 experimental models (low traffic).
Click
✅

3 critical → KServe Serverless; 30 experimental → ModelMesh pool.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Critical models (KServe):
deploymentMode: Serverless
minReplicas: 1  # zero cold start
# 3 models × 1 GPU = 3 GPUs
# Experimental models (ModelMesh):
deploymentMode: ModelMesh
# 30 models on 2 GPU pool = 2 GPUs
# Total: 5 GPUs vs 33 GPUs if all KServe = 6.6× cost savings

Chapter 24: Beyond Basic Serving

For specialized use cases — maximum throughput, custom preprocessing, streaming inference, and edge deployment — OpenShift supports advanced serving patterns beyond KServe and ModelMesh.

24.1 Triton Inference Server

🔬 NVIDIA Triton — Max Throughput Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    NVIDIA TRITON INFERENCE SERVER                   │
│                                                                     │
│  👤 Requests ──▶ [Dynamic Batcher] ──▶ [Model Scheduler]           │
│                       │                      │                      │
│            Batching Window: 100μs     Concurrent Models: 8         │
│                                                                     │
│         ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌─────────┐       │
│         │PyTorch  │  │TensorRT │  │  ONNX   │  │   TF    │       │
│         │ Runtime │  │ Runtime │  │ Runtime │  │ Runtime │       │
│         └─────────┘  └─────────┘  └─────────┘  └─────────┘       │
│              │             │            │            │              │
│              ▼             ▼            ▼            ▼              │
│         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
│         │           GPU Memory Pool (CUDA)                  │      │
│         │   Model1 [VRAM] Model2 [VRAM] Model3 [VRAM]      │      │
│         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                     │
│  📊 Performance: 2-5× throughput vs standard model servers         │
│  ⚡ Dynamic Batching: Combine 100+ requests into 1 GPU pass       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Deploy as a ServingRuntime CR on OpenShift. Triton supports dynamic batching, concurrent model execution, TensorRT optimization, and all major frameworks. Best for: maximum throughput, multi-framework shops, GPU-accelerated inference at scale.

24.2 Custom Servers (FastAPI)

Python — Custom FastAPI Inference Server on OpenShift📋
# app.py — Custom FastAPI inference server
from fastapi import FastAPI
import joblib, numpy as np
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()
model = joblib.load("/models/anihpj-skill-ranker.joblib")

class JobInput(BaseModel):
    title: str; skills: list[str]; experience: int
    location: str; salary_range: str

class Prediction(BaseModel):
    score: float; explanation: dict

@app.post("/predict", response_model=Prediction)
@app.get("/healthz")  # Liveness probe
def health(): return {"status": "ok"}

@app.get("/ready")    # Readiness probe
def ready():
    return {"status": "ready", "model_loaded": model is not None}

# Deploy: oc new-app python:3.11~https://github.com/anihpj/inference.git
# oc expose svc/anihpj-inference → Route for external access
# oc autoscale deploy/anihpj-inference --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70

Trade-off: you manage model loading, scaling, and monitoring yourself — but get unlimited flexibility for custom preprocessing and business logic. Best when KServe's patterns don't fit your pipeline.

│  new job post│     │  anihpj.jobs.new  │     │  (Kafka consumer) │
└──────────────┘     └──────────────────┘     └────────┬─────────┘

                                               ┌──────────────────┐

                                               └────────┬─────────┘

                                                        ▼

                                               └──────────────────┘
Pipeline: Strimzi Operator → KafkaTopic CRs → KServe Kafka Event Source
Latency: <100ms end-to-end (Kafka → infer → Kafka)

Real-time classification: every new job posting published to Kafka → inference pod classifies → results written to output topic. Install Strimzi (Kafka Operator) from OperatorHub, create KafkaTopic CRs, configure KServe with Kafka event source.

For anihpj edge: deploy ONNX/TensorRT models on SNO at regional locations. Models pushed from central registry via ImageStream. Benefits: data locality (GDPR), offline resilience, <10ms latency for instant job-skill matching.

What are the key differences between deploying a model with Triton ServingRuntime vs a custom FastAPI server?
Click
✅

Triton: KServe-managed, auto-scaling. FastAPI: You manage everything, unlimited flexibility.

📖 EXPLANATION
Triton (KServe):              FastAPI (Custom):
- KPA auto-scaling             - HPA (manual config)
- Dynamic batching free         - You write batching logic
- Multi-framework built-in      - Only your code's frameworks

Q4
What is dynamic batching in Triton and how does it improve inference throughput?
Click
✅

Dynamic batching combines individual requests into one batch for a single GPU pass — 2-10× throughput.

📖 EXPLANATION
# config.pbtxt:
dynamic_batching {
  max_queue_delay_microseconds: 100  # Wait up to 100μs for more requests
  preferred_batch_size: [8, 16, 32]   # Preferred batch sizes
}
# Without: 100 requests = 100 GPU kernel launches
# With: 100 requests batched into 3-4 kernel launches → 25-33× faster
# Trade-off: adds latency = batching window (100μs negligible)

kind: KafkaTopic

24.5 Distributed Inference — llm-d for Large-Scale LLM Serving (Red Hat v3.4)

🆕 From Official Red Hat Docs — "Deploy models using Distributed Inference with llm-d"

llm-d (LLM Distributed) enables serving large language models across multiple GPUs and nodes — splitting the model across GPUs when it's too large for a single GPU. This is essential for serving models like Llama-70B or Mixtral 8x22B that exceed single-GPU VRAM limits.

🚀 Distributed Inference — Model Parallelism vs Data Parallelism
DATA PARALLELISM (vLLM/TGI):              MODEL PARALLELISM (llm-d):
┌──────────┐┌──────────┐                 ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ GPU 0    ││ GPU 1    │                 │ GPU 0: Layers 0-15           │
│ Full 7B  ││ Full 7B  │                 │ GPU 1: Layers 16-31          │
│ Requests ││ Requests │                 │ GPU 2: Layers 32-47          │
│ A-M      ││ N-Z      │                 │ GPU 3: Layers 48-63 + Head   │
└──────────┘└──────────┘                 └──────────────────────────────┘
Each GPU has full model copy             Model SPLIT across GPUs — tensor parallelism
Best when: model fits on 1 GPU           Best when: model > 1 GPU VRAM (70B+)

When to use llm-d: Your model (e.g., Llama-70B at FP16 = 140GB) doesn't fit on a single H100 (80GB). llm-d splits the model across 2+ GPUs using tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, or both. For anihpj: If you deploy a large custom job-matching LLM that exceeds single-GPU capacity, llm-d distributes it across your GPU nodes with automatic load balancing.

Chapter 25: GPU Architecture for AI🔴 Advanced

Chapter 25: Understanding the Hardware That Powers AI

GPUs are the engines of modern AI. Understanding their architecture — CUDA cores, Tensor Cores, memory hierarchy, and interconnects — helps you make informed decisions about model training, inference optimization, and hardware sizing.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🎮 GPU

25.1 GPU Fundamentals

🎮 GPU vs CPU — Why GPUs Win at AI
CPU (Intel Xeon):                    GPU (NVIDIA A100):
├── 64 cores @ 3.5 GHz               ├── 6,912 CUDA Cores + 432 Tensor Cores
├── Sequential processing             ├── Massively parallel
├── ~100 GB/s memory bandwidth        ├── ~2,039 GB/s memory bandwidth
├── Great for: OS, web servers        ├── Great for: Matrix math, deep learning
└── Training BERT: ~2 weeks           └── Training BERT: ~2 hours (168x faster!)

Unlike CPUs (few cores, high clock speed, optimized for sequential tasks), GPUs have thousands of simpler cores optimized for parallel computation — perfect for matrix operations in ML. Key concepts: CUDA Cores (general parallel processing), Tensor Cores (specialized for matrix multiply-accumulate — the heart of deep learning), VRAM (GPU memory — stores model weights, activations, and batch data).

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "Why Do I Need a GPU for AI?"

Matrix multiplication is 99% of deep learning. A single forward pass through a neural network is just a chain of matrix multiplications. CPUs can do 10-20 operations at a time (cores). GPUs can do 10,000+ operations simultaneously (CUDA/Tensor cores). The difference for training a model: CPU = 2 weeks, GPU = 2 hours. Tensor Cores specifically are designed to multiply two 4×4 matrices in a single clock cycle — making them 10x faster than CUDA cores for the FP16/FP8 math used in modern AI.

VRAM is your limiting factor. If your model + batch data doesn't fit in GPU memory, training simply won't start. This is why model size determines GPU requirements — not training speed. For EX267: know that GPU scheduling requires nvidia.com/gpu resource requests and that the GPU Operator must be installed first.

25.2 NVIDIA GPU Families

GPUVRAMTensor CoresFP16 TFLOPSBest For
A10040/80 GB3rd Gen312Training + Inference
H10080 GB HBM34th Gen (FP8)989LLM Training, GenAI
L40S48 GB4th Gen362Inference, Fine-tuning
A1024 GB3rd Gen125Small models, dev

25.3 MIG & Time-Slicing for GPU Sharing

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU): Hardware-level partitioning — splits one A100/H100 into up to 7 isolated instances, each with dedicated memory and compute. Perfect for multi-tenant production. Time-slicing: Software-level GPU sharing — GPUs alternate between workloads. Simpler but no memory isolation — one workload can OOM others. For EX267: know that MIG requires the GPU Operator with MIG strategy enabled.

25.4 NVLink, NVSwitch, InfiniBand

NVLink: Direct GPU-to-GPU interconnect — 600 GB/s (vs 64 GB/s PCIe 5.0). Critical for multi-GPU training where gradient sync is the bottleneck. NVSwitch: Connects all GPUs in a node at full NVLink speed (DGX systems). InfiniBand: High-speed networking for multi-node GPU clusters — 400 Gb/s with RDMA for cross-node gradient communication.

25.5 Inside the NVIDIA H100 GPU

132 Streaming Multiprocessors

Each SM contains: 128 CUDA cores + 4 Tensor Cores. Total: 16,896 CUDA cores + 528 Tensor Cores. SMs execute threads in warps of 32.

4th Gen Tensor Cores (FP8)

FP8 delivers 2x throughput over FP16 with Transformer Engine. 989 TFLOPS FP8 vs 495 FP16. Critical for LLM training/inference.

HBM3 Memory 80GB

3.35 TB/s bandwidth. L2 Cache: 50 MB. Model + KV cache + batch data must fit in 80GB. Llama-70B (140GB) needs 2+ H100s with model parallelism.

NVLink 4.0 + NVSwitch

900 GB/s per GPU pair. NVSwitch connects all 8 GPUs in DGX H100. Cross-node via InfiniBand NDR400.

🎯 EX267 + NCP-AII Exam Focus — Chapter 25

Must-know numbers: A100=80GB/312 TFLOPS, H100=80GB/989 TFLOPS, MIG max=7, NVLink=900GB/s. Gotcha: VRAM formula = params × bytes × 4. Llama-70B FP16 = 560GB → needs 7× A100.

📝 Chapter 25 Practice Questions

Q1
Why can't you run Llama-70B on a single H100 (80GB) without model parallelism?
Click
✅

Llama-70B in FP16 requires ~140GB VRAM (70B × 2 bytes). H100 has 80GB. You need at least 2 H100s with model parallelism or FP8/INT4 quantization.

📖 EXPLANATION
VRAM = params × bytes_per_param × overhead_factor
Llama-70B FP16:  70B × 2 = 140GB (doesn't fit 80GB)
Llama-70B FP8:   70B × 1 = 70GB  (fits on 1× H100!)
Llama-70B INT4:  70B × 0.5 = 35GB (fits on 1× A10 24GB? No — add KV cache)
# Reality check: KV cache for 4096 tokens adds ~20GB more
# FP8 + KV cache = 70 + 20 = 90GB → needs 2× H100 still
Q2
What's the difference between MIG and time-slicing for GPU sharing?
Click
✅

MIG: Hardware-level — dedicated VRAM + compute. Time-slicing: Software-level — no memory isolation.

📖 EXPLANATION
MIG (ClusterPolicy):               Time-Slicing (ConfigMap):
spec:                               apiVersion: v1
  mig:                              kind: ConfigMap
    strategy: mixed                 data:
  migManager:                         default: |-
    enabled: true                       timeSlicing:
Isolation: ✅ VRAM+Cache+Err          replicas: 4
GPU types: A100/H100 only             Isolation: ❌ shared VRAM
Max instances: 7 per GPU              GPU types: ALL NVIDIA GPUs
Best for: Production multi-tenant     Max instances: Unlimited
Q3
You have an A100 80GB GPU. How many 1g.10gb MIG instances can you create?
Click
✅

Up to 7 MIG instances. Each gets 1/7 compute + 10GB VRAM. Hardware-isolated.

📖 EXPLANATION
# A100 40GB MIG Profiles:        # H100 80GB MIG Profiles:
1g.5gb  × 7 = 35GB total        1g.12gb × 7 = 84GB
2g.10gb × 3 = 30GB total        2g.24gb × 3 = 72GB
3g.20gb × 2 = 40GB total        3g.47gb × 2 = 94GB (fits 80GB? no, max 2)
4g.20gb × 1 = 20GB              4g.47gb × 1 = 47GB
7g.40gb × 1 = 40GB (full)       7g.80gb × 1 = 80GB (no MIG)

# Verify: nvidia-smi mig -lgi   # List GPU Instances

Q4
What interconnect technologies are used for multi-GPU training in a DGX H100 system?
Click
✅

Three layers: NVLink 4.0 (900 GB/s intra-node), NVSwitch (3.6 TB/s all-to-all), InfiniBand NDR400 (400 Gb/s cross-node via GPUDirect RDMA).

📖 EXPLANATION
DGX H100 Interconnect Hierarchy:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Layer 1: NVLink 4.0 — GPU↔GPU (intra)  │ 900 GB/s per link
│ Layer 2: NVSwitch   — All 8 GPUs        │ 3.6 TB/s bisection
│ Layer 3: CX-7 IB    — Node↔Node         │ 400 Gb/s NDR
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
# NCCL uses best available path:
# Same node → NVLink (auto-detected by topology)
# Cross node → InfiniBand with GPUDirect RDMA (NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5)
# Verify: nvidia-smi topo -m → shows NVLink + NIC topology
Q5
Why does FP8 training on H100 deliver 2× throughput over FP16 on A100?
Click
✅

H100's 4th Gen Tensor Cores + Transformer Engine dynamically cast FP8↔FP16. 989 TFLOPS FP8 vs A100's 312 TFLOPS FP16.

📖 EXPLANATION
GPU Comparison (FP16 unless noted):
A100: 312 TFLOPS FP16  (3rd Gen Tensor Cores)
H100: 495 TFLOPS FP16  (4th Gen, 1.6× A100)
H100: 989 TFLOPS FP8   (Transformer Engine, 3.2× A100)
B200: ~2,250 TFLOPS FP8 (5th Gen, projected)

# Transformer Engine auto-manages precision:
# Forward pass → FP8 (fast, less precise)
# Backward pass → FP16 (accurate for gradients)
# Master weights → FP32 (full precision)
Q6
What is VRAM and why is it the limiting factor for AI?
Click
✅

VRAM = GPU memory. Must hold model weights + activations + batch data + KV cache. If model > VRAM, training fails. This determines GPU choice.

📖 EXPLANATION
VRAM = params × precision × (1 model + 1 optimizer + 1 gradient + 1 activation)
7B FP16: 7B × 2 × 4 = 56GB → A100 80GB ✅
70B FP16: 70B × 2 × 4 = 560GB → needs 7× A100 (model parallel)
Q7
What is NVSwitch and how does it help multi-GPU training?
Click
✅

NVSwitch connects ALL GPUs in a DGX node at full NVLink speed (3.6 TB/s). Eliminates GPU-to-GPU communication bottleneck.

📖 EXPLANATION
Without NVSwitch: GPU0→GPU3 = multiple hops, ~200 GB/s
With NVSwitch:    GPU0→GPU3 = direct, 900 GB/s
# DGX H100: 8 GPUs × NVSwitch = all-to-all at full bandwidth
Q8
How do Tensor Cores differ from CUDA Cores?
Click
✅

CUDA Cores = general parallel compute. Tensor Cores = specialized for 4×4 matrix multiply-accumulate (99% of deep learning). 10x faster for ML ops.

📖 EXPLANATION
CUDA Core: 1 multiply-add per clock
Tensor Core: 4×4 matrix multiply-add (64 ops) per clock
# A100: 6,912 CUDA Cores + 432 Tensor Cores → 312 TFLOPS FP16
Q9
When would you choose an A100 over an H100?
Click
✅

A100: Mature, widely available, MIG support. H100: 2-3× faster for FP8, newer. Choose A100 for stability/cost; H100 for max performance.

📖 EXPLANATION
A100: 80GB HBM2e, 312 TFLOPS FP16, MIG up to 7, available everywhere
H100: 80GB HBM3, 989 TFLOPS FP16, 3,958 FP8, new, harder to get
# For anihpj BERT fine-tuning: A100 is plenty. For LLM training: H100 needed.
Q10
What is InfiniBand and why is it critical for multi-node GPU clusters?
Click
✅

InfiniBand is high-speed interconnect (400 Gb/s) for cross-node GPU communication. Critical for multi-node training where gradient sync crosses node boundaries.

📖 EXPLANATION
Ethernet: 100 Gb/s, ~50μs latency
InfiniBand NDR400: 400 Gb/s, <1μs latency, RDMA support
# Multi-node training: 40% time = gradient communication. IB reduces this to <10%.

Chapter 26: NVIDIA GPU Operator 🎯🔴 Advanced · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 26: The NVIDIA GPU Operator — Your GPU Autopilot on OpenShift

The NVIDIA GPU Operator is the single most important operator for AI workloads on OpenShift. It automates the ENTIRE GPU lifecycle: detecting GPU hardware via NFD, installing the correct driver version for each GPU model, configuring CRI-O to recognize NVIDIA runtimes, deploying the Kubernetes device plugin so pods can request nvidia.com/gpu: 1, and setting up DCGM for GPU metrics export to Prometheus. Without it, you'd manually install drivers on each node, configure runtimes, deploy device plugins, and handle driver updates — hours of error-prone work per node. One ClusterPolicy CR controls everything. This chapter is critical: GPU management is 35% of EX267 and 35% of NCP-AII.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🔺 GPU Operator🎯 EX267 35%🔺 NCP-AII

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "What Does the GPU Operator Do, Step by Step?"

Think of the GPU Operator as an automated mechanic for each GPU node: Step 1: NFD (Node Feature Discovery) scans the PCI bus and labels nodes with GPU info (feature.node.kubernetes.io/pci-10de.present=true — 10de is NVIDIA's PCI vendor ID). Step 2: The GPU Operator sees these labels and deploys driver containers to matching nodes. Step 3: Drivers compile against the node's kernel (RHEL CoreOS) and load. Step 4: The NVIDIA Container Toolkit configures CRI-O to pass GPUs through to containers. Step 5: The device plugin advertises nvidia.com/gpu: 8 (or however many GPUs the node has) to the Kubernetes scheduler. Step 6: DCGM Exporter starts streaming GPU metrics to Prometheus. All of this is controlled by a single ClusterPolicy CR — change the driver version and the Operator performs a rolling update across all GPU nodes automatically. This is the Operator pattern at its finest: encode human operational knowledge into software that runs 24/7.

26.1 Installing the GPU Operator

🔧 GPU Operator Install Flow
1️⃣ NFD Operator → Labels GPU nodes (pci-10de.present=true)
2️⃣ GPU Operator → Installs drivers + toolkit + device plugin
3️⃣ ClusterPolicy CR → Triggers driver deployment on GPU nodes
4️⃣ DCGM Exporter → GPU metrics → Prometheus
5️⃣ Verify: oc describe node | grep nvidia → nvidia.com/gpu: 1

Order matters: 1. Node Feature Discovery (auto-labels GPU nodes). 2. NVIDIA GPU Operator. 3. ClusterPolicy CR (triggers driver deployment). Verify: oc get pods -n nvidia-gpu-operator, nvidia-smi from test pod, oc describe node | grep nvidia.

26.2 GPU Driver Management

📦
ClusterPolicy CR

Single CR controls driver version, toolkit, device plugin across ALL GPU nodes. Change spec.driver.version to upgrade/downgrade all nodes.

🔄
Rolling Update Strategy

GPU Operator drains pods → uninstalls old driver → installs new driver → reboot node → uncordon. One node at a time. Zero-downtime for multi-node clusters.

⚠️
Version Pinning

Pin driver version for production: spec.driver.version: "550.54.15". Auto-update only in dev. Driver mismatch = GPU pods stuck in Pending.

✅
Verification

nvidia-smi inside any GPU pod. oc describe node gpu-node | grep nvidia. Both must show expected driver version and GPU count.

Driver versions controlled via spec.driver.version in ClusterPolicy. Updates: rolling, one node at a time with pod draining. Pin version for stability; auto-update for latest CUDA features. Driver mismatch = GPU unavailable.

26.3 GPU Monitoring with DCGM

MetricKeyAlert If
GPU UtilizationDCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL<10% for 30min (idle = waste)
VRAM UsedDCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED>90% (risk of OOM)
GPU TemperatureDCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP>85°C (throttling)
ECC ErrorsDCGM_FI_DEV_ECC_CURRENT>0 (hardware issue)

26.4 GPU Node Labeling

NFD auto-labels: nvidia.com/gpu.present=true, nvidia.com/gpu.count=N, nvidia.com/gpu.product=A100-SXM4-40GB. Use for nodeSelectors. Always taint GPU nodes: oc adm taint node gpu-node nvidia.com/gpu=true:NoSchedule — prevents CPU workloads from wasting expensive GPUs.

🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 26

Core task: Install NFD → GPU Operator → ClusterPolicy. Verify: oc describe node | grep nvidia, nvidia-smi from test pod. Gotcha: Driver mismatch = GPU unavailable. Pin version in ClusterPolicy for stability.

Q1

What DCGM metric alerts for overheating GPU before it throttles?
Click
✅

DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP — Warning 80°C, Critical 85°C. Also monitor DCGM_FI_DEV_SLOWDOWN_TEMP.

📖 EXPLANATION
# PrometheusRule for GPU thermal alerting:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata: { name: gpu-thermal-alerts, namespace: nvidia-gpu-operator }
spec:
  groups:
  - name: gpu-thermal
    rules:
    - alert: GPUHighTemperature
      expr: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP > 85
      for: 5m
      labels: { severity: critical }
      annotations:
        summary: "GPU {{ $labels.gpu }} at {{ $value }}°C — THROTTLING"
    - alert: GPUWarmTemperature
      expr: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP > 80
      for: 10m
      labels: { severity: warning }

✅

ClusterPolicy controls: driver version/install, toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter, MIG strategy, GPU Feature Discovery labels.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: { name: gpu-cluster-policy }
spec:
  driver: { enabled: true, version: "550.54.15" }
  toolkit: { enabled: true }
  devicePlugin: { enabled: true }
  dcgmExporter: { enabled: true }
  mig: { strategy: mixed }

Chapter 27: Hardware Sizing & Capacity Planning🔴 Advanced

Chapter 27: Right-Sizing Your AI Infrastructure

GPU hardware is the single largest cost in any AI platform. A single H100 costs ~$30K and draws 700W. Multiply by 8 for a DGX, then by racks for a cluster — you're making million-dollar decisions. Over-provisioning wastes hundreds of thousands yearly; under-provisioning bottlenecks your entire data science team, where each hour of idle GPU time from a $200K/year ML engineer represents real business cost. This chapter gives you the concrete formulas, strategies, and rules of thumb to size exactly right.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours📐 Sizing💰 Cost

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "Why Is GPU Sizing So Hard?"

Unlike CPU sizing (where 1 core = 1 thread and you just count), GPU sizing involves four interdependent variables that all affect each other:

1. Model size (params × precision): A 7B parameter model in FP16 needs ~14GB just to load. But training needs 4× more (model + gradients + optimizer + activations). Inference needs less but must fit the full model in VRAM.

2. Batch size: Bigger batches = better GPU utilization = faster training. But bigger batches = more VRAM. You're always trading batch size against model size within a fixed VRAM budget.

3. Concurrency: 10 data scientists don't use 10 GPUs simultaneously. Real concurrency is ~60% at peak. But when they ALL need GPUs (demo day, deadline week), you need burst capacity.

4. Workload type: Notebook exploration (1 GPU, bursty), training jobs (GPUs, hours), inference (fractional GPU via MIG, 24/7). Each has different utilization patterns and cost profiles.

The golden rule: Monitor DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL weekly. Target 60-80% average. Below 40% = over-provisioned (wasting money). Above 85% sustained = under-provisioned (bottlenecking your team).

27.1 Estimating Requirements

📐 GPU Sizing Formula
VRAM_required = params × bytes_per_param × 4 × batch_overhead
├── params: 7B (Llama-7B), 70B (Llama-70B), 175B (GPT-3)
├── bytes: FP32=4, FP16=2, INT8=1, INT4=0.5
├── ×4 factor: model + gradients + optimizer_states + activations
└── batch_overhead: +10-20% for batch data + KV cache

Examples:
7B FP16:  7B×2×4 = 56GB  → 1× A100 80GB ✅
70B FP16: 70B×2×4 = 560GB → 7× A100 80GB (model parallel)
70B INT4: 70B×0.5×4 = 140GB → 2× A100 80GB + KV cache ≈ 2-3× A100

VRAM formula: model_params × bytes_per_param × 4 (model + gradients + optimizer + activations). FP16: ~8 bytes/param. Example: 7B model = 56GB minimum + 20% batch overhead = ~67GB. anihpj (<1B): 1× A10 (24GB). LLM fine-tune (7B): 1× A100 (80GB). LLM train (70B): 8+× H100.

27.2 Cluster Sizing for AI — A Systematic Approach

Step-by-step sizing methodology:

1️⃣
Count Users & Workloads

How many concurrent notebook users? How many training jobs run daily? How many inference endpoints are always-on? Example: 20 DS × 60% concurrency = 12 active GPUs for notebooks.

2️⃣
Profile Model Sizes

What's the largest model the team trains? 7B LoRA (~25GB) or 70B full (~560GB)? This determines minimum GPU VRAM. Multiply by precision (FP16=2, INT4=0.5).

3️⃣
Add Concurrency Buffer

Peak vs average: add 30% headroom above average concurrent usage. For 12 active GPUs → provision 16. Use MIG to subdivide: 2 A100 × 7 MIG slices = 14 logical GPUs.

4️⃣
Separate Training & Inference

Training needs full GPUs for hours. Inference needs fractional GPUs 24/7. Use node taints + tolerations to dedicate GPU nodes to each workload type — prevents resource contention.

Key sizing factors: concurrent notebook users (1 GPU each minimum), pipeline training jobs (full GPU for duration), inference endpoints (GPU fraction via MIG or time-slicing), 30% dev headroom. Dedicate GPU nodes with taints — keep CPU workloads on separate nodes to avoid wasting expensive GPU capacity on non-AI tasks. A $30K GPU running a web server is a $30K mistake.

27.3 Cost Optimization — 6 Strategies That Actually Work

💰 GPU Cost Optimization Pyramid — From Easy Wins to Advanced
                        ▲ 6. Schedule Off-Peak (20% savings)
                       ▲▲ 5. KPA Scale-to-Zero (50%+ savings for sporadic)
                      ▲▲▲ 4. ModelMesh Multi-Tenancy (1 GPU → 50+ models)
                     ▲▲▲▲ 3. Idle Notebook Culling (saves $60/day/GPU)
                    ▲▲▲▲▲ 2. MIG Partitioning (1 A100 → 7 isolated GPUs)
                   ▲▲▲▲▲▲ 1. Spot/Preemptible Instances (60-80% cheaper)

    COMBINED: $100/hr on-demand → as low as $5/hr (95% reduction)
    But: spot can terminate → requires checkpointing + fault tolerance

1. Spot/Preemptible instances — 60-80% cheaper but can terminate. Use with checkpointing: save model every N steps, resume on new instance. AWS Spot A100: ~$1.00/hr vs $3.76/hr on-demand.

2. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) — Hardware-level GPU partitioning. 1 A100 → up to 7 isolated instances, each with dedicated memory and compute. 7 data scientists share 1 GPU without interference. Each gets guaranteed VRAM and compute slice.

3. Idle notebook culling — Auto-stop notebooks after inactivity (default: 24h, set to 1h). GPU pods terminate → no GPU charges. Workspace PVC persists. User relaunches when needed. Easy 50%+ savings for overnight idle.

4. ModelMesh multi-tenancy — 1 GPU serves 50+ models simultaneously by sharing the runtime. Models loaded/unloaded on demand. 50× more efficient than 1 GPU per model.

5. KPA scale-to-zero — Inference pods scale to 0 when idle → zero cost. Cold start penalty: ~30s on first request. Use for internal/dev models; avoid for user-facing (latency-sensitive) endpoints.

6. Schedule training off-peak — Run large training jobs at night/weekends when spot prices drop and on-prem GPUs would otherwise be idle. Kubernetes CronJob or pipeline schedule: schedule: "0 2 * * 0" (Sunday 2 AM).

27.4 Multi-Cloud GPU Strategy

WorkloadPrimary CloudBurst/BackupStrategy
Training (predictable)On-prem DGXAWS p4d (spot)On-prem first, burst when queue > 4hrs
Training (elastic)AWS spot (60% off)Azure ND (spot)Multi-cloud spot with checkpointing
Inference (always-on)Primary cloud GPU nodesN/ASmall fixed pool, no scale-to-zero
Inference (sporadic)KPA scale-to-zeroFallback to CPU if GPU unavailableScale-to-zero → no cost when idle

Primary GPUs on main cloud. Burst to secondary when spot instances available. On-prem DGX for predictable workloads. Avoid single-cloud lock-in for GPU availability.

Chapter 28: Beyond NVIDIA — The Broader AI Hardware Landscape

While NVIDIA dominates the AI hardware market with ~85% share, a deeper understanding of the full hardware landscape makes you a better AI platform engineer. This chapter explores WHY different hardware exists (the physics behind it), what alternatives are emerging, how to evaluate them, and what the future holds — all through the lens of OpenShift integration.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour🔬 HardwareNCP-AII

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "Why Can't We Just All Use the Same Chips?"

The short answer: Different AI tasks have radically different hardware needs. Training a GPT-scale model requires massively parallel matrix multiplication (NVIDIA/AMD GPUs). Running that model on a phone needs ultra-low power (Apple Neural Engine). Real-time video AI in a factory needs deterministic microsecond latency (FPGAs). Massive-scale cloud inference needs the lowest cost per query (Google TPUs, AWS Inferentia). There is no "one chip to rule them all" — each is optimized for a different point on the power × performance × cost × flexibility spectrum.

For your EX267 exam: Only NVIDIA GPU management is tested. But understanding why NVIDIA dominates (CUDA ecosystem, 15+ years of library maturity, first-class K8s operator) helps you reason about GPU scheduling decisions and justify infrastructure choices to stakeholders.

28.2 FPGA & ASIC Acceleration — When GPUs Are Overkill

FPGAs (Field-Programmable Gate Arrays) and ASICs (Application-Specific Integrated Circuits) represent the "custom hardware" end of the spectrum. They sacrifice programmability for extreme efficiency on a narrow set of operations.

TypeLatencyPowerFlexibilityDev ComplexityUse Case
FPGA (Xilinx Alveo)<1ms25-75WReprogrammable (VHDL/Verilog)High (hardware design skills)Financial trading, real-time video transcoding, network inference at edge
ASIC (Google TPU, AWS Inferentia)<0.5msVery lowFixed functionLow (use their SDK)Cloud-scale inference, specific model architectures
GPU (NVIDIA A100)1-10ms300-700WGeneral purpose (CUDA/PyTorch)Low (Python)Training + inference, any model, any framework

FPGA Deep Dive: FPGAs contain arrays of programmable logic blocks that you configure at the hardware level. This means you can build a circuit that does EXACTLY your model's forward pass — no instruction fetch/decode overhead, no cache misses, no branch prediction failures. The result is deterministic, single-digit-microsecond inference latency that no GPU can match. The trade-off: you need hardware engineers who write VHDL/Verilog. Tools like Xilinx Vitis AI bridge this gap by compiling TensorFlow/PyTorch models directly to FPGA bitstreams.

ASIC Deep Dive: ASICs are the ultimate optimization — a chip designed for ONE thing. Google's TPU is an ASIC optimized for TensorFlow's XLA compiler operations: matrix multiplication (systolic array architecture) and convolution. AWS Trainium/Inferentia are ASICs for the Neuron SDK. The downside: you can't run PyTorch on a TPU (easily), and you can't run TensorFlow on Inferentia. ASICs create platform lock-in — but for cloud-scale deployments, the 30-50% cost savings justify it.

On OpenShift: The Xilinx Alveo FPGA Operator exists in OperatorHub, allowing FPGA acceleration for specific workloads. However, it's extremely niche — only use when you have a documented latency requirement under 1ms that GPUs can't meet.

28.3 Future AI Hardware Trends — What's Coming and Why It Matters

Why you should care: Hardware evolution directly shapes what's possible in AI. The reason ChatGPT exists isn't just better algorithms — it's H100 GPUs with FP8 Tensor Cores and 900 GB/s NVLink. Understanding hardware trends helps you plan infrastructure 3-5 years ahead.

In-Memory ComputingMatrix multiplication inside RAM cells — data never moves to a compute unit. Eliminates the von Neumann bottleneck entirely.Samsung, Mythic, Untether AI2026+Potentially eliminates VRAM constraints for inference. Could run LLMs on CPU-class hardware.
