Deep-Dive: Multi-Node GPU Training, Networking, Storage & Cluster Management

This chapter amplifies your NCP-AII preparation with advanced NVIDIA infrastructure topics: NCCL tuning for multi-node training, InfiniBand/RoCE configuration, GPUDirect Storage, NVIDIA Base Command, power management, and production GPU cluster operations.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🔺 NCP-AII Core35%
🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "Why does NCP-AII care so much about networking and storage?"

When training a 70B+ parameter model across 8+ GPUs, the GPUs spend ~40% of their time communicating gradients, not computing. Slow networking = wasted GPU time = wasted money. At $30,000+ per H100, every millisecond of GPU idle time matters. NCCL tuning (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) and InfiniBand/RoCE are how you maximize GPU utilization in multi-node setups. GPUDirect Storage bypasses CPU memory when loading training data — crucial when your dataset is terabytes and you're paying for GPU hours.

28B.1 Multi-Node GPU Training — NCCL Deep Dive

🔄 NCCL — How GPUs Communicate During Distributed Training
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    NCCL COMMUNICATION PATTERNS                             │
│                                                                            │
│  All-Reduce (gradient sync):  All GPUs sum gradients → distribute         │
│  ┌─────┐    ┌─────┐    ┌─────┐    ┌─────┐                                │
│  │GPU 0│◄──▶│GPU 1│◄──▶│GPU 2│◄──▶│GPU 3│   ← Ring topology               │
│  └─────┘    └─────┘    └─────┘    └─────┘     ← Most common pattern       │
│                                                                            │
│  Node 1 (DGX H100)              Node 2 (DGX H100)                         │
│  ┌──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┐    ┌──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┐                 │
│  │G0│G1│G2│G3│G4│G5│G6│G7│    │G0│G1│G2│G3│G4│G5│G6│G7│                 │
│  └──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┘    └──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┴──┘                 │
│       │ NVSwitch (3.6 TB/s)         │ NVSwitch (3.6 TB/s)                  │
│       │                             │                                      │
│       └───── InfiniBand NDR400 ─────┘  ← 400 Gb/s cross-node              │
│                                                                            │
│  NCCL Tuning Parameters:                                                   │
│  NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0        Enable InfiniBand                                │
│  NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5     GPUDirect RDMA (GPU→NIC, bypass CPU)            │
│  NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0  Network interface                                │
│  NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5_0,mlx5_1  InfiniBand adapters                           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
NCCL Env VarRecommended ValueWhat It Controls
NCCL_DEBUGINFO (WARN in prod)Logging verbosity for diagnosing comm issues
NCCL_IB_DISABLE0Enable InfiniBand (0=enabled, 1=fallback to TCP)
NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL5GPUDirect RDMA: 0=off, 5=GPU→NIC direct (fastest)
NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAMEeth0 or ib0Network interface for GPU comms
NCCL_IB_HCAmlx5_0,mlx5_1Specific InfiniBand HCAs to use
NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX3 (RoCEv2)GID table index for RoCE
NCCL_TOPO_FILE/var/run/.../virtualTopology.xmlGPU topology for optimal routing
NCCL_NSOCKS_PERTHREAD4Sockets per thread for multi-rail networking
Shell — Multi-Node Training Launch with NCCL📋
# Node 0 (master): 192.168.1.10
torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc_per_node=8 \
  --node_rank=0 --master_addr=192.168.1.10 --master_port=29500 \
  train.py --backend=nccl

# Node 1 (worker): 192.168.1.11
torchrun --nnodes=2 --nproc_per_node=8 \
  --node_rank=1 --master_addr=192.168.1.10 --master_port=29500 \
  train.py --backend=nccl

# Verify NCCL topology:
nvidia-smi topo -m          # GPU topology map
nccl-tests/build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 128M -f 2 -g 8  # Bandwidth test

28B.2 InfiniBand & RoCE Configuration

TechnologySpeedLatencyGPU DirectBest For
InfiniBand HDR200 Gb/s~1μsGPUDirect RDMA ✅A100 clusters
InfiniBand NDR400 Gb/s~1μsGPUDirect RDMA ✅H100/DGX clusters
InfiniBand XDR800 Gb/s<1μsGPUDirect RDMA ✅Next-gen (2025+)
RoCE v2100-400 Gb/s~2-5μsGPUDirect RDMA ✅Ethernet-based, lower cost
Standard TCP/IP25-100 Gb/s~50μs❌ CPU bounceSmall clusters, dev only

RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) uses standard Ethernet switches with RDMA-capable NICs — 50% cheaper than InfiniBand but 2-5μs higher latency. For NCP-AII: know that GPUDirect RDMA is the key advantage — it lets GPU memory talk directly to the network card, bypassing CPU entirely. Configure via NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5 and NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0.

28B.3 GPUDirect Storage — Bypassing CPU for Data Loading

📦 GPUDirect Storage vs Traditional Data Loading
Traditional (CPU bottleneck):
  NVMe ──▶ CPU RAM ──▶ GPU VRAM   (CPU copies every byte, ~25 GB/s max)

GPUDirect Storage (DMA):
  NVMe ──────────────────▶ GPU VRAM   (DMA engine bypasses CPU, ~100+ GB/s)

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  GPUDirect Storage Benefits:                                      │
│  • 4× faster data loading (bypasses CPU)                         │
│  • CPU freed for compute tasks                                   │
│  • Critical when dataset > GPU VRAM (streaming from NVMe)        │
│  • Requires: NVIDIA GPU Driver 525+, CUDA 12+, supported NVMe    │
│  • Enable: nvidia-fs.ko kernel module                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Use case for anihpj: When training on millions of job postings, GPUDirect Storage streams data directly from local NVMe drives to GPU VRAM — eliminating the CPU as a bottleneck. This is especially important for multi-modal models processing job descriptions + images.

28B.6 NVIDIA Container Toolkit Deep Dive

🐳 NVIDIA Container Toolkit — How GPU Containers Work
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Container (e.g., PyTorch training)                               │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │  PyTorch → CUDA → libcuda.so → /dev/nvidia0            │     │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│       │                                                           │
│       │ nvidia-container-runtime (OCI hook)                       │
│       ▼                                                           │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │  nvidia-container-toolkit                                │     │
│  │  • Mounts: /dev/nvidia*, /usr/lib64/libcuda*            │     │
│  │  • Sets: NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1                     │     │
│  │  • Configures: cgroups, device nodes                    │     │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│       │                                                           │
│       ▼                                                           │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │  Host: NVIDIA Driver + CUDA Toolkit + GPU Hardware      │     │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The GPU Operator deploys the NVIDIA Container Toolkit automatically. For NCP-AII: understand that nvidia-container-runtime is an OCI-compliant runtime hook that injects GPU drivers and device nodes into containers at creation time — this is why you don't need CUDA installed inside the container image.

🔺 NCP-AII Exam Focus — Chapter 28B

NCCL env vars: NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5, NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0. Gotcha: Multi-node training = 40% time in gradient communication. GPUDirect RDMA + InfiniBand reduces this to <10%.

Q1
What NCCL environment variable enables GPUDirect RDMA, and what level provides maximum performance?

Q2
When would you choose RoCE v2 over InfiniBand for GPU cluster networking?
Click
✅

RoCE when: budget constrained (50% cheaper), existing Ethernet, 2-5μs OK. IB when: max perf, <1μs latency.

📖 EXPLANATION
RoCE v2 (400GbE):               InfiniBand NDR400:
Latency: 2-5μs                   Latency: <1μs
Cost: ~$5K/port                  Cost: ~$10K/port
Infra: Uses existing Ethernet    Infra: Separate IB fabric needed
NCCL: NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX=3        NCCL: Native IB verbs
# Both support GPUDirect RDMA; choose based on latency/cost tradeoff
Q3
How does GPUDirect Storage improve training throughput?
Click
✅

NVMe→GPU VRAM DMA, bypassing CPU. 4× faster, CPU-free data loading.

📖 EXPLANATION
Without GDS: NVMe → CPU RAM → GPU VRAM  (~25 GB/s, CPU-loaded)
With GDS:    NVMe → GPU VRAM            (~100 GB/s, CPU-free!)
Requirements: NVIDIA driver 525+, CUDA 12+, nvidia-fs.ko, supported NVMe
# 4× faster, CPU available for other compute during data loading
Q4
What happens when a GPU hits its thermal throttle threshold (85°C)?
Click
✅

GPU auto-reduces clock speeds → 10-30% performance drop. Alert when DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP > 85.

📖 EXPLANATION
Monitor: nvidia-smi dmon -s pucvmet
Alert: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP > 85 → warning → action
Fixes:
1. Improve DC cooling (lower ambient to 25°C target)
2. Set power cap: nvidia-smi -pl 250  (reduce TDP)
3. Reduce workload density per GPU
# Every 10°C above 75°C = ~5% clock reduction
Q5
How does the NVIDIA Container Toolkit enable GPU access in containers without CUDA installed in the image?
Click
✅

nvidia-container-runtime OCI hook injects host GPU drivers/libraries into container at creation.

📖 EXPLANATION
Container Runtime Hook:
1. Mounts /dev/nvidia* device nodes
2. Mounts /usr/lib64/libcuda* + cuBLAS, cuDNN from host
3. Sets NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all
4. Configures cgroups for GPU access
# Container image only needs CUDA app layer (cuBLAS/cuDNN), not kernel driver
# Saves 500MB+ in image size; driver from host, never in container
Q6
What NCCL_DEBUG level should you use for troubleshooting?
Click
✅

NCCL_DEBUG=INFO for troubleshooting; WARN for production. VERBOSE/TRACE for deep debugging communication issues.

📖 EXPLANATION
export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO     # Shows: ring formation, bandwidth, topology
export NCCL_DEBUG=WARN     # Production: only warnings/errors
export NCCL_DEBUG=TRACE    # Extreme detail — for NCCL bug reports only
Q7
How does NCCL ring topology work for all-reduce?
Click
✅

GPUs form a logical ring. Each GPU sends gradients to next, receives from previous. After N-1 steps, all GPUs have the summed result.

📖 EXPLANATION
GPU0→GPU1→GPU2→GPU3→GPU0 (ring)
Step1: GPU0 recvs G3, sends G0; GPU1 recvs G0, sends G1...
Step2: Each GPU now has 2 gradients summed
Step3: After N-1 steps, all GPUs have complete sum
# Ring all-reduce: O(N) bandwidth, optimal for large messages
Q8
What is GPUDirect RDMA and when is it needed?
Click
✅

GPUDirect RDMA allows GPU memory → NIC direct DMA without CPU involvement. Needed for multi-node training to avoid CPU bounce buffer bottleneck.

📖 EXPLANATION
Without GDR: GPU→CPU RAM→NIC→network (bottleneck at CPU, ~25 GB/s)
With GDR:    GPU→NIC→network (CPU-free, ~100+ GB/s)
# Enable: NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5, NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0
Q9
How do you configure NCCL for RoCE v2 networks?
Click
✅

Set NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX=3 (RoCEv2), NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0, and ensure PFC/ECN QoS is configured on the network.

📖 EXPLANATION
export NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0
export NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX=3      # RoCEv2 GID index
export NCCL_IB_HCA=mlx5_0       # Specific HCA
export NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0
# RoCEv2 needs: PFC + ECN on switch, lossless Ethernet
Q10
What tools validate GPU cluster health before production?
Click
✅

DCGM diagnostics (Level 3), NCCL tests (all_reduce_perf), nvidia-smi topo -m, bandwidthTest. Run ALL before deploying production workloads.

📖 EXPLANATION
dcgmi diag -r 3              # Full GPU diagnostic (memory, PCIe, thermal)
all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 128M -g 8  # NCCL bandwidth test
nvidia-smi topo -m           # GPU topology + affinity
bandwidthTest --device=all   # Host↔Device bandwidth
# All must pass before accepting GPU nodes into production

28C.1 CUDA Programming Model — Infrastructure Perspective

🧩 CUDA Execution Model — Thread Hierarchy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CUDA KERNEL LAUNCH: myKernel<<<grid, block>>>(args)             │
│                                                                    │
│  Grid (entire GPU)                                                 │
│  ├── Block 0 ── SM 0                                              │
│  │   ├── Warp 0 (32 threads) → SIMD unit                          │
│  │   ├── Warp 1 (32 threads) → SIMD unit                          │
│  │   └── ... (up to 32 warps/block)                                │
│  ├── Block 1 ── SM 1                                              │
│  │   └── Warps...                                                  │
│  └── Block N ── SM N                                              │
│                                                                    │
│  Key Metrics for Infrastructure Operators:                        │
│  • Occupancy: active_warps / max_warps_per_SM (target >50%)       │
│  • Register pressure: too many registers → fewer warps → low occ  │
│  • Shared memory: 48-164 KB/SM (H100: 228 KB/SM)                  │
│  • Grid-stride loops: efficient for large datasets                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
ConceptWhat It MeansInfrastructure Impact
ThreadSingle execution unit — runs CUDA instructionMillions active simultaneously
Warp32 threads executing in lockstep (SIMD)Scheduling unit — 4 warps/SM on H100
BlockGroup of threads sharing shared memoryMust fit on single SM's resources
GridAll blocks for one kernel launchSpans entire GPU across all SMs
StreamSequence of operations (kernels + mem copies)Concurrent execution via multiple streams
Occupancy% of maximum warps active per SMHigher = better latency hiding; tune via registers/shared mem

#!/bin/bash
# GPU cluster acceptance test
echo "=== GPU Inventory ===" && nvidia-smi -L
echo "=== GPU Topology ===" && nvidia-smi topo -m

echo "=== NCCL All-Reduce Bandwidth ==="

echo "=== GPU Acceptance Complete ==="

28C.3 MIG Partitioning — Production Strategies

MIG ProfileVRAMComputeInstances/GPUBest For
1g.5gb5 GB1/7 compute7Light inference, dev notebooks
1g.6gb6 GB1/77 (A100)Small model inference (BERT, etc.)
1g.12gb12 GB1/77 (H100)LLM inference (7B FP8)
2g.12gb12 GB2/73Training small models
3g.20gb20 GB3/72Training medium models
4g.24gb24 GB4/71Full GPU for training
7g.80gb (full)80 GB7/71LLM training (no MIG)
✅ MIG Best Practices
  • Pin inference to 1g instances, training to 2g/3g
  • Label nodes with MIG profile for scheduling
  • Use MIG for multi-tenant production
  • MIG instances are hardware-isolated — no noisy neighbor
⚠️ MIG Limitations
  • A100/H100 only — not on L40S or A10
  • Cannot mix MIG and non-MIG on same GPU
  • Reboot required to change MIG config
  • NVLink unavailable between MIG instances

vGPU use case: Virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) for data scientists who need GPU workstations, cloud providers offering GPU VM instances. Uses NVIDIA GRID/vGPU driver with license server. For NCP-AII: know the difference between vGPU (VM-level), MIG (container-level), and time-slicing (software-level).

28C.6 Slurm + GPU Clusters — HPC Integration

Shell — Slurm GPU Job Submission📋
# Request 4 GPUs on 2 nodes for PyTorch training
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-training
#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=4
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:4           # 4 GPUs per node
#SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1      # 1 GPU per task
#SBATCH --partition=gpu-h100
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00

# Load NVIDIA environment
module load cuda/12.2 nccl/2.19

# Launch distributed training
srun --mpi=pmi2 torchrun --nnodes=$SLURM_NNODES \
  --nproc_per_node=$SLURM_NTASKS_PER_NODE \
  --node_rank=$SLURM_NODEID \
  --master_addr=$(scontrol show hostname $SLURM_NODELIST | head -n1) \
  --master_port=29500 \
  train.py --backend=nccl

Slurm is the dominant scheduler in HPC GPU clusters. It handles GPU allocation via GRES (Generic Resource Scheduling) — similar to Kubernetes resource requests but optimized for HPC batch workloads. NCP-AII expects familiarity with Slurm's GPU scheduling model alongside Kubernetes.

# Reboot required                       nvidia.com/gpu: 4
# MIG: prod multi-tenant              # SW sharing, no VRAM isolation
                                      # Any GPU, no reboot needed
                                      # Time-slicing: dev/test/experiments
Q4
What's the difference between vGPU, MIG, and time-slicing for GPU sharing?
Click
✅

vGPU: VM-level (GRID+license). MIG: Hardware-level (free). Time-slicing: Software-level (free).

📖 EXPLANATION
vGPU: Hypervisor (VMware/KVM) → VMs share GPU → needs GRID license + license server
MIG: GPU hardware partition → K8s pods → free, A100/H100 only
Time-slicing: GPU time share → K8s pods → free, any GPU, no VRAM isolation
# Choose: vGPU for VDI/VM infra, MIG for production K8s, time-slicing for dev
Q5
How do you configure Slurm to allocate specific GPU types (e.g., H100 for training, A10 for inference)?
Click
✅

GPU-specific partitions in slurm.conf + gres.conf → #SBATCH --gres=gpu:h100:4.

📖 EXPLANATION
# slurm.conf:
PartitionName=gpu-h100 Nodes=node[01-08] MaxTime=24:00:00
PartitionName=gpu-a10 Nodes=node[09-16] MaxTime=UNLIMITED
GresTypes=gpu
# gres.conf:
NodeName=node01 Gres=gpu:h100:8
NodeName=node09 Gres=gpu:a10:4
# Submit: #SBATCH --gres=gpu:h100:4 --partition=gpu-h100
# Result: Training→H100, Inference→A10, never conflict
Q6
What is CUDA stream concurrency and why does it matter?
Click
✅

CUDA streams allow concurrent kernel execution + memory transfers. Overlapping compute with data movement hides latency and improves GPU utilization.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Without streams (sequential):
H2D_copy → kernel → D2H_copy → H2D_copy → kernel → ...  (GPU idle during transfers)
# With streams (concurrent):
Stream1: H2D_copy → kernel → D2H_copy
Stream2:     H2D_copy → kernel → D2H_copy    # Overlap hiding transfer latency
Q7
What MIG profile would you use for BERT inference?
Click
✅

1g.10gb or 2g.20gb on A100. BERT (~400M params) needs ~2GB for model + KV cache. 1g.10gb is sufficient.

📖 EXPLANATION
BERT-base: 0.4B params × 2 bytes = 0.8GB + KV cache(2GB) + overhead = ~4GB
1g.10gb: fine for BERT inference (10GB > 4GB)
2g.20gb: for BERT fine-tuning (need optimizer states + gradients)
Q8
How does vGPU differ from GPU passthrough?
Click
✅

vGPU: hypervisor partitions GPU for VMs (time-sliced or MIG-backed). Passthrough: entire GPU assigned to one VM. vGPU = sharing; passthrough = dedicated.

📖 EXPLANATION
vGPU: GRID license + license server → 1 A100 → 16 vGPU profiles (time-sliced)
Passthrough: PCIe device assigned to VM → 1 GPU = 1 VM
# OpenShift uses MIG (HW-level) for containers, not vGPU (VM-level)
Q9
What NVIDIA Magnum IO components are relevant for AI?
Click
✅

GPUDirect Storage (NVMe→GPU DMA), GPUDirect RDMA (GPU→NIC), NCCL (GPU collective comms), NVSwitch (all-to-all fabric).

📖 EXPLANATION
Magnum IO Stack:
├── GPUDirect Storage: NVMe → GPU (100+ GB/s, bypass CPU)
├── GPUDirect RDMA: GPU → NIC → network (bypass CPU)
├── NCCL: GPU collective communications library
└── NVSwitch: 8-GPU all-to-all at 3.6 TB/s
Q10
What is NVAIE licensing and what does it include?
Click
✅

NVIDIA AI Enterprise: licensed GPU Operator, certified drivers, 24/7 support, NGC catalog access, RMA coordination. Per-GPU annual subscription.

📖 EXPLANATION
NVAIE includes:
- GPU Operator (production license)
- Certified drivers (R550/R560 branches)
- NGC private registry access
- 24/7 enterprise support + RMA
- RHEL/RHCOS kernel compatibility guarantee
# Pricing: ~$4,500/GPU/year (list), volume discounts available

Chapter 29: Keeping Your AI Systems Healthy

Monitoring is critical for production AI — you need visibility into GPU utilization, model performance, pipeline success rates, and resource consumption. OpenShift provides a comprehensive monitoring stack with Prometheus, Grafana, AlertManager, and DCGM for GPU metrics.

OpenShift's built-in monitoring: Prometheus (metrics collection, 15-day retention), Thanos (long-term storage), Grafana (dashboards), AlertManager (alert routing). For GPU: DCGM exports GPU metrics. For user workloads: enable user-workload monitoring to scrape your model serving and pipeline metrics.

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "What Should I Actually Monitor?"

You don't need 100 dashboards. Focus on 4 key questions: 1) Is the hardware healthy? (GPU utilization, memory, temperature — DCGM dashboard). 2) Are my models working? (inference latency, error rate, prediction drift — custom metrics). 3) Are pipelines succeeding? (success/fail rate, duration — pipeline dashboard). 4) Am I wasting money? (idle GPUs, oversized instances, unused PVCs — cost dashboard). If you can answer these 4 questions in under 30 seconds, your monitoring is good enough for production.

29.2 Custom AI Metrics

Python — Expose Prometheus Metrics in Inference Pod📋
from prometheus_client import Histogram, Counter, Gauge, start_http_server
import time

# Define metrics
pred_latency = Histogram('prediction_latency_seconds', 'Inference latency',
                         buckets=[0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.5, 5.0])
pred_total = Counter('predictions_total', 'Total predictions served')
model_ver = Gauge('model_version', 'Serving model version')
drift_score = Gauge('drift_score', 'Data drift score (KL divergence)')

start_http_server(8000)  # Expose on :8000/metrics

@pred_latency.time()
def predict(text):
    result = model(text)
    pred_total.inc()
    model_ver.set(2)      # Update version when deployed
    drift_score.set(0.03) # From monitoring pipeline
    return result

After exposing, create a ServiceMonitor to scrape :8000/metrics, then a PrometheusRule to alert: drift_score > 0.3 → warning, prediction_latency_seconds{quantile="0.99"} > 1.0 → critical.

29.3 Grafana Dashboards

OpenShift ships with pre-built Grafana dashboards. For AI: NVIDIA DCGM Dashboard (auto-deployed with GPU Operator) and the OpenShift AI Dashboard (model serving metrics). Custom dashboards: create in Administrator → Monitoring → Dashboards or via GrafanaOperator CR.

29.3a AI Dashboard Blueprint

🔹 GPU Health Row

GPU utilization %, memory used, temperature, power draw, ECC errors. Red alert if GPU temp > 85°C or utilization < 10% (idle GPU leaking cost).

🔹 Cluster Health Row

Node CPU/RAM, pod restarts, PVC usage %, ClusterOperator status. Amber alert if any operator Degraded.

🔹 Model Performance Row

Inference latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput (req/s), error rate (4xx/5xx), prediction drift score. Red alert if p99 latency > 500ms or error rate > 1%.

🔹 Pipeline Status Row

Pipeline runs (success/fail), run duration, artifact size. Amber alert if failure rate > 10%.

🔹 Alerts Row

Active firing alerts from AlertManager. Grouped by severity: Critical (page on-call), Warning (Slack notification), Info (ticket created).

Define via PrometheusRule CR. Silence during maintenance: oc create -f silence.yaml or via AlertManager UI. Stay out of alert fatigue: only pages should wake people up at night.

29.5 Logging & Audit

Stack: Vector (collector) → Loki (store) → Grafana (query). Structured JSON logging recommended. Key log queries: {pod=~"inference-.*"} |= "ERROR", {namespace="anihpj-prod"} | json | latency > 1. Retention: app logs 7d, audit logs 30d minimum (compliance). Enable audit logging via ClusterLogForwarder CR.

29.6 DCGM Integration

DCGM is deployed by the GPU Operator. Metrics flow: GPU → DCGM daemon → nvidia-dcgm-exporter pod → Prometheus → Grafana. Key metrics: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL (utilization %), DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED (VRAM bytes), DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP (°C), DCGM_FI_DEV_ECC_CURRENT (error count). Access via Monitoring → Dashboards → NVIDIA DCGM Exporter Dashboard. ServiceMonitor auto-created by GPU Operator — no manual config needed.

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata: { name: model-accuracy-alert }
spec:
  groups:
  - name: ai-metrics

      labels: { severity: critical }
      annotations:

29.8 Bias & Drift Monitoring — Red Hat's AI Monitoring Framework (v3.4)

🆕 From Official Red Hat Docs — "Monitoring your AI Systems"

Red Hat OpenShift AI includes built-in bias and data drift monitoring. Configure metrics, set thresholds, and visualize drift over time. This is what separates "we deployed a model" from "we operate a model responsibly." EX267 tests your ability to set up monitoring for production AI.

MetricWhat It DetectsExample AlertFix
Data DriftInput data distribution changing from training baseline"Feature 'salary' mean shifted 2.3 std devs"Retrain on recent data
Concept DriftRelationship between features and labels changing"Model predictions diverging from actuals"Retrain with new labels
Prediction DriftModel output distribution shifting over time"% positive predictions dropped from 65% to 30%"Investigate, possible data issue

For anihpj: Monitor if job recommendations maintain consistent quality across job categories and demographics. If "Tech" jobs consistently rank higher than "Healthcare" jobs for similar queries → bias alert. If model predictions shift after a new batch of job postings → drift alert → trigger automated retraining pipeline.

Chapter 30: Troubleshooting AI Workloads 🎯🔴 Advanced · 🎯 EX267

Chapter 30: Diagnosing and Fixing AI Issues — The Platform Engineer's Superpower

When something breaks — and it will — the difference between a 5-minute fix and a 5-hour debugging session is having a systematic methodology. AI workloads add unique failure modes: GPU driver mismatches, CUDA out-of-memory errors, NCCL communication timeouts, model download failures from S3, cold-start latency spikes. This chapter teaches you the diagnostic framework, universal commands, and common failure patterns that turn chaos into clarity.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🔧 Troubleshoot🎯 EX267 10%

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — The Troubleshooting Mindset

The #1 mistake: jumping to conclusions. You see "CrashLoopBackOff" and immediately edit the Deployment YAML. Don't. The pod that crashed has logs — but the pod that's currently crashing may have already overwritten them.

The golden sequence that solves 80% of issues:

1. Verify context: oc whoami && oc project. Are you even in the right namespace? This simple check prevents hours of confusion.

2. Check the cluster diary: oc get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -20. Kubernetes records EVERY significant event — pod scheduled, image pulled, OOM kill, volume mounted. The root cause is often in the last 5 lines. This is the most underused debugging tool.

3. Look at the LAST crash, not the current state: oc logs <pod> --previous. If a pod is crash-looping, the current logs might be empty (container hasn't started yet). The --previous flag shows what happened in the previous instance.

4. Describe tells the story: oc describe pod <name> — look at the Events section at the bottom. It's a chronological narrative: "Scheduled on node X → Pulling image → Created container → Started → ... → OOMKilled." Read it like a story.

5. Never change two things at once. If you change the memory limit AND the SCC AND the image tag simultaneously and the problem goes away, you don't know which fixed it. One change, one verify, one document.

30.0 Troubleshooting Decision Tree

Notebook Won't Start

Check: PVC bound? → GPU available? → Image pull succeeds? → Resource quota not exceeded? → oc describe notebook → events section.

Pipeline Step Fails

Check: Pod logs → Artifact S3 access → Resource limits → Input data schema → oc describe pipelinerun → failed step details.

Model Serving Timeout

Check: Pod CPU/memory → GPU utilization → Cold start? → Scale-to-zero delay? → oc describe inferenceservice → conditions.

Universal First Commands

oc get pods → oc describe pod → oc logs --tail=50 → oc get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'. These 4 commands solve 80% of issues.

30.1 Systematic Troubleshooting Methodology

🔍 6-Step AI Troubleshooting Decision Tree
START: Something is broken
│
├─ Step 1: oc whoami && oc project        → Wrong context? Fix and retry.
│
├─ Step 2: oc get pods -o wide            → Pod CrashLoopBackOff? Pending? OOMKilled?
│    ├─ Pending → oc describe pod → check Events for "Insufficient GPU" / "Scheduler"
│    ├─ CrashLoop → oc logs --previous → check traceback
│    └─ OOMKilled → Check resource limits; increase memory
│
├─ Step 3: oc get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -20
│    → The cluster diary — often reveals root cause in first 5 lines
│
├─ Step 4: oc describe pod/notebook/serving → Volumes, Env, Images, Limits, SCC
│
├─ Step 5: oc debug pod/<name> -- /bin/bash  → Interactive diagnosis inside the pod
│
└─ Step 6: Fix, verify (oc get), and document (oc annotate)

Follow this order: 1) Check context (oc whoami, oc project). 2) Check pod status (oc get pods). 3) Check events (cluster diary). 4) Check logs (oc logs --previous if crashed). 5) Describe resource (oc describe). 6) Debug interactively (oc debug). Never skip steps — the event log often shows the root cause before you check logs.

Predictor crashOOM — model too large for memoryoc describe pod → OOMKilledIncrease memory limit or use smaller model
Cold start timeoutScale-to-zero delay too long on first request503 → eventually 200 after ~30sSet minReplicas: 1 or increase timeout
GPU not availableNode taints not toleratedPod Pending — no GPU nodesAdd toleration for GPU taint in IS spec
High latencyUndersized GPU or too many modelsp99 latency > 1sUse bigger GPU, enable MIG, or reduce model count

30.5 GPU Troubleshooting — The Deep End

GPU issues are the hardest to diagnose because the failure can be at any layer: physical hardware → driver → container runtime → Kubernetes device plugin → pod SCC → application code. Here's how to systematically isolate each layer:

🔺 GPU Debugging Layers — Top to Bottom
LAYER 6: Application  → "RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory" → torch.cuda.memory_summary()
LAYER 5: Framework    → "CUDA error: no kernel image available" → Check CUDA version vs PyTorch
LAYER 4: Pod/Container→ "nvidia-smi: command not found" → Wrong base image, no CUDA tools
LAYER 3: Device Plugin→ "nvidia.com/gpu: 0" → GPU Operator not running, ClusterPolicy broken
LAYER 2: Driver       → "NVIDIA-SMI has failed" → Driver mismatch, needs reinstall
LAYER 1: Hardware     → GPU not detected at all → PCIe issue, power, physical failure
LAYER 0: Node/Kubelet → Node NotReady → kubelet down, disk pressure, network partition

🎯 RULE: Always diagnose bottom-up. Layer 0-2 affect ALL pods. Layer 3-5 affect some pods. Layer 6 is per-workload.
ProblemRoot Cause ChainDiagnostic CommandsFix
GPU not on nodeNFD missing → GPU Operator missing → ClusterPolicy not created → driver not installedoc describe node \| grep nvidia → oc get pods -n nvidia-gpu-operatorInstall NFD → Install GPU Operator → Create ClusterPolicy → Wait for driver pods
Pod can't use GPUSCC not privileged → quota exhausted → node taint not tolerated → device plugin not readyoc describe pod \| grep -A5 Events → oc describe quotaoc adm policy add-scc-to-user privileged -z default or create custom SCC
nvidia-smi fails in podDriver not loaded on host → NVIDIA runtime not configured → container lacks CUDA toolsoc debug node/<gpu-node> -- nvidia-smi → oc exec <pod> -- nvidia-smiUse nvidia/cuda:12.x-runtime base image; verify driver on host
GPU visible but unusedModel doesn't use CUDA → .to('cpu') instead of .to('cuda') → wrong framework configtorch.cuda.is_available() in notebook → nvidia-smi dmon while runningCheck code: model.to('cuda'), device='cuda' in training config
MIG not workingMIG mode not enabled in ClusterPolicy → wrong MIG profile → GPU doesn't support MIGoc get clusterpolicy -o yaml \| grep mig → nvidia-smi mig -lgipEnable MIG in ClusterPolicy → reboot GPU nodes → create MIG instances
CUDA Out of MemoryModel too large for VRAM → batch size too big → memory leak → no gradient checkpointingtorch.cuda.memory_summary() → nvidia-smi → check VRAM usageReduce batch size, enable gradient checkpointing, use LoRA, increase GPU count
🎯 EX267 Exam Focus — Chapter 30 (10% of exam!)

Universal 4 commands: get pods → describe pod → logs --previous → get events. Gotcha: Cold start 503 = minReplicas:0. Fix with minReplicas:1 or increase scaleDownDelay.

Q1

oc describe pod  | grep -A10 Events   # Step 1: Why Pending?
# Events: 0/3 nodes: insufficient nvidia.com/gpu, PVC not bound, etc.
oc get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -20  # Step 2: Cluster view

Q2
A pipeline step fails with OOMKilled. What's the fix?
Click
✅

Check actual memory → Increase limit OR optimize (chunks, Dask/Spark).

📖 EXPLANATION
# Diagnose:
oc describe pod  | grep OOMKilled
oc logs  --previous  # Check what was running at OOM
# Fix options:
1. Increase: resources.limits.memory: 16Gi → 32Gi
2. Optimize: process data in chunks, use Dask for out-of-core
3. Reduce batch size: batch_size: 64 → 32
Q3
A deployed model endpoint returns 503 for 30 seconds, then starts working. What happened and how do you fix it permanently?
Click
✅

Cold start from scale-to-zero. minReplicas: 1 or increase scaleDownDelay.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Problem:
minReplicas: 0 + idle > scaleDownDelay → pod terminated → cold start on next req
# Fix:
minReplicas: 1  # Always warm, costs GPU, eliminates cold starts
# OR:
scaleDownDelay: 300s  # Keep pod 5 min after last request, reduces cold starts
# anihpj: user-facing recommendations → minReplicas≥1 always
Q4
You run nvidia-smi inside a GPU pod and get "command not found." The GPU operator is installed and running. Why?
Click
✅

SCC mismatch or container image lacks CUDA tools.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Check 1: SCC
oc adm policy add-scc-to-user privileged -z default -n 
# Check 2: Image — use CUDA base
FROM nvidia/cuda:12.0-base  # includes nvidia-smi
FROM python:3.11             # does NOT include nvidia-smi!
# Check 3: Verify driver on host (bypass container)
oc debug node/ -- nvidia-smi
Q5
An InferenceService shows "StorageNotAccessible" in conditions. What are the possible root causes?
Click
✅

Check in order: 1) oc get secret — does the Data Connection secret exist? Is it in the right namespace? 2) oc describe secret <dc-name> — correct keys? (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY). 3) S3 bucket permissions — does the IAM role/user have s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket? 4) Network — can the cluster reach S3 endpoint? (check egress NetworkPolicy). 5) storageUri syntax — must match s3://bucket/key exactly. Use oc describe inferenceservice to see the exact error message in the conditions section.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Diagnostic chain:
oc get secret -n  | grep aws         # Secret exists?
oc describe secret aws-connection        # Correct keys?
oc describe isvc  | grep -A5 Conditions  # Exact error
# Fix: oc create secret generic aws-connection --from-literal=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... --from-literal=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
# Labels: opendatahub.io/dashboard: "true", opendatahub.io/managed: "true"

31.1 Backup & Disaster Recovery

🔐 AI Platform DR Strategy — RPO/RTO by Component
COMPONENT            RPO (Max Data Loss)     RTO (Max Downtime)     METHOD
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
etcd (cluster brain)   < 1 hour                < 4 hours             etcd backup + S3
Model Registry DB      < 15 minutes            < 2 hours             DB replication
PVCs (training data)   < 24 hours              < 8 hours             CSI snapshots
InferenceServices      0 (re-deploy)            < 10 min              GitOps (ArgoCD)
Notebooks              < 24 hours              < 1 hour              PVC backup
GPU drivers/config     0 (Operator re-applies)  < 30 min              OperatorHub

🔑 Key: etcd backup is non-negotiable. Without it, you can't rebuild the cluster.
    oc get backup -n openshift-etcd → verify last successful backup.
WhatToolFrequencyRPO
PVC snapshots (notebooks, DB)CSI VolumeSnapshotsDaily<24h
S3 buckets (artifacts, models)NooBaa replication / VeleroContinuous<1h
Model Registry metadataVelero (etcd + CRs)Daily<24h
Cluster state (etcd)OpenShift built-in (etcd backup)Every 15 min (auto)<15min
Custom resources (DSC, DSProjects)Velero / GitOps backupOn change (Git)<5min (git push)

DR test: Monthly — restore a PVC snapshot to a new namespace, verify notebooks launch and models load. If you haven't tested restore, you don't have a backup.

31.2 Upgrading OpenShift AI

Shell — OpenShift AI Upgrade Procedure📋
# 1. Check current version
oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator
# NAME                              DISPLAY           VERSION
# rhods-operator.v2.8.0             Red Hat OpenShift AI   2.8.0

# 2. Change subscription channel (if needed)
oc patch subscription rhods-operator -n redhat-ods-operator \
  --type merge -p '{"spec":{"channel":"stable-2.9"}}'

# 3. Approve new InstallPlan
oc get installplan -n redhat-ods-operator
oc patch installplan install-xxxxx -n redhat-ods-operator \
  --type merge -p '{"spec":{"approved":true}}'

# 4. Verify reconciliation
oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator   # Must show Succeeded
oc get dsc                           # All components Ready
oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications  # All Running

Always: test in staging first, backup before upgrade, check release notes for breaking changes. Never upgrade on a Friday.

Secret encryptionetcd encryption at restoc patch apiserver cluster --type merge -p '{"spec":{"encryption":{"type":"aescbc"}}}'

✅

Velero backup:                     CSI VolumeSnapshot:

Includes: CRs, Deployments, PVCs   Includes: PVC data only

Upgrade Plan (skipped 6 months = ~3 minor versions):
1. Read release notes: stable-2.6→2.7→2.8→2.9 (ALL changes)
2. Deploy staging cluster, replicate prod
3. Backup: Velero full + CSI snapshots
4. Upgrade: 2.6→2.7 → health check → 2.7→2.8 → health check → 2.8→2.9
   Health check: oc get dsc, launch notebook, run pipeline, test inference

Q6
How do you set up automated daily PVC snapshots?
Click
✅

Create a CronJob that creates VolumeSnapshots with timestamped names. CSI driver must support snapshots.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata: { name: daily-pvc-snapshot }
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"  # 2 AM daily
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: snapshot
            image: bitnami/kubectl
            command: [sh, -c]
            args: ["oc create volumesnapshot notebook-snap-$(date +%Y%m%d) --pvc-name notebook-workspace"]

Chapter 32: Performance Tuning for AI Workloads🔴 Advanced

Chapter 32: Squeeze Every Drop of Performance from Your AI Platform

Performance tuning is what separates a functional AI platform from a production-grade one. This chapter covers optimizing training throughput, inference latency, storage I/O, and network bandwidth — each can be worth 3-10× speed improvements when tuned correctly.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours⚡ Performance🛠️ Production
🎯 The Four Dimensions of AI Performance Tuning
                    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │         AI PERFORMANCE TUNING                 │
                    │                                              │
                    │  🧠 Training         🚀 Inference            │
                    │  ├─ Mixed precision  ├─ Batching & queue    │
                    │  ├─ Gradient accum   ├─ Quantization (INT8)  │
                    │  ├─ Data loader opts ├─ TensorRT / vLLM      │
                    │  └─ NCCL tuning      └─ KPA/HPA scaling      │
                    │                                              │
                    │  💾 Storage           🌐 Network             │
                    │  ├─ PVC IOPS/through  ├─ CNI plugin choice   │
                    │  ├─ Local SSD vs NFS  ├─ NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME  │
                    │  ├─ S3 parallel reads ├─ Jumbo frames (MTU)  │
                    │  └─ CSI driver choice └─ InfiniBand/RoCE     │
                    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

32.1 Optimizing Training Performance

TechniqueSpeedupHow to EnableTrade-off
Mixed Precision (FP16/BF16)2-3×torch.cuda.amp() or --fp16 flagSlight accuracy loss (<0.5%)
Gradient AccumulationFits larger batches--gradient_accumulation_steps 4Slower convergence per step
DataLoader Workers1.5-3×num_workers=4-8, pin_memory=TrueHigher CPU usage
TF32 on A100/H1003-5×Auto-enabled — tensor core accelerated FP32None (same accuracy)
NCCL Tuning1.3-2×NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=NVL NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0Complexity
FSDP/DeepSpeedLinear with GPUs--fsdp full_shard or DeepSpeed configCommunication overhead

32.2 Optimizing Inference Performance

📦
Batching Strategies

Static batching: Fixed batch size, predictable latency. Dynamic batching: Accumulates requests for N ms then processes together. 2-10× throughput improvement. Configure in KServe: runtime.knative.dev/batching-max-size: "32"

⚡
Quantization

INT8: 4× smaller, 2-3× faster. INT4: 8× smaller, 3-4× faster. Accuracy: INT8 <1% loss, INT4 1-3% loss. Use bitsandbytes for LLMs, TensorRT for vision models.

🚀
TensorRT/vLLM

TensorRT: NVIDIA's inference optimizer — kernel fusion, precision calibration, kernel auto-tuning. vLLM: PagedAttention for LLMs — 24× higher throughput than naive HuggingFace.

📊
Autoscaling Tuning

KPA: Scale-to-zero after idle. HPA: CPU/GPU-based. Set target: "60" (CPU) or DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL > 80. Min replicas = 1 for latency-sensitive; 0 for cost-sensitive.

32.3 Storage Performance Tuning

Storage TypeIOPSThroughputBest ForConfig
Local NVMe SSD500K+3-7 GB/sTraining data, swapHostPath or LocalVolume CSI
Network Block (EBS/PD)16K-64K250-4750 MB/sPVCs for notebooksgp3/Performance tier
NFS/Filestore5K-50K100-1200 MB/sShared datasetsReadWriteMany PVC
S3 (NooBaa/MinIO)VariableVariableModel artifacts, checkpointsParallel reads (boto3 config)
GPUDirect StorageNVIDIADirect GPU↔StorageLarge model loadingGDS-enabled CSI driver

Key tuning: Use storageClassName: gp3-csi with iops: 16000 and throughput: 1000 for training PVCs. For S3: enable parallel reads with boto3 TransferConfig.

32.4 Network Performance Tuning

🌐 Multi-Node GPU Communication — NCCL Environment Variables
# Critical NCCL tuning for multi-node GPU training:
NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0           # Use correct network interface
NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0                 # Enable InfiniBand (0=on)
NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5              # GPUDirect RDMA (max performance)
NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=NVL                # NVLink for intra-node
NCCL_NSOCKS_PERTHREAD=4           # More sockets = faster all-reduce
NCCL_SOCKET_NTHREADS=2            # Thread count for socket ops
NCCL_MIN_NCHANNELS=4              # Min channels for ring all-reduce

# Performance tiers:
# 🥇 GPUDirect RDMA over InfiniBand: 200+ GB/s (H100 NVLink)
# 🥈 RoCE v2: 100 GB/s
# 🥉 Standard Ethernet: 25-100 Gbps
# Before tuning: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO to see what's actually being used
InterconnectBandwidthLatencyMulti-Node Scaling
NVLink 4.0 (H100)900 GB/s~1 µsIntra-node only
InfiniBand NDR400400 GB/s<1 µsExcellent (linear to 1000s GPUs)
RoCE v2100-200 GB/s1-3 µsGood (needs DCQCN tuning)
Ethernet 100GbE100 Gbps10-50 µsModerate (ECMP hashing issues)
⚡ EX267 Speed Tip — Performance Tuning

On EX267: performance tuning questions are usually straightforward — enable mixed precision, set num_workers, configure KPA scale-to-zero. Memorize: NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME, num_workers=4, --fp16 flag. Always verify with oc describe pod | grep -A5 Limits that GPU limits are set correctly.

📝 Chapter 32 Practice Questions

Q1
What is mixed precision training and how much speedup does it typically provide?
Click
✅

Mixed precision uses FP16/BF16 for most operations while keeping critical computations in FP32. Speedup: 2-3× on A100/H100 GPUs with Tensor Cores.

📖 EXPLANATION
import torch
scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()
with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
    output = model(input)
    loss = criterion(output, target)
scaler.scale(loss).backward()
scaler.step(optimizer)
scaler.update()
# Or CLI: python train.py --fp16  (HuggingFace Trainer)
Q2
How do you configure DataLoader workers for optimal GPU training?
Click
✅

Rule of thumb: num_workers = 4 × GPUs. Set pin_memory=True for faster CPU→GPU transfer. Use persistent_workers=True to avoid worker restart between epochs.

📖 EXPLANATION
train_loader = DataLoader(
    dataset, batch_size=64,
    num_workers=8,       # 4×GPUs (for 2 GPUs)
    pin_memory=True,     # CPU pinned → GPU faster
    persistent_workers=True,  # Reuse workers across epochs
    prefetch_factor=4    # Prefetch 4 batches per worker
)
Q3
What is NCCL and why does tuning it matter for multi-GPU training?
Click
✅

NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) handles GPU-to-GPU communication for all-reduce, all-gather, broadcast ops. Tuning NCCL can yield 1.3-2× training speedup on multi-GPU setups.

📖 EXPLANATION
NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=NVL       # Use NVLink for GPU-GPU (intra-node)
NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0        # Enable InfiniBand (inter-node)
NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0  # Correct network interface
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO           # Verify what NCCL is using
# In OpenShift: set via env in Deployment/Pod spec
Q4
What is model quantization and when should you use INT8 vs INT4?
Click
✅

Quantization reduces model precision from FP32 to INT8 (4× smaller, 2-3× faster) or INT4 (8× smaller, 3-4× faster). INT8: production inference with <1% accuracy loss. INT4: edge deployment or extreme cost savings (1-3% accuracy loss).

📖 EXPLANATION
# Using bitsandbytes for LLM quantization:
from transformers import BitsAndBytesConfig
bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,           # INT4 quantization
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True  # Double quantization
)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "meta-llama/Llama-2-7b",
    quantization_config=bnb_config
)
Q5
How do you configure autoscaling for KServe inference services?
Click
✅

Use KPA (Knative Pod Autoscaler) for scale-to-zero or HPA for resource-based scaling. Configure via annotations on InferenceService.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-recommender
  annotations:
    autoscaling.knative.dev/min-scale: "1"
    autoscaling.knative.dev/max-scale: "10"
    autoscaling.knative.dev/target: "50"     # Concurrency target
    autoscaling.knative.dev/scale-down-delay: "300s"
Q6
What storage class is best for AI training PVCs and why?
Click
✅

Local NVMe SSD-backed storage (e.g., AWS gp3 with high IOPS, or local CSI driver) for training data. High IOPS (16K+) and throughput (1+ GB/s) are critical to keep GPUs fed with data.

📖 EXPLANATION
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: { name: training-data-fast }
spec:
  storageClassName: gp3-csi  # AWS EBS gp3
  resources: { requests: { storage: 500Gi } }
  # On AWS: gp3 defaults 3000 IOPS, 125 MB/s
  # For training: provisioned 16000 IOPS, 1000 MB/s (extra cost)
Q7
What is GPUDirect Storage (GDS) and when does it help?
Click
✅

GDS enables direct data transfer between GPU memory and NVMe storage, bypassing CPU. Helpful for: loading large models (70B+ params), streaming training data from fast NVMe arrays, checkpoint saving/loading.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Requisites: NVIDIA GPU (A100+), NVMe SSD, GDS-enabled CSI driver
# Enabling in CUDA:
cuFileDriverOpen()
cuFileBufRegister(gpu_buffer, size, 0)  # Register GPU memory
cuFileRead(fh, gpu_buffer, size, offset, 0)  # Direct GPU read
# In OpenShift: use GDS-enabled CSI driver, mount NVMe with HostPath
Q8
What NCCL environment variables are most critical for multi-node GPU training?
Click
✅

NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME (network interface), NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0 (enable InfiniBand), NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=NVL (NVLink for intra-node), NCCL_DEBUG=INFO (verify configuration).

📖 EXPLANATION
# Pod env spec for multi-node training:
env:
- name: NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME
  value: "eth0"          # Must match actual network interface
- name: NCCL_IB_DISABLE
  value: "0"             # 0 = InfiniBand enabled
- name: NCCL_P2P_LEVEL
  value: "NVL"           # NVLink for GPU-to-GPU within node
- name: NCCL_DEBUG
  value: "INFO"          # Verify: shows which transport NCCL uses
Q9
How does TensorRT optimize inference and what speedup can you expect?
Click
✅

TensorRT applies: layer fusion (merges ops), precision calibration (FP32→FP16/INT8), and kernel auto-tuning (selects best CUDA kernels). Speedup: 3-10× for vision models, 2-5× for LLMs vs naive PyTorch inference.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Convert ONNX to TensorRT engine:
trtexec --onnx=model.onnx --saveEngine=model.trt --fp16
# In KServe: use Triton with TensorRT backend
# InferenceService spec → format: triton, runtime: tensorrt
# Expected: 5-10× faster than raw PyTorch ONNX inference
Q10
What are the key storage and network bottlenecks for AI workloads on OpenShift?
Click
✅

Storage: Insufficient IOPS causing GPU idle time (GPUs wait for data), network-attached storage latency, S3 single-threaded reads. Network: Wrong NCCL interface, missing InfiniBand config, Ethernet bottlenecks for all-reduce.

📖 EXPLANATION
# Diagnose GPU idle from storage:
nvidia-smi dmon -s pucvmet -d 2  # Watch GPU utilization
# If GPU util drops to 0% periodically → data loading bottleneck
# Fix: increase num_workers, use local SSD, enable GDS

# Diagnose network bottleneck in NCCL:
NCCL_DEBUG=WARN python train.py 2>&1 | grep "NCCL"
# Look for: "using Network" (Ethernet) vs "using NET/IB" (InfiniBand)

Chapter 33: EX267 Exam Deep Dive🎯 EXAM

Chapter 33: Everything You Need to Know About EX267

EX267 — Red Hat Certified Developer in AI — is a 2-hour, performance-based exam. You perform real tasks on a live OpenShift cluster. This chapter covers the exam format, screen layout, objectives breakdown, and proven exam-day strategies.

🎯 EXAM⏱️ ~30 min📋 Prep

33.0 Exam Screen Layout

Question Panel (Left 40%)

Task description with specific requirements. Read carefully — keywords like "configure," "create," "verify" tell you exactly what to do. Tasks are grouped by domain.

Terminal (Bottom Left)

Multiple terminal tabs available. Pre-configured with oc already logged in. You can open additional terminals. oc explain is your best friend.

Browser + Console (Right 60%)

OpenShift Console + official Red Hat documentation. Documentation is PROVIDED — use it! Search for CRD specs, API references, and examples.

33.1 Exam Format

DetailValue
Duration2 hours
FormatPerformance-based (hands-on)
Passing Score68% (210 out of 300 points)
EnvironmentLive OpenShift cluster with AI components
DocumentationProvided — official Red Hat docs accessible

33.2 Exam Objectives Breakdown

DomainWeightCovered In
Manage OpenShift AI installation & configuration35%Ch 5, 6, 11, 13
Manage data science pipelines30%Ch 9, 10, 15, 19
Manage model development & serving25%Ch 14, 17, 18, 22, 23
Monitor & troubleshoot10%Ch 29, 30

33.3 Scoring & Passing

Each task has a point value. Partial credit is sometimes awarded. Tasks are NOT weighted equally — installation tasks (35%) carry more weight. Prioritize high-weight domains. You need 210/300 to pass. Unfinished tasks score 0 — always submit SOMETHING.

33.4 Exam Day Strategy

🎯 Proven EX267 Strategy
  1. First 5 min: Scan ALL tasks. Flag easy ones (quick wins). Note high-point tasks.
  2. Next 30 min: Complete all easy tasks first — build confidence and rack up points.
  3. Next 60 min: Tackle medium/hard tasks grouped by domain. Stay in the same mental context.
  4. Next 15 min: Review and verify. Run oc get on every resource you created.
  5. Final 10 min: Submit partial work on unfinished tasks. Something > nothing.
  6. DO: Use oc explain constantly, check docs for YAML examples, verify each task before moving on. DON'T: Get stuck on one task >10 min, forget to switch projects, leave tasks blank.
🎓 Beyond EX267 — NCP-AII Certification Path

This guide also prepares you for the NVIDIA-Certified Professional: AI Infrastructure (NCP-AII) exam. Key NCP-AII topics covered: GPU architecture (Ch 25), GPU Operator (Ch 26), DCGM monitoring (Ch 29), MIG configuration (Ch 25), multi-GPU training (Ch 17/20), and hardware sizing (Ch 27). NCP-AII focuses more on infrastructure and GPU management, while EX267 focuses on the OpenShift AI application layer. Together they provide complete AI platform expertise.

Chapter 37: Production AI Architecture🛠️ Practical

Chapter 37: Designing Production AI Systems

Moving from prototype to production requires thoughtful architecture — data pipelines, training infrastructure, serving endpoints, observability, and security all working together. This chapter provides the blueprint.

🛠️ Practical⏱️ ~1 hour🏗️ Architecture

37.0 Complete AI Platform Architecture

Data Layer

S3 (NooBaa/MinIO), PostgreSQL, Kafka streaming, DVC versioning. All data sources connected via Data Connections.

Training Layer

GPU nodes (A100/H100), Jupyter notebooks, Katib tuning, MLflow tracking, PyTorch DDP distributed training.

Serving Layer

KServe single-model, ModelMesh multi-model, vLLM/TGI for LLMs, Triton for max throughput.

Observability

Prometheus/Grafana, DCGM GPU metrics, TrustyAI bias/drift, AlertManager, Kibana logs.

Security + CI/CD

Tekton pipelines, GitOps (ArgoCD), RBAC/SCC, NetworkPolicy, image scanning, audit logs.

37.1 End-to-End MLOps Pipeline

🔄 Complete MLOps Loop on OpenShift AI
Data Collection        Feature Eng         Training              Eval          Registry        Deploy         Monitor
    │                      │                  │                   │               │               │              │
    │  S3/Postgres/Kafka   │ Jupyter          │ GPU Nodes         │ Katib        │ MLflow        │ KServe       │ Prometheus
    │  ──────────────────▶ │ ───────────────▶ │ ────────────────▶ │ ───────────▶ │ ────────────▶ │ ───────────▶ │ ─────┐
    │                      │                  │                   │               │               │              │      │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                                                    ▲                                                                  │
                                                                    └──────────── Retraining Trigger (drift > threshold) ───────────┘

Tekton Pipeline: [Data Check] → [Preprocess] → [Train] → [Evaluate] → [Register] → [Build Serving Image] → [Canary Deploy]
GitOps (ArgoCD): watches model registry → auto-syncs InferenceService with new model version

37.2 Multi-Environment Deployments

EnvInfraGPUDataPromotion Gate
DevCRC or shared clusterNone / MIG sliceSynthetic / sampledTests pass + model > baseline
StagingDedicated project, prod-like1× A10/L4Anonymized prod sampleLoad test pass + accuracy > 85%
ProductionHA, multi-AZ, dedicated GPU nodes2+× A100/L40SFull production dataCanary 10% → 50% → 100%

Image promotion: oc tag anihpj:staging anihpj:production. Model promotion: Model Registry stage transition. Never build in production — promote to it.

37.3 High Availability for AI

LayerHA StrategyRPORTO
TrainingCheckpoint every N steps → resume from last checkpointN steps of work<5 min (reschedule)
ServingMulti-replica KServe (minReplicas=2), anti-affinity across AZsZero (stateless)<30s (KPA rescale)
StorageS3 cross-region replication (NooBaa), CSI snapshots for PVCs<1 hour<15 min
Control Plane3 master nodes (etcd quorum), Operator Lifecycle Manager auto-recoveryZero<5 min
GPU NodesN+1 redundancy, node cordon + PodDisruptionBudget, spare node poolZero<2 min (reschedule)

37.4 Multi-Tenant AI Platform

Isolation MechanismWhat It ProtectsExample
Data Science ProjectsNamespace-level isolationteam-search, team-recommend
Resource QuotasCPU/GPU/RAM limits per teamteam-search: 2 GPU, team-recommend: 4 GPU
Network PoliciesPod-to-pod communicationteam-search pods can't reach team-recommend DB
MIG PartitioningGPU memory/bandwidth isolationA100 → 7× MIG slices (1 per data scientist)
RBACWho can do whatDS team: edit in their project, view in staging
GPU Node PoolsDedicated hardwareNodeSelector + taints per team GPU pool

Golden rule: one Data Science Project per team. Lock down with NetworkPolicy deny-all then allow specific egress. MIG prevents noisy-neighbor GPU interference.

38.4 Security Implementation

anihpj Security Configuration
# NetworkPolicy: Django can only talk to Postgres + Redis
kind: NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
metadata: { name: django-egress, namespace: anihpj-prod }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: anihpj } }
  egress:
  - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: postgres } } }]
    ports: [{ port: 5432 }]
  - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: redis } } }]
    ports: [{ port: 6379 }]
  policyTypes: [Egress]

# RBAC: CI/CD SA has edit, developers have view
oc policy add-role-to-user edit -z cicd-sa -n anihpj-prod
oc policy add-role-to-user view -z developer -n anihpj-prod

# Secret rotation via External Secrets Operator:
# AWS Secrets Manager → Sync → Kubernetes Secret

38.6 Complete Production Dockerfile

anihpj Production Dockerfile
# Stage 1: Build
FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/python-311 AS builder
USER 0
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Stage 2: Runtime
FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/python-311
USER 1001
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app /app
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/healthz || exit 1
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8080", "--workers", "4", "--timeout", "120"]

38.7 Kubernetes Manifests

anihpj Core Manifests
# Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1; kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: anihpj, namespace: anihpj-prod }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: anihpj } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: anihpj } }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: anihpj:latest
        ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
          limits: { cpu: 1000m, memory: 512Mi }
        livenessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }, initialDelaySeconds: 30 }
        readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }, initialDelaySeconds: 10 }
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef: { name: django-config }
        - secretRef: { name: db-credentials }
---
# HPA
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2; kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: anihpj-hpa, namespace: anihpj-prod }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { kind: Deployment, name: anihpj }
  minReplicas: 3; maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 } }

38.8 Tekton CI/CD Pipeline

Tekton Pipeline Definition
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1; kind: Pipeline
metadata: { name: anihpj-ci-cd, namespace: anihpj-prod }
spec:
  params:
  - { name: git-url, type: string }
  - { name: image-tag, type: string }
  workspaces: [{ name: source }]
  tasks:
  - name: clone
    taskRef: { name: git-clone }
    params: [{ name: url, value: "$(params.git-url)" }]
  - name: build
    taskRef: { name: s2i-python }
    runAfter: [clone]
    params: [{ name: IMAGE, value: "image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/anihpj-prod/anihpj:$(params.image-tag)" }]
  - name: test
    taskRef: { name: pytest }
    runAfter: [build]
  - name: deploy-staging
    taskRef: { name: oc-deploy }
    runAfter: [test]
    params: [{ name: ENV, value: staging }]
  - name: smoke-test
    taskRef: { name: curl-test }
    runAfter: [deploy-staging]
  - name: promote-prod
    taskRef: { name: oc-tag }
    runAfter: [smoke-test]
    params: [{ name: FROM, value: "anihpj-staging/anihpj:$(params.image-tag)" },
             { name: TO, value: "anihpj-prod/anihpj:prod" }]

Chapter 39: AI Platform Engineering (SRE)🛠️ Practical

Chapter 39: Running AI Platforms Like a Pro

AI Platform Engineering combines MLOps with SRE (Site Reliability Engineering). This chapter covers SLIs/SLOs, incident response, capacity planning, team structure, and the future of AI platforms.

🛠️ Practical⏱️ ~1 hour🔧 SRE

39.1 SLIs, SLOs, SLAs for AI Platforms

SLI (Indicator)SLO (Objective)SLA (Agreement)
Inference p95 latency<200ms99.9% of requests <200ms
Model accuracy (F1)>85%Monthly accuracy audit >85%
Training job success rate>95%Failed jobs retried within 1hr
Inference availability99.9%99.5% — penalty if breached
GPU utilization50-70%Alert if <10% or >90% sustained

Start loose, tighten over time. First month: track SLIs without SLOs. Second month: set SLOs at p90 actual. Third month: tighten to p95/p99. Error budgets: SLO 99.9% = 43min downtime/month allowed. Use it for planned maintenance.

39.2 Incident Response for AI Systems

IncidentSymptomImmediate ActionRoot Cause Fix
Model Accuracy DropDrift score alert firesRollback model to previous versionRetrain with new data, investigate drift source
GPU Node FailureGPUUnavailable alertCordon node, pods reschedule automaticallyReplace GPU, verify DCGM metrics
Inference Latency Spikep99 > 1s alertScale up replicas immediatelyProfile model, optimize batch size, check GPU VRAM
Pipeline Cascade Fail3 consecutive failuresStop dependent pipelines, check root step logsFix root step, backfill data, resume pipeline

Incident Command: 1. Acknowledge alert. 2. Assess impact (how many users affected?). 3. Mitigate (restore service first, investigate later). 4. Resolve + postmortem. Each incident type has a runbook with exact commands to run.

39.3 Capacity Planning

MetricTrack PeriodTrigger to Add CapacityLead Time
GPU-hours/weekWeekly trend>70% sustained for 2 weeks4-6 weeks (GPU procurement)
Inference req/sDaily peakGrowth >20% month-over-month1 week (add replicas)
Model training frequencyMonthlyNew model type added2 weeks (GPU provisioning)
Storage growthWeekly>20% month-over-month1 week (expand PVC/S3)

Pre-provisioning: For anihpj, if "Black Friday" brings 10× traffic, pre-warm 10 inference replicas. Use spot instances for elastic training capacity (60-80% cheaper, with checkpointing to handle preemption).

39.8 AI Platform Engineer's Manifesto

🔹 Automate Everything

Manual steps don't scale. Tekton pipelines + GitOps (ArgoCD) + Operator Lifecycle Manager. If it's not in Git, it doesn't exist.

🔹 Monitor What Matters

Four questions: hardware healthy? models working? pipelines succeeding? money wasted? Answer in <30 seconds.

🔹 Design for Failure

Everything breaks eventually. Checkpoint training, multi-replica serving, cross-AZ storage, N+1 GPUs, automated rollback.

🔹 Version Everything

Code (Git), data (DVC), models (MLflow/Registry), configs (GitOps), images (ImageStream tags). Reproducibility = production safety.

🔹 Least Privilege Always

RBAC per Data Science Project, SCC for GPU access only, NetworkPolicy deny-all + allow-list, encrypted secrets at rest.

🔹 Data Scientists Are Your Customers

Make their lives easier — self-service notebooks, pre-configured images, auto-scaling inference. Platform should be invisible.

🔹 Keep Learning

AI infrastructure evolves monthly. New GPUs, new serving frameworks, new operators. Subscribe to OpenShift AI release notes + NVIDIA developer blog.

🔹 Ship It

Done is better than perfect. Deploy, monitor, iterate. Production feedback > endless optimization. Your users will tell you what matters.

📋 Appendix A: oc CLI Quick Reference — 50 Must-Know CommandsReference

Your EX267 Terminal Survival Kit

🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "Why oc instead of kubectl?"

oc is a superset of kubectl — every kubectl command works via oc, but not vice-versa. OpenShift-specific features like Routes, BuildConfigs, DeploymentConfigs, SecurityContextConstraints, and Projects are only accessible through oc. On the EX267 exam, you'll need oc for AI-specific commands like oc get dsc and oc get inferenceservice. Rule of thumb: If you're on OpenShift, always use oc — it does everything kubectl does, plus more.

🔧 Appendix B: AI Operator Installation & TroubleshootingReference

Install OpenShift AI Right — Every Time

This appendix provides the definitive step-by-step for installing the OpenShift AI Operator, creating the DataScienceCluster, and fixing the 10 most common failures.

📋 Reference⏱️ ~20 minEX267 35%
🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "What does the AI Operator actually install?"

The OpenShift AI Operator installs six major components into your cluster: Dashboard (web UI for data scientists), Workbenches (Jupyter notebooks), Data Science Pipelines (Tekton-based ML pipelines), KServe + ModelMesh (model serving), TrustyAI (bias/drift monitoring), and CodeFlare (distributed training). Each component is managed by the DataScienceCluster CR — you can enable/disable any component with a simple managementState: Managed or Removed. Think of it as a single switch that deploys an entire AI platform.

│  │ 1. OLM     │───▶│ 2. Subscription │───▶│ 3. InstallPlan   │             │
│  │ OperatorHub│    │ redhat-ods-op   │    │ (Manual approve) │             │
│  └────────────┘    └────────────────┘    └────────┬─────────┘             │
│                                                    │                       │
│                                                    ▼                       │

B.2 Step-by-Step Installation

🖥️ Via Web Console
  1. Administrator → Operators → OperatorHub
  2. Search: "Red Hat OpenShift AI"
  3. Click Install → namespace: redhat-ods-operator
  4. Channel: "stable" (or "fast" for preview)
  5. Approval: "Manual" (prod) / "Automatic" (dev)
  6. Click Install → wait for CSV "Succeeded"
⌨️ Via CLI
# Create namespace
oc create ns redhat-ods-operator

# Create OperatorGroup
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1
kind: OperatorGroup
metadata:
  name: redhat-ods-operator
  namespace: redhat-ods-operator
spec:
  targetNamespaces: []
EOF

# Create Subscription
cat <<EOF | oc apply -f -
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata:
  name: rhods-operator
  namespace: redhat-ods-operator
spec:
  channel: stable
  name: rhods-operator
  source: redhat-operators
  installPlanApproval: Manual
EOF

# Approve InstallPlan
oc get installplan -n redhat-ods-operator
oc patch installplan install-xxxxx -n redhat-ods-operator \
  --type merge -p '{"spec":{"approved":true}}'

🐳 Appendix C: anihpj Dockerfile — Multi-Stage BuildReference

Production-Ready Django Containerization

Multi-stage Dockerfile for the anihpj/jobpost Django application using Red Hat UBI (Universal Base Image) — optimized for OpenShift with non-root user, health checks, and build caching.

📋 Reference⏱️ ~15 minanihpj
🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "Why multi-stage and why UBI?"

Multi-stage builds keep your final image small by separating the build environment (Stage 1: compilers, pip, dependencies) from the runtime environment (Stage 2: only what's needed to run). Result: a 400MB image instead of 1.2GB. Red Hat UBI (Universal Base Image) is the only container base image you can freely redistribute and is officially supported on OpenShift. It comes pre-configured for OpenShift's security model (random user IDs, restricted SCC compatibility). Using UBI means no "security context" errors when deploying — the image just works.

C.1 Complete Annotated Dockerfile

Dockerfile — Multi-Stage UBI Build📋
# Stage 1: Build dependencies
FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/python-311 AS builder
WORKDIR /opt/app-root/src
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --user -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Production image
FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/python-311:latest
LABEL name="anihpj" \
      vendor="Anihs" \
      version="2.0" \
      description="AI-powered job board on OpenShift"

# Non-root user (OpenShift best practice)
USER 1001
WORKDIR /opt/app-root/src

# Copy dependencies from builder
COPY --from=builder /opt/app-root/.local /opt/app-root/.local
COPY --chown=1001:0 . .

# Collect static files during build
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Health check
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/healthz || exit 1

EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8080", \
     "--workers", "4", \

# Build image
podman build -t anihpj:v2.0 .

# Login to OpenShift internal registry
oc registry login

  default-route-openshift-image-registry.apps.example.com

✅ DO: OpenShift Best Practices
  • Use UBI base images (Red Hat certified)
  • Run as non-root user (USER 1001)
  • Define liveness + readiness probes
  • Use multi-stage builds for smaller images
  • Expose on port 8080 or 8443
  • Set resource requests = limits in dev
❌ DON'T: Common Mistakes
  • Run as root (blocked by SCC)
  • Use :latest tag in production
  • Store secrets in image layers
  • Skip .dockerignore (bloated builds)
  • Bind to localhost only (0.0.0.0 needed)
  • Use port 80/443 (requires privileged)

☸️ Appendix D: anihpj Kubernetes ManifestsReference

Complete Production YAML Templates

Every manifest you need to deploy the anihpj/jobpost Django application on OpenShift — Deployment, Service, Route, PostgreSQL StatefulSet, Redis, ConfigMap, Secret, HPA, and PDB.

📋 Reference⏱️ ~20 minanihpj
🧑‍🏫 Novice's Corner — "Why so many YAML files?"

A production Kubernetes deployment isn't one file — it's a set of specialized resources that each handle one concern. Deployment manages the app (pods, replicas, updates), Service gives it a stable internal address, Route exposes it to the internet with TLS, StatefulSet handles databases with persistent storage, ConfigMap holds non-secret settings, Secret holds passwords/tokens, HPA auto-scales pods by CPU, and PDB prevents accidental downtime. This is the separation of concerns pattern — each YAML does one thing well. Apply them all together and you have a complete, production-grade application stack.

D.1 Django Deployment + Service + Route

YAML — deployment.yaml + service.yaml + route.yaml📋
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  labels: { app: anihpj, tier: frontend }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: anihpj }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: anihpj, tier: frontend }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/anihpj-prod/anihpj:v2.0
        ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef: { name: anihpj-config }
        - secretRef: { name: anihpj-secret }
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
          limits: { cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi }
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
          initialDelaySeconds: 15, periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
          initialDelaySeconds: 5, periodSeconds: 5
---
# service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj
spec:
  selector: { app: anihpj }
  ports:
  - port: 8080, targetPort: 8080, name: http
---
# route.yaml
apiVersion: route.openshift.io/v1
kind: Route
metadata:
  name: anihpj
spec:
  host: anihpj.apps.example.com
  to: { kind: Service, name: anihpj }
  port: { targetPort: http }
  tls:
    termination: edge
    insecureEdgeTerminationPolicy: Redirect

D.2 PostgreSQL StatefulSet + Service + PVC

YAML — PostgreSQL StatefulSet📋
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
spec:
  serviceName: postgres
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: postgres }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: postgres }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        ports: [{ containerPort: 5432 }]
        envFrom:
        - secretRef: { name: postgres-secret }
        volumeMounts:
        - name: pgdata
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }
          limits: { cpu: 1000m, memory: 1Gi }
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata: { name: pgdata }
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
      resources:
        requests: { storage: 50Gi }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgres
spec:
  selector: { app: postgres }
  ports:
  - port: 5432, targetPort: 5432

D.5 HPA & PodDisruptionBudget

ResourcePurposeKey Setting
HPAAuto-scale Django pods by CPUminReplicas: 3, maxReplicas: 10, CPU 70%
PDBPrevent too many pods from going down at onceminAvailable: 2 — at least 2 pods always running
YAML — HPA + PDB📋
# hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: anihpj-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: anihpj
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
---
# pdb.yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: anihpj-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: anihpj }
